21686-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Volume one of Stevenson's works, in the Swanston Edition of 1911, opens with Andrew Lang's introduction. The set ran to twenty-five volumes, with two thousand copies for sale. This copy is number sixteen hundred and seventy-eight of the printing.

An Inland Voyage leads the contents, Stevenson's canoe trip from Antwerp toward France. Colvin's memoir tells how illness ordered the young writer south to Mentone. There the born wayfarer wrote on roads for Hamerton's Portfolio. Walter Crane designed the title page of the voyage. The volume shows Stevenson at the start of his road, a traveller before he was a romancer.
23055-the-slanderer-1901:
Anton Chekhov catches a schoolmaster in The Slanderer, his story dated 1901 here. A voice from the adjoining room calls out at a wedding feast. Vankin's cropped head soon appears in the doorway. He is the assistant instructor, and he has heard enough to start trouble. Someone has been kissing in here, Vankin announces, alone with a lady, no less.

A kiss, a witness, and a panic about reputation set Chekhov's little machine running. The slanderer of the title fears gossip so much that he manufactures it himself, begging, explaining, and spreading the story everywhere. Chekhov needs only a few pages to strip a man's dignity with perfect comic timing. The tale is a miniature of his method, funny on the surface, pitiless underneath, and done before the reader wants it to end.
a-select-bibliography-of-chemistry-1492-:
A Select Bibliography of Chemistry, 1492-1897, published in 1901, continues Henry Carrington Bolton's great listing of chemical literature. This portion is Section 8 of the second series, devoted to academic dissertations. It extends Bolton's coverage five years beyond his first bibliography, which had closed in 1892, and gathers the university theses of chemistry into one place.

Academic dissertations are among the hardest chemical writings to trace, since they were printed in small numbers by universities across Europe and America. Bolton's section gives them a single ordered list, by the same bibliographer who mapped the science's books. For historians, it opens a view of how chemistry was taught and examined in the universities of the nineteenth century.
abraham-lincoln-a-history-volume-01:
John G. Nicolay and John Hay, Lincoln's own secretaries, dedicate their great history to Robert Todd Lincoln in token of lifelong friendship. Their preface, written a generation after Lincoln's death, says the judgment of contemporaries has already hardened into tradition: he was incomparably the greatest man of his time. This first volume covers the making of the man.

The contents run from lineage and Kentucky boyhood through Indiana pioneer life, New Salem, the Black Hawk War, surveying, the legislature, early law practice, marriage, and the Shields duel, toward Congress. Nicolay and Hay worked from papers no one else held, and their ten-volume life remained the standard Lincoln for decades. Volume one gives the frontier roots in full.
apotelesmata-philosophica-mercvrii-trivm:
Apotelesmata Philosophica Mercurii Triumphantis, printed in 1601 by Martinus Copus, is the key to the author's earlier work Mercurius Triumphans. That book first appeared at Magdeburg in 1599 and was issued in an enlarged edition the next year. The present work's five sections correspond to the five books of the 1599 edition, unlocking them in order.

Its Latin title promises the true and supreme medicine of the most ancient philosophers, the heart of the alchemical quest. The dedication, addressed to the Emperor Rudolph the Second, is signed with the initials of Martinus Copus, doctor of medicine. A woodcut coat of arms of the Copi de Calvis family ornaments the book, a piece of the learned alchemy of Rudolfine Europe.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-01:
Richard F. Burton published the first volume of his Thousand Nights and a Night in 1885. His literal, unexpurgated translation of the Arabic Alf Layla wa Layla became the most famous English Arabian Nights. Shahrazad, wedded to a king who kills his brides, saves her life by telling tales that never quite end at dawn.

Volume one sets that frame and opens the early cycles of merchants, jinn, and porters. Burton kept the verse, the slang, and the frankness that earlier versions cut. His notes draw on years in the East and a scholar's appetite for custom. The full set runs to ten volumes, with six supplemental ones after. This first volume is where the great frame begins.
arabian-nights-burton-supplemental-1886-:
Burton's Supplemental Nights began in 1886, adding tales from Arabic manuscripts outside the main cycle. Volume one of the supplement is famed for holding Aladdin and Ali Baba in Burton's full rendering. Those two tales, known to every child in short forms, come here with their complete Arabic frames and details.

Aladdin's lamp and the forty thieves' cave gain depth, violence, and humor in the uncut text. Burton drew these stories from the Wortley Montague manuscript and other sources he names. The supplement was no afterthought: it rounds the Nights toward completeness. Readers who know only the famous pair will find them stranger and richer here. Six volumes carry the supplement to its end.
arxiv-2509-00001:
K. Mahesh Krishna, working alone, extends a core idea from sparse signal theory to measure spaces in a short 2025 note. Donoho and Elad set out the spark of a frame in 2003, a count tied to the smallest set of frame parts that depend on each other. From spark they derived an uncertainty principle and a sharp test for when a sparse answer to a hard problem is the sole one.

Krishna shows that spark makes sense for linear maps whose domain is a measure space, a set with a size rule. From that broad form he derives a new uncertainty principle. He also gives a condition that ensures sparse solutions exist for linear systems on such spaces. The note widens a classic tool to far broader settings.
arxiv-2509-00301:
Ninh Van Thu, working alone, gives an explicit account in 2025 of how key complex functions behave near the edge of a weakly pseudoconvex domain. Such a domain is a region in complex space whose edge meets a mild curve condition, held only in a loose sense. The study follows set sequences of points that tend toward a special edge point, called h-extendible.

Three linked objects are tracked along those sequences. The first is the Bergman kernel, a core function that encodes the domain's complex shape. The second is the Bergman metric, a way to measure distance built from the kernel. The third is the set of curvatures tied to that metric. Explicit boundary formulas for all three aid work on how complex domains behave at their edges.
arxiv-2509-00701:
Kun Qiu, with three co-authors, Ying Wang, Baoqian Li, and Wenjun Zhu, presents an unsupervised framework for cleaning encrypted traffic data. Classifying network flows into categories helps enterprise and carrier networks, but encryption defeats deep packet inspection, and machine learning methods need clean training data without useless flows.

Existing cleaning relies on manual inspection of every packet, which is costly and slow. Qiu and his co-authors automate the removal of irrelevant protocols, background activity, control messages, and long-lived sessions from encrypted mobile traffic, without labeled examples. On real-world datasets, their cleaning costs only about two to two and a half percent in classification accuracy compared with manual cleaning, making it an efficient preprocessing step.
arxiv-2509-00801:
Hyungbo Shim, with two co-authors, proposes parameter adaptation for multi-agent systems. The agents differ in their internal dynamics. Such systems are called heterogeneous. Unlike identical agents, they cannot reach perfect synchronization. Strong coupling can still induce approximate consensus among them. That shared behavior is governed by blended dynamics.

The team adds an adaptation law to align the agents' parameters. The law needs no direct exchange of parameters. It reuses the same coupling signal used for state synchronization. The process is thus plausible as a biological or social model. Under a persistent excitation condition, they prove convergence. The agents' dynamics converge to each other over time. The system becomes homogeneous in the limit, with exact consensus of states.
arxiv-2509-01001:
Zhi Zhao, with three co-authors, proposes a generalized promotion time cure model for cancer data. Single-cell tools reveal interplay between cancer cells and their surroundings. The data span survival, cell composition, and single-cell omics. No prior model joined all three scales at once. Their model aims to find cell-type-specific genes for prognosis.

The class is Bayesian in form, as the title states. It joins multiscale data to find cell-type-linked factors. It also aims to improve survival prediction for patients. Simulations cover both low- and high-dimensional settings. They show the models can identify such factors. Survival prediction improves as well in those tests. The framework links cell-level measures to patient outcomes in one model.
arxiv-2509-01301:
Tests of how well language models handle culture often shrink it to trivia questions with short answers. Juhyun Oh, with five co-authors, argues that this trivia-centered habit fails as models grow stronger and spread wider. Culture is not a static list of facts; it shapes even tasks that look neutral.

The authors call for intentionally cultural evaluation, a systematic check of the cultural assumptions built into every part of testing. They map what kinds of cultural questions arise, how they arise, and under what circumstances. They also stress researcher positionality, the way a test maker's own background shapes the test. Oh and the team close with directions for more inclusive, culturally aware language research beyond current benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-01401:
Recognizing emotion in spoken Arabic is hard because data and research for the language are scarce, and large models are costly to run. Ali Abouzeid, Bilal Elbouardi, Mohamed Maged, and Shady Shehata introduce ArabEmoNet, a lightweight model for that task. It reads Mel spectrograms, pictures of sound over time and pitch, with two-dimensional convolutions that keep fine emotional cues.

An attention-equipped bidirectional LSTM then reads those features in both directions to catch how emotion unfolds. With only about one million parameters, the model is many times smaller than large speech systems such as HuBERT base and Whisper, yet the authors report superior results. That small size suits phones and other limited devices. ArabEmoNet aims to bring strong speech emotion tools to a low-resource language in real-world settings.
arxiv-2509-01501: Jingjun Han, Jihao Liu, and Ziquan Zhuang prove the effective termination of minimal model programs of general type in dimension at most five. The minimal model program is a stepwise method in algebraic geometry for simplifying shapes. For dimension at most four, they also give explicit bounds, in terms of topological invariants and divisor volumes, on how many steps the program can take.
arxiv-2509-01601:
Sudden catastrophic shifts, from collapsing structures to failing ecosystems, often arrive without warning in quiet, low-noise systems. Tapas Bar, with four co-authors, studies early warning signals for such tipping points in athermal systems, systems without thermal jitter. Their models are a zero-temperature random field Ising model and thermally deposited cobalt films, both prone to avalanche failures.

As the system nears its tipping point, avalanche activity shows clear critical signs: slowing down, growing variance, and a lengthening spatial correlation range. Those hallmarks can serve as warnings of impending collapse. Crucially, raising disorder in the system made it less vulnerable to catastrophic failure, and in highly disordered regimes the warnings emerged well before the transition. Disorder, usually seen as a flaw, here buys both safety and time to act.
arxiv-2509-01701:
Kazi Hassan Shakib, Muhammad Asfand Hafeez, and Arslan Munir design AmphiKey, a key exchange protocol for smart power grids. Key exchange is how two devices agree on a secret code for safe messages. AmphiKey mixes newer quantum safe methods with classic ones so safety holds if either holds. It runs in two modes: one proves who sent a message, the other lets a sender plausibly deny it.

The signed mode pairs short lived keys with long term keys built to resist side channel leaks, where attackers learn from device behavior. The deniable mode guards privacy while still checking identity during setup. Tests span a strong server and a small low power board. Handshakes finish in well under a few thousandths of a second in most roles.
arxiv-2509-01901:
Saieed Akbari, Jonny Aloni, Arash Beikmohammadi, and Alexander Clow tighten bounds on splitting graphs into cycles and single edges. A long standing conjecture claims any graph splits into a number of such pieces that grows only with its point count. The covering version was proven decades ago with a near matching bound. Best known split bounds still carry a small extra factor.

For graphs where each point has at most four links, the team proves the clean bound conjectured. Claw free graphs, which lack a point tied to three separate others, split into few two-regular pieces and edges. They also improve the covering bound for any graph that holds a cycle. Only trees still need the older covering count.
arxiv-2509-02101:
Matic Fucka, Vitjan Zavrtanik, and Danijel Skocaj present SALAD, a semantics aware detector for logical anomalies in images. Surface detectors catch dents and scratches well but miss logical flaws like missing or misplaced parts. Top logical methods lean on pooled pretrained features or handcrafted descriptors that discard spatial and semantic detail. SALAD adds a composition branch that models how object parts are arranged.

A new extraction procedure builds composition maps without hand labels or category specific data. Modeling the distribution of those maps teaches the system semantic relationships among parts. On the standard logical anomaly benchmark, SALAD sets a strong new image level score. The gain shows composition modeling beats feature pooling for logical checks. Code is released for reuse.
arxiv-2509-02401:
Josefa Lia Stoisser and eight co-authors wrote a 2025 biomedical AI paper on agents that summarise complex multi-table data, such as combined omics datasets in cancer research. Language model agents often sound fluent while overstating what the data supports.

Their agent tracks two doubt signals. Retrieval uncertainty measures spread across repeated table choices, while summary uncertainty blends self-consistency with perplexity, a fluency-based score. Summary doubt feeds reinforcement learning training, and both signals filter outputs at run time and help build cleaner synthetic data. On multi-omics benchmarks, the count of claims that were both correct and useful roughly tripled per summary. Downstream survival prediction also improved sharply. The work treats uncertainty as a control signal for abstaining and reporting confidence.
arxiv-2509-02601:
Piotr Giedziun and nine co-authors present a 2025 computational pathology paper on telling normal mitotic figures from atypical ones in tissue images, the second track of the MIDOG 2025 challenge. Shape cues are subtle, and models must work across hospitals and scanners.

Their entry leans on H-optimus-0, a pathology foundation model chosen after cross-domain benchmarks and local tests. Cheap low-rank fine-tuning adapts it, while MixUp augmentation blends training images. Soft labels encode how strongly human experts agreed on each case. Hard negative mining, focal loss, metric learning, and domain adaptation all support robustness. The authors report reasonable preliminary performance, and they frame the work as evidence of both promise and difficulty for foundation models in this task.
arxiv-2509-02701:
Mathieu Gross, Md Riajul Haque, and Yann Mambrini wrote a 2025 cosmology paper. It computes the gravitational wave background expected from primordial black holes. The inflaton, the field that drove early cosmic expansion, adds its own waves. Signals from several sources overlap across frequencies.

For the first time, the authors combine three sources. They add waves from black hole decay. They add waves from the black holes' own density fluctuations. And they add inflaton waves from before and after inflation ends. The reheating era uses a power-law inflaton potential. A possible memory burden effect is folded in. That effect slows black hole evaporation as information builds up. It reshapes the spectrum. The full picture helps future searches read early-universe history.
arxiv-2509-02801:
Christopher Ewasiuk and Stefano Profumo wrote a 2025 particle physics paper asking how a huge hidden sector of light particles would betray itself through gravity alone. General relativity, read as an effective theory, predicts small quantum corrections to Newton's law from loops of matter fields.

With very many light species, those corrections can grow to levels that precision laboratory and astrophysical tests can see. The authors translate the predictions into the standard language of Yukawa-type deviations from the inverse-square law. Current fifth-force limits then bound how many hidden species can exist and how heavy they may be. Massless hidden states still allow enormous multiplicities, while finite masses face tighter limits. The framework complements cosmological probes, since lab tests constrain the spectrum regardless of cosmic history.
arxiv-2509-03001:
Elena Brylyakova and 4 co-authors searched old low-frequency radio data in 2025 for signals from five quiet binary systems. Each pair holds a visible low-mass star and an unseen companion whose mass fits a neutron star. Finding radio pulses would confirm what those hidden partners really are.

The archive came from a large phased array telescope near Pushchino in Russia. No steady or repeating emission showed up from any of the five systems. One single short burst did appear near one target, bright and brief. Its delay pattern, though, pointed to a distance that does not match that system. The authors weigh other explanations for the burst, leaving its source open.
arxiv-2509-03101:
Chris Blake and Ryan J. Turner examined in 2025 how galaxy motions add error to measurements of the universe's expansion rate. Standard sirens are cosmic events with known loudness, such as colliding neutron stars, whose distance can be read off directly. Pairing that distance with a host galaxy's redshift gives the Hubble constant, the current expansion rate.

Host galaxies also drift with their own peculiar velocities, which distort their redshifts. Reconstructing those motions from nearby matter leaves errors that are linked across galaxies by large flows. The authors show how to carry that full linked error into expansion estimates. In simulations of near-future sirens, ignoring the linkage could understate the error by about a factor of two. Nearby sources with precise distances suffer most.
arxiv-2509-03201:
Abdul Rahoof and 3 co-authors built CapsBeam in 2025, a capsule network beamformer for ultrasound imaging that runs on a programmable chip. Beamforming combines signals from many sensor elements into one image. Newer learning-based versions give cleaner pictures but are too heavy for small edge devices.

CapsBeam works on raw radio-frequency data from non-steered plane wave imaging, where the ultrasound pulse is sent out flat rather than aimed. In living tissue tests it reduced artifacts against the standard delay-and-sum method. In lab and simulated data it raised contrast and sharpened detail along both image directions. The team pruned the model with their multi-layer look-ahead method, cutting most parameters without hurting quality. A custom accelerator then delivered strong throughput on a commercial chip.
arxiv-2509-03601:
In a 2025 theoretical physics paper, Mara Lozano and two co-authors examine topological excitons in flat electronic bands, and on which light they can absorb. An exciton is a bound pair of an electron and a missing electron, called a hole. Topological excitons carry a swirling pattern, or vorticity, in momentum space, set by the band structure's topology.

Selection rules state which kinds of light can create or destroy such excitons. The authors derive them for three model systems, including Hamiltonians whose pseudo-spin textures wrap like skyrmions, plus flattened BHZ and Haldane models. With skyrmion-like textures, every exciton is bright, and the handedness of light it couples to is fixed by the swirl direction. In the BHZ case, bright excitons take circularly polarised light regardless of interaction range. The Haldane case couples to elliptically polarised light, with a phase diagram mapping how polarisation depends on model parameters.
arxiv-2509-04301:
Praveen Muralikrishnan and four co-authors explain how sugars keep proteins folded, using simplified computer models in a 2025 research paper. Vaccines and protein drugs need stabilizers, called excipients, and sugars are common choices. Four sugars enter the study: two glucose forms, fructose, trehalose, and sucrose counted among them. A coarse polymer stands in for the protein while free-energy bookkeeping separates the forces at play.

At low sugar levels, sugar-polymer contacts help folding, while solvent effects push the other way. At higher levels, entropy penalties, the cost of lost disorder, take control. Mixing two sugars added a stabilizing entropy effect favoring the folded state. Formulation designers gain a clearer recipe logic.
arxiv-2509-04401:
Andreas Raab, writing alone, develops classical Monte Carlo methods that mimic a flagship quantum computing task in a 2025 research paper. Random circuit sampling asks quantum machines to draw bit strings from the wild output patterns of random quantum circuits. Such sampling is often cited as evidence of quantum advantage. Raab derives exact probability formulas whose large-system limit matches the expected Porter-Thomas distribution, then builds importance sampling algorithms around them.

Systems from seventy qubits up to more than a million were simulated on an ordinary personal computer at minimal cost, without noise. On that basis, Raab argues the sampling task can be conveniently performed classically. The claim challenges how quantum advantage demonstrations should be judged.
arxiv-2509-04501:
Rohit Patel, writing alone, offers a from-scratch guide to the reinforcement learning methods used to train language models in a 2025 exposition paper. Instruction tuning pipelines stack algorithms with confusing names: supervised fine-tuning, rejection sampling, REINFORCE, TRPO, PPO, GRPO, and DPO. Explanations often assume background knowledge or gloss over details. Patel develops each method step by step in simplified notation aimed squarely at language models, cutting detours into the wider reinforcement learning literature.

A literature review then surveys newer techniques beyond the core seven. The closing section presents GRAPE, a proposed generalization of relative advantage policy evolution, as fresh research directions. Students and engineers gain one self-contained map of the post-training toolbox.
arxiv-2509-05801:
Can a forecasting model be steered to imagine a crash it never saw in the current data? Debdeep Sanyal and four co-authors take up that question in a 2025 paper on time series foundation models. These large models predict routine patterns well, but rare, high-stakes events are exactly what users most need to test.

Their method, activation transplantation, edits the model's hidden states mid-prediction, imposing the statistical shape of one event, such as a past crash, onto a calm stretch of data. Forecasts respond in kind: crash features push predictions down, while calm features restore stability. The team also finds that models grade severity, with stronger shocks tied to larger internal vectors. Results held on two different model designs, supporting direct what-if stress tests.
arxiv-2509-05901:
An open-source solver for the one-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation is presented in a 2025 paper led by Sandy H. S. Herho with four co-authors. That equation governs waves in fiber optics, ultracold atomic gases, and ocean swells. The authors prize clear, teachable code over raw speed, aiming at students and researchers learning nonlinear wave behavior.

The solver pairs a Fourier spectral treatment of space with an adaptive eighth-order time stepper, conserving mass to machine precision on smooth solutions. Four standard tests check it: a lone soliton, two solitons colliding elastically, a breather, and instability growing from noise. Entropy measures and phase-space pictures then gauge how complex each solution becomes. Full code, documentation, and example setups are released for reproducible experiments.
arxiv-2509-06201:
A robot hand that keeps adjusting as it closes is the controller Grasp-MPC, presented in a 2025 paper led by Jun Yamada with five co-authors. Open-loop grasping fails in clutter when predictions err or objects shift; earlier closed-loop systems handled only simple scenes. Grasp-MPC plans continuously with model predictive control, guided by a learned value function over visual input.

That value function trains on two million synthetic grasp trajectories, successes and failures alike. Combined with collision-avoidance and smoothness costs, it steers six-degree-of-freedom grasps of novel objects in clutter. On the FetchBench suite and in real-world trials, success rises by up to about a third over open-loop, diffusion, transformer, and offline reinforcement baselines, including under noisy conditions.
arxiv-2509-06401:
Commonsense in a language model is strongest in English and thins in smaller languages, measure Ivan Martínez-Murillo and three co-authors in a 2025 paper. Their benchmark, MULTICOM, extends an existing dataset to English, Spanish, Dutch, and Valencian. The task: generate a commonsensical sentence containing a given triplet of words.

A range of open models, from LLaMA and Qwen to regional entries like Salamandra, are scored by automatic metrics, model judges, and human annotators. English wins consistently, less-resourced languages lag significantly, and adding context gives mixed help that tends to favor the underrepresented languages. The dataset is released publicly, and the authors frame the gap as a standing limitation of multilingual generation.
arxiv-2509-06501:
Training web agents that can hunt through many pages for one answer is the subject of a 2025 artificial intelligence paper led by Junteng Liu, with fourteen co-authors. Language models increasingly act as agents that browse the web, but hard, long searches expose weak spots. Good training examples for such searches are scarce.

The authors build data by letting a model explore and then evolving questions from long to short forms, creating query-answer pairs that demand many steps. Training on this data, first with supervised learning and then reinforcement learning, yields an eight-billion-parameter agent. It handles very long contexts and up to a hundred tool calls in one task. On several search benchmarks it beats much larger rivals, and it also generalizes well to a broad knowledge test.
arxiv-2509-06701:
Hidden sub-agents inside large neural networks are given a mathematical theory by Su Hyeong Lee and two co-authors in a 2025 paper on artificial intelligence foundations. The authors model an agent as a distribution over outcomes, scored by a log-score utility that rewards accurate beliefs. Combining agents means pooling their distributions.

Weighted logarithmic pooling, they prove, can strictly improve every member's welfare, something linear pooling cannot do, and binary outcome spaces rule it out too; three or more outcomes are needed. The framework supports recursive structure through cloning invariance, continuity, and openness. As an application to language models, they formalize a persona effect: prompting a benevolent character can summon an antagonistic counterpart. A strategy that first elicits then suppresses the counterpart cuts misalignment more than reinforcing the good persona alone. The theory aims to explain how sub-agents merge into coherent larger agents.
arxiv-2509-07401:
When boson stars collide, the merger can stir up swirling vortices, much like eddies in water. Yuanyuan Zeng, Bokai Zhang, and Jiajun Chen simulate those mergers in a 2025 research paper. Boson stars are hypothetical clumps of dark matter particles. The team solves the Gross-Pitaevskii-Poisson equations, which govern such quantum fluids, and varies the self-interaction strength between particles.

Vortices form in every merger they ran. Their size depends strongly on the interaction strength. With repulsive interactions, stronger coupling makes the vortex region expand. With attractive interactions, stronger coupling makes it shrink. The team confirms the pattern through velocity correlations, energy spectra, and vorticity maps. The result connects a basic particle property to a visible feature of dark matter collisions, which future observations might one day test.
arxiv-2509-08001:
When one banker quits, nearby colleagues often follow, and that clustering may be predictable. Abdulla AlKetbi and 3 co-authors study turnover contagion in Hong Kong finance in a 2025 research paper. They built temporal networks from the Securities and Futures Commission public register. The data cover well over one hundred thousand professionals and nearly five thousand firms across seventeen years.

Their graph-based method spreads features across the network to capture peer influence and firm stability. A clear contagion effect appeared: professionals grew much more likely to leave once many peers had recently departed. Adding network signals to machine learning models improved turnover prediction substantially over baselines. The authors suggest uses in regulatory monitoring, talent management, and systemic risk assessment. Workforce moves, it seems, ripple like information through a market.
arxiv-2509-09501:
Coloring a manga page automatically requires knowing which inked region on one page is the same coat, face, or room on the next. Yingxuan Li and 3 co-authors define that matching task in a 2025 research paper. Manga line art holds only sparse black strokes, none of the shading and color cues natural images offer. No annotations exist to learn from directly.

Their transformer framework trains on region correspondences generated automatically at large scale. It learns to drop noisy matches and reinforce structural links that agree. At use time, each drawing is segmented, then regions are matched through edge-aware clustering. Hand-annotated benchmarks confirm strong patch accuracy and region matching well above chance. The task also feeds in-between frame generation for animation. Teaching machines the identity of a line region is a quiet prerequisite for automating the labor-intensive corners of manga and anime production.
arxiv-2509-09901:
N. L. Samuelson and 7 co-authors report measurements from a graphene quantum Hall interferometer in this 2025 physics paper. In such a device, interference patterns carry information about particles trapped inside the loop and how they couple to the edge current. Earlier work assumed those particles enter and leave quickly, so the system stayed near balance during each measurement.

Working at two filling factors, the team watched the interference phase jump as single quasiparticles entered the bulk. Some jumps come from particles joining a shared puddle that couples to the whole edge, others from particles caught at a defect near one part of the edge. At times the settling time stretched to several minutes, far slower than the standard picture assumes.
arxiv-2509-10101:
T. J. Hicken and 15 co-authors pin down the hidden defects inside a candidate quantum material in this 2025 paper. The compound Pr2Zr2O7 is a possible quantum spin ice, a state prized for quantum technology. Disorder inside the crystal is thought to boost its quantum behavior, but nobody knew exactly which defect does the work.

Using neutron and X-ray scattering, backed by density functional theory, the team found the main defect. Praseodymium ions sit on zirconium sites. Oxygen vacancies balance the charge, and a nearby oxygen is pushed out of place. That structure explains the single-ion magnetism seen in tests and the extra features in crystal field spectra. It also broadens the magnetic scattering pattern in a way once blamed on quantum effects alone.
arxiv-2510-00001:
Broestl and colleagues bring the idea of code coverage from software testing to retrieval-augmented generation systems, asking whether a test question set actually covers the knowledge base it is meant to probe. Their practical framework embeds document chunks and test questions into one shared vector space using standard embeddings and clustering. It turns the vague worry about blind spots into numbers a developer can act on in their work.

Three complementary metrics are computed, basic proximity coverage, content-weighted coverage that accounts for how much material each area holds, and multi-topic coverage for questions spanning several clusters. Outlier detection flags irrelevant questions for removal. Demonstrated on two distinct use cases, the method pinpoints specific content areas with inadequate test representation and recommends concrete new questions. It helps teams build more genuinely robust test suites for high-stakes systems in practice.
arxiv-2510-00101:
Francesco D'Eugenio and thirteen colleagues published this 2025 astronomy paper on a bright early galaxy nicknamed Irony. The James Webb Space Telescope took the deepest spectra yet of this object, a so-called Little Red Dot. Such dots host growing black holes from the universe's first billion years. Irony shines from a time when the cosmos was very young.

The spectra show hydrogen lines that are both broad and partly absorbed. The absorption splits in speed, with one part moving toward us and another away. Line strengths imply the black hole may outweigh what its host galaxy's mass would suggest. Odd line ratios point to collisions in dense gas rather than plain dust dimming. Rare iron lines also appear, adding clues about the gas around the black hole. The study shows how messy the gas feeding early black holes can be.
arxiv-2510-00501:
Kaixin Wang and eight colleagues published this 2025 paper on helping code models write in programming languages they barely know. Models ace popular languages but stumble on low-resource ones with little training data. Their framework, CodeChemist, transfers know-how at test time instead of retraining. It first writes and runs code in a strong language to build revealing test cases.

Those tests capture what correct behavior looks like, in executable form. The model then drafts candidate solutions in the weak language at several sampling temperatures. Each candidate faces the test suite, and the best passer wins. Benchmarks on multilingual code suites showed consistent gains over rival test-time methods. The boost grew largest exactly where the language gap was widest. No weights changed during the whole process, the authors stress. The recipe gives rare languages a borrowed competence drawn from their richer cousins.
arxiv-2510-00701:
Lin, Zhang, and Lu make concept bottleneck models multimodal and relational in this 2025 arXiv paper on interpretable deep learning. Concept bottleneck models predict human-readable concepts first, then answer from those concepts, which lets people inspect and correct the reasoning. Classic versions handle one modality and treat concepts as isolated slots, ignoring how concepts relate to each other and to the question. The authors' framework, MoE-SGT, adds structure on both fronts.

They build answer-concept and answer-question graphs, then run a Graph Transformer over them to capture multi-level dependencies between concepts. A Mixture-of-Experts module replaces the plain feed-forward layers, routing each input to specialized sub-experts matched to its complexity. On multiple benchmark datasets the model beat other concept bottleneck networks on accuracy. Crucially, it kept end-to-end interpretability, so the concept layer still explains every prediction in plain terms.
arxiv-2510-00801:
Tsuzuki and Ohki settle a long-open question about Oja's flow in this 2025 arXiv paper on applied mathematics. The Oja flow is a continuous-time algorithm that extracts the leading components of data, much like principal component analysis. Its theory was complete only for symmetric positive-definite matrices, where it behaves as a gradient flow. For general square matrices, only local convergence near the answer was known.

The authors prove global convergence for general matrices, showing the flow settles exponentially fast from almost every starting point. In that setting it finds the invariant subspace tied to the eigenvalues with the largest real parts. They also propose a modification that improves numerical stability in practice. As applications, they build new methods for reducing large linear dynamical systems and for designing low-rank stabilizing controllers.
arxiv-2510-01101:
Mazzucato, Wang, and Wei study what happens as fluid viscosity shrinks toward zero in this 2025 arXiv paper on partial differential equations. Viscous flow follows the Navier-Stokes equations, while ideal flow follows the Euler equations. Near a solid wall the two can differ sharply, because friction creates a thin boundary layer. Their setting is harder still, since fluid may enter and leave through permeable boundaries at a general angle.

The authors prove that Navier-Stokes solutions converge to the Euler solution in the energy norm as viscosity vanishes. Interior convergence holds in both the L2 and Sobolev H1 norms at the same rates known for flow normal to the boundary. Their proof builds boundary layer correctors from Prandtl-type equations and pushes the expansion to higher order. A remark shows the method can reach arbitrarily high precision under stronger compatibility conditions.
arxiv-2510-02101:
Lukeš and Krtouš study point particles threaded on cosmic strings in a three-dimensional universe in this 2025 relativity paper. The BTZ solution describes a black hole in two space dimensions plus time. Continuing it analytically removes the horizon and leaves a conical deficit, read as a massive point particle. A cosmic string can hold such a particle in static equilibrium.

The authors define an additive notion of local mass for these static spacetimes. That bookkeeping lets them analyze particles and strings as one mechanical system. A bound pair, two particles joined by a string of finite length, becomes tractable. Going further, they use a cut-and-glue construction to build two particles oscillating on a string. That dynamical system leaves the static realm entirely. The constructions clarify how mass, deficit angles, and strings trade against each other.
arxiv-2510-02301:
Sullivan and co-authors model the radio jets of two candidate double black hole systems. Their 2025 astrophysics paper studies blazars PKS 2131-021 and PKS J0805-0111. Long radio monitoring showed both sources pulsing on a steady beat. Such clocks hint at two giant black holes in orbit. No single source of the known gravitational wave hum is confirmed yet. The authors propose a shared jet picture. A slow wind carves a helical channel outward. A much faster jet then travels along that channel. Viewing angle effects create most of the observed pulsing.

The model reproduces the main features of both sources. Lower radio tones vary later, as seen in data. That delay follows from emission at larger distances. The team predicts radio polarization and imaging signatures. Future telescopes can test those predictions directly. Confirmed binaries would anchor the gravitational wave background.
arxiv-2510-02401:
Szewczyk, Gallo Fernandez, and Townsend generate long music clips with linear recurrent networks. Their 2025 paper models raw audio one step at a time. Audio waveforms are extremely long sequences. Structure lives at many time scales at once. Older recurrent and attention models struggled with that load. Linear recurrent models, also called state space models, run far more efficiently. The team tests design choices across that family. Context parallelism lets them train on full minute long clips. Those clips reach about one million tokens each.

Their model, HarmonicRNN, set new marks on small datasets. It led on likelihood scores and perceptual quality measures. A Beethoven piano set was one test bed. A mixed YouTube music set was the other. Raw waveform generation stays hard at large scale. Efficient sequence models make the task newly practical.
arxiv-2510-02601:
Rim and co-authors capture 3D hand motion in real world settings with a camera rig. Their 2025 computer vision paper attacks a dataset problem. Hand tracking models train mostly on tidy lab recordings. Wild environments break those models quickly. The team built a backpack rig with eight outward cameras. A worn headset adds two first person views. Together they watch hands from ten angles at once. The wearer can move freely outdoors. A tracking pipeline fuses the views into 3D hand poses. Those poses serve as ground truth for training data.

Their annotated dataset pairs synced images with poses. Quality checks validated the pipeline carefully. The setup shrinks the trade-off between realism and accuracy. Future releases will add object poses and contact labels. Text descriptions of interactions are also planned. Augmented reality needs hands understood outside the lab. This rig shows how to gather that evidence.
arxiv-2510-02801:
Chen and a team of co-authors report a close look at a rare nearby galaxy that mimics a puzzling class of distant objects. The distant objects are called Little Red Dots. The James Webb Space Telescope found them in the early universe. The nearby galaxy, named J2048, sits at a redshift near 0.43, far behind the cluster. The team studied it with the Gemini North telescope.

The data show bright blue light spread across the galaxy. That light comes from a fierce burst of new stars. The burst forms stars at a rate near 400 solar masses each year. Fast gas also streams out of the galaxy. At its center sits a black hole that looks far too heavy for its host. The black hole holds about six tenths of the mass of all the stars. Nearby cases like this one help scientists test ideas about the far-off dots.
arxiv-2510-03101:
Tenison and co-authors pick which layers of a network to retrain on small devices. Phones and wearables must adapt models to their owners. Full retraining is too heavy for their chips and batteries. Retraining a few key layers is the usual escape. Picking those layers often needs labels or a full gradient pass. Their method, AdaBet, needs neither labels nor gradients. It reads the shape of each layer's activity instead.

Betti numbers count holes and loops in that activity cloud. Layers with rich topology hold more learning capacity. Forward passes alone supply all the needed data. Sixteen model and data set pairs tested the idea. AdaBet beat gradient-based pickers on accuracy by a clear margin. Peak memory use fell by two fifths at the same time. Retraining thus fits inside tight device budgets. Privacy gains follow, since data never leaves the device.
arxiv-2510-03201:
Jettkant and Søjmark set up a system of Brownian particles whose own death odds move the walls that kill them. Each wandering particle is absorbed when it hits its boundary. The boundary positions depend on absorption chances before a deadline. Those chances are computed backward from the final time. The coupling forms a singular forward-backward equation system. Its analysis yields a tiered moving boundary problem instead.

Each tier of the problem fixes one absorption pattern. The boundary and its condition come from the tier before. The authors prove classical well-posedness for the whole tower. That solution then solves the original particle system. Uniqueness of the forward-backward system follows from it too. Absorption of one particle shifts every other boundary. A weighted connection matrix encodes those mutual influences. Finance and physics both host such coupled hitting problems.
arxiv-2510-03301:
Sedek presents a 2025 arXiv paper on joining two kinds of machine learning models into one flexible team. Tree based XGBoost handles table data well, while neural networks catch complex patterns. Fixed mixing rules cannot adapt when data changes shape. The framework built here uses meta learning, which means a higher level model learns how to pick and blend the two workers for each new case.

The system weighs how unsure each worker is and which inputs matter most. It can choose XGBoost alone, the network alone, or a blend of both. On the California housing data set, the team cut forecast error by about two percent against XGBoost alone. The gain against the neural network alone reached about ten percent in the same tests. Clearer input rankings also made the blended choices easier to explain. The design suits fields where data mixes tables with tangled patterns.
arxiv-2510-03401:
Schoettler and Owen present an arXiv paper on what shakes up young systems of close in planets. Planets can scatter off each other inside a system, while passing stars can jolt a system from outside. The authors simulate four small planets near their star, with and without a distant giant planet. They then compare damage from a stellar flyby with damage from a stirred up giant. The runs follow the systems for five hundred million years.

The close in systems reached a similar favored end state no matter how they were perturbed. The giant's presence, spot, and mass did not change how inner planets weathered a flyby in their tests. Mass did matter for purely internal stirring, though. Lighter giants produced runs with no planet collisions at all. The findings suggest birth crowds leave a strong stamp on young planet systems, one that later evolution partly erases.
arxiv-2510-03701:
Goto and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper tackling a blind spot in vision language models: finding small objects described in words. Referring expression comprehension means drawing a box around the object a phrase describes. Targets, like cars in driving scenes, defeat models. The team built SOREC, a data set of one hundred thousand pairs for small objects in driving imagery. They built PIZA, a small adapter that teaches a model to zoom in progressively until the target is located.

PIZA fine tunes, updating parameters while the model stays frozen. Bolted onto the GroundingDINO model, it improved accuracy on the SOREC benchmark in experiments. Zooming mirrors how a person scans a scene for something. Driving systems must spot hazards described by passengers or logs, so the skill is practical. The data set, code, and trained models are public. Other tasks, from drones to microscopy, could borrow the zoom adapter idea.
arxiv-2510-03801:
Shen and Ushakov wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in group theory, a branch of algebra. They study HNN extensions, a standard way to build a larger group from a free group. Their focus is the word problem, which asks whether a product of group elements equals the identity. They consider the case where the two linked subgroups are equal and have finite index.

The authors prove that the word problem for these groups can be solved in polynomial time. Fast means the running time grows in a controlled way as inputs get longer. They extend the result to some non-normal cases, under one extra condition on the linking map. The result adds an efficiency guarantee for a class where only decidability was known. Word problems have been central to group theory since Dehn raised them in 1911.
arxiv-2510-03901:
Savaux and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on why affine frequency division multiplexing tolerates colored noise better than rival 6G waveforms. Next-generation systems need modulation robust to channels that vary in both time and frequency, plus disturbances that are not white. The authors analyze how each waveform's performance depends on its demodulation matrix's ability to whiten the noise. That ability, in turn, tracks how sparse the matrix is.

Affine frequency division multiplexing uses chirp carriers from the discrete affine Fourier transform, and its demodulation matrix is less sparse than those of OTFS or OFDM. The analysis therefore predicts an AFDM advantage before any simulation. Simulations confirmed it, with gains exceeding one decibel in most application scenarios. Use cases include signals and coexistence alongside legacy OFDM transmissions. As 6G waveform selection hardens, noise-color robustness is a criterion rather than a footnote.
arxiv-2510-04201:
Son and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on teaching image generators about concepts that appeared after their training ended. Text-to-image models render familiar subjects beautifully but mangle novel entities, new products, and long-tail terminology. Retraining for every emerging concept is hopeless. Their framework, World-To-Image, sends an agent to the live web instead.

The agent searches for reference images of the unknown concept in the prompt. Retrieved images then guide multimodal prompt optimization, steering the frozen generator toward an accurate depiction. An orchestrator chooses between refining the text prompt and grounding it visually, iterating only a few times. On their curated NICE benchmark of novel concepts, accuracy-to-prompt improved by about eight percent over strong baselines. The approach adds a knowledge interface around existing models rather than scaling them further. That interface could keep deployed generators current with a changing world.
arxiv-2510-04301:
Longo, Magrone, and Walchek present this 2025 arXiv paper on p-adic L-functions attached to families of quaternionic modular forms. A p-adic L-function packages arithmetic values across infinitely many related forms into one analytic object. Quaternionic forms live on division algebras rather than the classical upper half-plane, so tools from the GL2 theory do not transfer automatically. The authors work with ordinary families, where a Hida-style theory controls variation at the prime p.

Their construction uses Serre-Tate expansions to attach explicit power series to each quaternionic ordinary family. From those series they build a big p-adic L-function for the whole family. At classical specializations, it interpolates the p-adic L-functions constructed earlier by Burungale and Magrone. Such big L-functions are the usual route to Iwasawa-theoretic results about Selmer groups and ranks across a family.
arxiv-2510-04401:
Xuyang Guo and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a basic skill that AI vision models lack. Models that link images and text do well on many hard tasks. The team asked a simpler question: can such a model count objects in a picture? They built a benchmark with only basic shapes, such as triangles and circles. 

The results split sharply by task type. When a picture held one kind of shape, the models counted reliably and scored high. When two or more shape types appeared together, the models failed badly at counting each type. Changing color, size, or the wording of the prompt did not fix the failure. The authors call this combined task compositional counting, and they frame it as a core flaw. The paper argues that basic perception still lags far behind the fluent language of these models.
arxiv-2510-04701:
Jesper Lykke Jacobsen wrote this 2025 physics paper on exact formulas for correlations in critical loop models. Loop models describe tangles of non crossing curves at a phase transition, from magnets to polymers. Fields in these models can insert open loop segments, called legs, or change the weight of closed loops. The paper conjectures a formula for three point functions of such fields on a sphere. Those functions measure how three insertions influence each other.

In special cases, the formula matches known results from conformal loop ensembles. The author then computed the same quantities on cylinder shaped lattices. Transfer matrix methods carried the numerics. The numbers agreed with the conjecture in almost all cases tested. The few mismatches trace to degenerate ground states in the algebra behind the lattice model. Three point data is prime input for the conformal bootstrap program. It helps pin down families of two dimensional critical theories.
arxiv-2510-05201:
Harley Katz and twenty-four co-authors unveil a new simulation suite for the first galaxies in this 2025 arXiv paper. MEGATRON follows Milky Way-mass galaxies from the first stars to cosmic noon. It couples radiation transport to a vast non-equilibrium chemistry network. Starting from zero metals at parsec resolution, it predicts galaxy spectra directly.

The team built a library of more than 175,000 simulated galaxy spectra. That library naturally reproduces the spectral diversity JWST observes at high redshift. Population III star formation continues somewhere in the region down to the lowest simulated redshift. The simulations still miss some oddballs, like massive mini-quenched galaxies and nitrogen emitters. Even so, they sharpen direct comparisons between theory and the early universe.
arxiv-2510-05701:
Kusano and colleagues map the black holes of an alternative theory of gravity. Weyl conformal gravity stretches spacetime locally while keeping its equations intact. The authors give the charged Reissner-Nordström solution both electric and magnetic charge. Their 2025 study derives its horizons, photon spheres, and temperature limits.

They obtain analytic formulas for photon sphere radii and horizon positions. Extremal limits and Hawking temperatures follow from the same parameters. The missing inverse-square term in the metric removes the usual guarantee about the innermost horizon. One surprise is a nested black hole, with a Cauchy horizon trapped between two event horizons. General relativity offers no such structure. At a critical charge, the stable and unstable photon spheres merge. In other limits, three horizons collide at once. The charged case yields more spacetime varieties than the uncharged one. Conformal gravity aims to ease dark matter and dark energy tensions.
arxiv-2510-05801:
Caballero and two coauthors study how liquid climbs inside a thin tube in their 2025 mathematics paper. The classic model for this rise uses a Volterra equation with a memory term. Their version lets the kernel and the response stay rough and not smooth. They work in integral Holder spaces, which suit functions that lack clean slopes. Such equations also track processes where the present state depends on the past.

The authors prove that a solution exists under weak rules on the inputs. They also give the first sharp bounds on error for straight line fits in these spaces. One solver joins short straight pieces and provably closes in on the true curve. A second solver uses Legendre nodes and converges at an exponential rate when solutions are smooth. Tests on sample problems match the theory and hold up for rough cases.
arxiv-2510-05901:
Benfeghoul and five coauthors examine a cheap way to speed up large language models in their 2025 study. Full attention grows fast in cost as texts get long, so linear attention is attractive. Rather than train new models from scratch, teams convert trained models after the fact. Most conversions mix linear attention with a small sliding window of full attention.

The team shows that these mixed models mostly ignore their linear part. Tests that switch each part off reveal that the window does nearly all the work. Scores on six common sense tasks thus credit the wrong part of the model. The authors offer three fixes, among them random dropout of the window in training. Their fixes keep most of the base model scores on Mistral and Llama models. The study restores honest credit for speed gains in future conversions.
arxiv-2510-06001:
Pistotti and colleagues revisit whether language models know parasitic gap syntax. The Argument from the Poverty of the Stimulus asks what syntax is learnable from data. Two surprisal-based studies reached opposite conclusions using different metrics. Their 2025 paper argues the direct minimal pair metric is more transparent.

A refined eight-permutation paradigm of parasitic gap stimuli is generated. GPT-2, the model from the earlier studies, is evaluated systematically. A Wilcox-style wh-effect analysis compares minimal pairs directly. The model succeeds across all four tested conditions. That indicates robust knowledge of filler-gap licensing principles. The difference-in-differences metric had obscured this competence behind ambiguity. Metric choice, the authors conclude, can decide the verdict on competence. Stimulus quality matters as much as the metric itself. Applying the framework to worse-performing models is the logical next step. Rigorous foundations for learnability claims are the broader goal.
arxiv-2510-06401:
Umar and four co-authors measure how label noise changes information inside neural representations in a 2025 machine learning paper. Real datasets carry annotation errors, and label noise affects test performance. Its effect on hidden representations was poorly understood.

The team compares representations using Information Imbalance, a proxy for conditional mutual information. One striking pattern appears first. Hidden layers' information content follows a double descent in network size, mirroring the test-error curve. In the underparameterized regime, noisy-label representations are more informative than clean-label ones. In the overparameterized regime, noisy and clean representations match. Big networks' representations are robust to label noise. Networks trained on random labels did worse than random features. Such training pushes weights beyond lazy learning to encode meaningless labels. The results give generalization research a new information-theoretic lens.
arxiv-2510-06501:
Seunghyun Lee, Rajarshi Mukherjee, and Sumit Mukherjee study a basic question in statistics. Their 2025 paper looks at Gaussian mixture models, which describe data drawn from two overlapping bell-shaped groups. Each data point carries a hidden label that says which group it came from. Most past theory assumed those labels were independent, or followed a simple chain.

The authors ask how the best possible accuracy changes when labels depend on each other in richer ways. For labels with any dependence, a simple estimator still reaches the usual rate of accuracy. Under labels from an Ising model, they find a sharp phase transition. When dependence stays below a threshold, the best estimator matches the independent case exactly. When dependence grows stronger, estimation becomes easier, and the simple estimator stops being best. They propose a new estimator for that strong-dependence case.
arxiv-2510-06701:
Antonio Bjelčić, Nicolas Schunck, and Marc Verriere simulate what happens when an atomic nucleus splits in two. Their 2025 paper studies nuclear fission in plutonium-240. When a nucleus breaks apart, the two fragments carry excitation energy that later escapes as neutrons and photons. That energy cannot be measured directly, because scission happens too fast.

The team predicts it with time-dependent density functional theory, a microscopic simulation method. A new, faster solver let them run hundreds of fission trajectories. Those runs covered nearly every possible split of the nucleus. The predicted total kinetic energy matched experiment only for the most likely split. At small and large asymmetries, the theory badly underestimated that energy. Changing the underlying energy formula barely helped, in either of its channels. The authors conclude the theory itself is limited, since it cannot mix different configurations. Nuclear data users now know where this trusted tool underperforms.
arxiv-2510-07001:
Jihang Zhu and Chunli Huang show that a classic response formula in electron physics is pure geometry at heart. Their 2025 paper studies how interacting electron systems answer a magnetic field. The analysis stays within mean-field theory, the approximation for such systems. The density matrix, which encodes the electron state, shifts when the field arrives.

That shift turns out to depend only on wavefunction geometry. It involves Berry connections between filled and empty states, and nothing about the interaction strength. The quasiparticle energies drop out of the answer entirely. From this clean response, compact formulas follow for two quantities. One is the Středa formula linking magnetization to electron density changes. The other is orbital magnetization, the magnetism from electrons circling in place. The paper also clarifies how exchange and self-consistency shape the current vertices. Mean-field theory, quantum geometry, and topological band theory meet in one result.
arxiv-2510-07101:
Casaburi, Piccioli, and Vivo ask a simple question with a strange answer: what is data worth? Their 2025 paper treats data as a good that can be copied at almost no cost. Normal price rules fail for such goods. The authors model rivals who bet on a random process. Some rivals know more of the past record than others do.

In the model, a well-informed player can sell part of her data to a weaker rival. The authors solve for the price range where both sides gain from the trade. Some results defy textbook logic. A seller can give data away for free and still earn more. Rivalry among the well-informed can even help the uninformed. The work gives firms a clearer way to price the data they trade. It also warns that more data does not always mean more profit.
arxiv-2510-07201:
McCormack, Teimurazov, Shishkina, and Linkmann study how liquid metal in a magnetic field first starts to churn. Their 2025 paper models a heated metal layer in a box with insulating walls. A vertical magnetic field holds the metal still at first. The authors show the box walls change that story. Stable moving states can exist below the threshold where stillness first fails.

As heating grows, the branch born at the threshold loses stability. Flow then jumps to the most strongly early-born branch instead. That branch takes a quasiperiodic route into chaos. Its spatial symmetry shapes the large-scale pattern of the later turbulence. In short, the turbulent state owes nothing to the first linear wobble. The effect should grow stronger at higher field strengths. The result matters for metal processing and lab models of planetary cores.
arxiv-2510-07501:
Park, Lu, and Yang build a framework for learning treatment sequences for patients who may die before the sequence ends. Their 2025 paper confronts truncation by death, a notorious problem in critical care research. When a patient dies mid-study, later outcomes are not merely missing; they are undefined, which breaks standard methods for evaluating dynamic treatment regimes. The authors adopt principal stratification, judging strategies by their value among the patients who would survive under any strategy. That always-survivor value is the quantity clinicians actually mean when comparing long care pathways for the sickest patients.

For that target, they derive an estimator that is both semiparametrically efficient and multiply robust across multi-stage regimes. Robustness here means several independent chances for the modeling assumptions to hold. Simulations validate the estimator's behavior. An application to electronic health records demonstrates personalized treatment optimization under realistic messiness.
arxiv-2510-07901:
Diamantopoulos, Tziritas, Bahsoon, and Theodoropoulos wrote this 2025 paper on managing blockchains without a central controller. Blockchains must adapt as conditions change, yet central management would break their core promise. The authors propose running management itself in a decentralized way. Digital twins of the system, controlled by different stakeholders, act as the managers. A second blockchain coordinates those twins and records their decisions.

The management chain reaches consensus on new configurations and passes them to the main chain. Nodes of the managed blockchain watch the management chain as observers. The active configuration simply follows the latest management block. Simulations showed decisions were reached quickly, and reconfiguration added only minimal overhead. Sensitivity tests probed how delays and costs scale with system conditions. The design completes a feedback loop in which a blockchain system watches, judges, and retunes itself while staying decentralized.
arxiv-2510-08001:
Ahadi, Esrafilian, Kaltenberger, and Malik wrote this 2025 paper on locating phones in 5G networks without labeled training data. Channel charting learns a positioning function from radio measurements. Walls and obstacles bend those measurements when the direct path is blocked, and charts distort. The authors enrich impulse response data with time-difference-of-arrival features and base station positions. Motion measurements from the device add continuity to the learned map.

A masking step identifies and discards measurements corrupted by blocked paths. Training is self-supervised, in a global coordinate frame. The team tested on a real 5G testbed with centimeter-grade reference positioning. Their method beat semi-supervised and self-supervised charting approaches. Errors stayed within two to four meters in ninety percent of cases across blocked-path ratios. They release the dataset. Self-taught positioning like this could serve factories and campuses where satellite signals never reach.
arxiv-2510-08501:
Christopher Vairogs and co-authors study how much entanglement can be concentrated onto part of a large quantum state in a 2025 arXiv paper. Localizing entanglement means measuring most qubits so the rest share a strong entangled state. Two measures govern this: localizable entanglement using local measurements, and entanglement of assistance using global ones. A prior polynomial-time test, based on assistance, checks whether graph states can be transformed by local measurements.

The authors show this test stays effective in large systems across a wide range of measured subsystem sizes. Applying it to linear cluster states yields a surprising negative result. General local unitaries with global measurements typically give no advantage over local Clifford unitaries with local Pauli measurements, when turning cluster states into GHZ states. They also derive concentration inequalities for both measures over random states. Localized entanglement structure depends strikingly on measurement locality, they find.
arxiv-2510-08801:
Honor and a large team of astronomers map where galaxies have stopped forming stars inside a huge distant cluster, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The cluster, nicknamed El Gordo, sits so far away that its light shows it as it was billions of years ago. It holds two massive clumps that are likely merging. Using Webb telescope images, the team measured what share of galaxies in two size ranges had gone quiet.

Distance from the cluster's overall center showed no link with the quiet share. But for smaller galaxies, the picture changed when distance was measured from the nearer of the two clumps. Galaxies closer to a clump were more likely to have shut down. The authors read this as proof that the cluster environment was already quenching galaxies at that early era. Smaller galaxies, with weaker gravity holding their gas, suffered the effect most.
arxiv-2510-08901:
John, Chihoub, and co-authors, including Kristin Dana, teach a vision model to chart how cranberries grow, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Growers and breeders judge growth, yield, and disease by eye, a slow manual routine. The team instead photographs the fruit repeatedly across a season and learns a compact map of its appearance over time. Their training needs no hand labels, which are tedious to produce for thousands of images.

They fine-tune a vision transformer, an image model built on attention, with two practice tasks: guess when a photo was taken, and name the variety shown. The learned space arranges images into readable tracks that follow each variety through the season. Those tracks can forecast growth and separate the habits of different varieties. The team also releases a time-lapse dataset covering eight varieties watched fifty-two times over about four months, annotated with spray records, yield, and rot.
arxiv-2510-09001:
Zhou and co-authors rethink how training rewards are weighted when a language model learns mathematics by trial and error, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The dominant method and its many variants all grade groups of attempts against each other. The team's analysis shows the variants differ mainly in how they weight easy and hard problems. Fixed weighting cannot follow a model whose skills change during training, so effort piles onto the wrong difficulty level.

Their method, DARO, watches the model's current learning state and continually rebalances how much each difficulty group contributes to the training loss. The weights themselves become adjustable rather than frozen in a formula. Experiments on three open models, two built for mathematics and one general, covered six math benchmarks. DARO beat four leading baselines, converging faster and finishing higher. The authors offer their unified view of the method family as a guide for future variants.
arxiv-2510-09101:
Sherman and colleagues hunt for faint gamma-ray companions to the most energetic neutrino ever recorded, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The KM3NeT detector, deep in the Mediterranean, caught a neutrino carrying about two hundred twenty peta-electronvolts in 2023. Such neutrinos are born alongside gamma rays, which then cascade down to energies that space telescopes can see. The team searched data from the Fermi telescope's main instrument around the neutrino's sky position.

They found three gamma-ray sources too faint for existing catalogs within a small patch around the event. One flickered into view only after the neutrino arrived, though it may be an unrelated flare from a nearby microquasar, a small black hole system. Another may coincide with a known radio blazar. Soberingly, three such faint sources could be expected by chance at that galactic latitude, and the fluctuations look consistent with background.
arxiv-2510-09201:
Choi and co-authors argue that tuning the instructions for multimodal AI models should tune the pictures too, not just the words, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Prompt optimization automates the search for instructions that make a model perform best. Existing methods only rewrite text, even when the model also consumes images, video, or molecular structures. The authors define multimodal prompt optimization, where text prompts and non-text prompts are improved together as a pair.

Their framework, MPO, updates both halves while preserving the alignment between them, so the image prompt and its caption keep matching. A Bayesian selection step uses scores from earlier candidate prompts as prior knowledge when choosing which candidates to try next. Across experiments spanning images, videos, and even molecules, MPO beat the leading text-only optimizers. The authors conclude that joint multimodal tuning is an essential step toward unlocking what these models can do.
arxiv-2510-09401:
Matthew Williams, F Hunter McGuire, and Terrance Savitsky work on survey statistics in a 2025 arXiv paper. Large surveys sample some groups more than others, which can bias estimates and distort measures of uncertainty. The authors study multi-level models, which estimate both overall parameters and local effects for each group, under such complex sampling designs.

Their focus is the survey-weighted pseudo-posterior, a Bayesian method that reweights the sample to correct the design. They test its limits and those of an existing automated fix for its uncertainty estimates. They then propose changes to that automated process and show the improvements in a simulation study. A real example from the National Survey on Drug Use and Health illustrates the method, and the team released an updated R software package for other analysts.
arxiv-2510-09601:
Min-Hsiu Hsieh, Xingjian Li, and Ting-Chun Lin simplify quantum weight reduction in a 2025 arXiv paper. Quantum error correction codes are checked by measurements, and codes whose checks touch many qubits are hard to run on real hardware. Weight reduction rewrites a code so its checks stay small, at some cost in size and distance.

Their streamlined geometric procedure rests on coning, a cone-shaped construction, and treats the two check types, called X and Z, symmetrically. It improves on Hastings' earlier approach and reaches bounds the authors show are optimal or near-optimal within this geometric framework. Applied to random dense codes of a standard family, it yields explicit codes that pass the square-root distance barrier. The constructions also embed in three dimensions at the best possible rate, and the technique reduces the helper qubits needed to measure logical operators fault-tolerantly.
arxiv-2510-09701:
Siyuan Guo and Taylor Jones measure a classic fractal construction in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Cantor set is built by repeatedly deleting middle thirds, and taking the Cartesian product of several copies gives a fractal dust in higher dimensions. Hausdorff measure generalises length and area to such jagged sets, and its exact value at the critical dimension is often elusive.

The authors bound that measure for the d-fold product of the one-third Cantor set, at the dimension given by d times the base logarithm ratio. They apply known theorems for fractals satisfying the strong open set condition. They also generalise what was previously done for the two-fold product, the planar case. The result is a pair of stricter upper and lower bounds for several small values of d. The paper adds precision to the measurement of one of the most studied families of fractals.
arxiv-2510-09801:
Valerie Chen and nine co-authors, among them Graham Neubig, study how to evaluate software agents with the humans who use them in a 2025 arXiv paper. Benchmarks grade agents on accuracy while assuming full automation, but real use is collaborative. Their framework, PULSE, makes human-centric evaluation efficient in three steps: collect user feedback, train a model to predict satisfaction, and combine real ratings with model-generated pseudo-labels.

They deployed PULSE in software engineering, on a large web platform built around OpenHands, an open-source agent. Across fifteen thousand users, they tested how three agent design decisions affected developer satisfaction. The method also tightened conclusions, reducing confidence intervals by forty percent compared with a standard A/B test. Wild results sometimes disagreed with benchmark rankings, including an anti-correlation between two leading models. The authors argue benchmark-driven evaluation alone misleads design.
arxiv-2510-10201:
Zhang and co-authors present RLFR in this 2025 arXiv paper on training language models with reinforcement learning. Verifiable rewards have improved reasoning, but a binary pass-or-fail reward can overlook valuable exploration along a reasoning path. Process reward models grade each step, yet gold step labels are costly to annotate.

RLFR extends reinforcement learning with a flow environment, and it shapes process-token rewards with auxiliary signals. Signals such as entropy and likelihood, collected from the model's own output distribution, stand in for expensive human labels. The authors aim to reward good reasoning steps without a golden process model. Finer rewards should guide models toward sound reasoning, not just lucky final answers.
arxiv-2510-10301:
Kazarnovskii revisits the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra in this 2025 arXiv paper in mathematics. The theorem says every complex polynomial has exactly as many roots, counted with multiplicity, as its degree. The paper also treats a probabilistic cousin for real roots of real polynomials, the Kac theorem of Littlewood and Offord from 1938.

Kazarnovskii develops the circle of ideas around both results. The probabilistic version asks how many real roots a random polynomial should have, a question with a strikingly small answer compared with the degree. Revisiting these classics exposes the tools, from counting arguments to potential theory, that still drive modern work on random polynomials and their zeros.
arxiv-2510-10501:
Heechan Yi and four co-authors explore quantum circuits as tools for the heavy numerical integration that particle physics demands, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Monte Carlo methods simulate collisions, model detectors, and evaluate multi dimensional integrals, but they converge slowly and lose precision on functions with sharp peaks. The team studies Quantum Integration Networks, which use quantum circuits whose gradients can be computed exactly through the parameter shift rule.

They compare adaptive sampling, which adjusts where points are drawn, against non adaptive sampling, and they test how different loss functions affect accuracy and convergence. They also examine three circuit designs: a data re-uploading model, a quantum signal processing protocol, and deterministic quantum computation with one qubit. Their results show how these choices interact, offering guidance for tuning such networks for high energy physics work.
arxiv-2510-10801:
Bahar İlgen and Georges Hattab propose judging simplified health texts the way readers actually experience them, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Text simplification should make public health information usable by people with limited health literacy. Standard metrics such as BLEU, FKGL, and SARI, however, mostly capture surface features. They miss clarity, trustworthiness, tone, cultural relevance, and whether a reader can act on the text, qualities that matter greatly in high stakes health communication.

Their Human-Centered Readability Score has five dimensions and is grounded in human computer interaction and health communication research. It combines automatic measures with structured human feedback, capturing the relational and contextual sides of readability. The authors outline the framework, describe how it fits into review workflows with readers involved, and present a protocol for validating it. Their aim is scoring that aligns language technology with readers' needs and lived experience, not surface statistics.
arxiv-2510-10901:
Ziad Ghanem designs a symmetric key cryptosystem whose algebra lives in the Burnside ring of a compact Lie group, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Classical linear ciphers like the Hill cipher act on fixed finite dimensional spaces, so known plaintext attacks recover the key, a fully determined linear operator. Ghanem's key instead bundles the group itself, a secret ordering of a natural basis, and a secret set of representation indices that define the encryption multiplier.
