For the circle symmetry group O(2), he proves encryption preserves the plaintext's support, avoiding ciphertext expansion and leakage. Against passive observers, any finite set of observations constrains the action only on a finite rank submodule, and the key is information theoretically unidentifiable from such data. But the verdict is not all positive: he proves the scheme is not IND-CPA secure, exhibiting a one query chosen plaintext distinguisher built from dihedral probes.
arxiv-2510-11001:
Tieyuan Chen and five co-authors give finished language models a second look at their hardest tokens, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their Dynamic Nested Depth method works with off the shelf models. At the end of a transformer layer, a small router picks the tokens that look most critical. Those tokens loop back for an extra round of processing, like a student rechecking hard questions, while easy tokens skip the redundant work. Two tricks keep selection precise: a loss that sharpens the router's choices, and a threshold scheme that keeps selections stable.

The method plugs into pretrained dense and mixture of experts models during a post training phase. On diverse benchmarks it lifted the dense Qwen3-1.7B model by 1.88 percent and the sparse Qwen3-30B-A3B by 0.87 percent in the reported experiments. The gains came with minimal added parameters and computing.
arxiv-2510-11501:
A racing car that learned against one style of opponent may fail against a different driving style, because the opponent's behavior changes the dynamics the learner planned around. Emran Yasser Moustafa and Ivana Dusparic study that transfer problem for model-based reinforcement learning in this 2025 arXiv robotics paper. They work in Roboracer, a simulated head-to-head autonomous racing environment, and frame the task as a contextual Markov decision process where the context is the adversary's driving behavior.

Benchmarking model-based methods in this setting, they find context-free methods generalize poorly to out-of-distribution adversary behaviors. Their add-on, called cMask, feeds the episode's context into the learned model. Context-aware methods did better on unseen adversary styles. cMask also improved performance relative to other context-aware approaches when racing against in-distribution opponents, showing that knowing the opponent's style helps both in familiar and in novel matchups.
arxiv-2510-12301:
Kronthaler and Held extend a p-value based method of meta-analysis so it accounts for uncertainty about study differences, in a 2025 arXiv statistics paper. Meta-analysis combines results from many studies. Edgington's method merges the studies' p-values into one joint function, from which estimates and intervals can be read off.

The authors adjust that method using a confidence distribution for the heterogeneity parameter, which measures how much true effects vary across studies. It is built from a generalized heterogeneity statistic, so uncertainty about variation feeds into the final intervals. Simulations show the ninety five percent intervals reach close to their nominal coverage in most cases with more than three studies and some heterogeneity. With no heterogeneity or only three studies the intervals overcover, yet often stay narrower than the standard Hartung Knapp Sidik Jonkman interval. Its point estimator showed small bias when the model was misspecified.
arxiv-2510-12501:
Cruz-Zamorano and Zarvalis characterize the holomorphic self mappings of the upper half plane whose orbits converge as slowly as possible, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. A self map sends the half plane into itself. Repeated application drives points toward a special point called the Denjoy Wolff point. Most maps approach it at some rate. The extremal ones approach at the slowest rate the theory allows.

The authors focus on the discrete hyperbolic and parabolic cases. They characterize the extremal maps using several tools in combination. These include the Herglotz representation, which expresses such maps through positive measures. They also include the conformality of the Koenigs map at the Denjoy Wolff point, and hyperbolic distance, which measures separation in the geometry natural to the half plane. The result identifies exactly which dynamics realize the boundary case of convergence speed, completing the picture of orbit rates.
arxiv-2510-12701:
Mercer analyzes a particle system where branching and selection act at both ends, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Its large scale behavior is governed by a free boundary problem with two moving walls. The classical model is N particle branching Brownian motion, where particles diffuse, split, and are culled to keep the population fixed. His generalization lets selection act on the leftmost and rightmost particles, set by a parameter between zero and one.

The main result shows that as the particle number grows, the empirical spread converges to a deterministic hydrodynamic limit. That limit is a free boundary problem on a bounded interval, with two moving walls and explicit conditions set by the selection parameter. The long run velocity of the particle system also converges to the unique traveling wave speed of the limiting problem. The results generalize earlier one sided models, and connect to free boundary problems in evolutionary dynamics.
arxiv-2510-13501:
Du and co-authors turn a language model's own confidence into a reward signal for judging answers. Their 2025 arXiv paper proposes CRew, short for Confidence-as-a-Reward, a training-free reward method. Trained reward models normally need large curated datasets and costly runs. Judge-style prompting avoids training but still trails trained reward models in quality.

CRew simply reads the model's token-level confidence in its final answer as the reward. This works best for close-ended problems with definite answers, such as mathematics. On MATH500 and RewardMATH, CRew topped all other training-free reward models. It even surpassed most trained reward models on those benchmarks. CRew scores also track closely with a model's actual reasoning performance. A variant, CRew-DPO, builds preference data from confidence and correctness to fine-tune judges further.
arxiv-2510-13701:
Herceg and co-authors compute the ringing tones of a charged black hole deformed by noncommutative geometry. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies Dirac quasinormal modes, the damped vibrations a black hole emits when disturbed. Noncommutative geometry blurs spacetime at tiny scales, a possible fingerprint of quantum gravity. The deformation adds an extra twist-like term to the black hole's metric.

The team follows massless Dirac fields, the relativistic waves of spin-half particles, around the deformed hole. They extract mode frequencies with a continued fraction method, boosted to handle six-term recurrences. Frequencies and damping rates shift clearly compared with the ordinary charged black hole. The spectrum also splits in a pattern like the Zeeman effect in atoms. That splitting is driven directly by the noncommutativity parameter. Such signatures could, in principle, let gravitational wave data test spacetime fuzziness.
arxiv-2510-13801:
Gil-García and Shahbazi pin down the algebraic square of a basic complex spinor in every size and sign pattern. Their 2025 arXiv paper continues the view of spinors as square roots of geometry. Squaring a spinor yields exterior forms, the language of differential geometry. Which forms arise this way, exactly, was only partly known before.

The square is written as a pair of exterior forms obeying exact algebraic rules. Those rules are stated neatly with the geometric product of the base space. The result is a general match-up between irreducible spinors and special forms. Explicit builds follow for flat Euclidean spaces up to size six. Generic chiral spinors in eight flat dimensions get their squares built too. The authors then define spinorial instantons within the same scheme. Those objects live on bundles with complex structure groups and on gerbes over six-dimensional Lorentzian spaces.
arxiv-2510-14001:
Miranda Carou Laiño, Veronika Chobanova, and Miriam Lucio Martínez explore quantum machine learning with qutrits for finding anomalies in particle collider data, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A qutrit is a quantum unit with three states instead of the qubit's two, giving more room to encode information. The coming High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider will produce data at rates that strain classical analysis.

The authors propose developing a qutrit-based quantum model for anomaly detection, the search for events the Standard Model cannot explain, which could signal exotic new phenomena. They benchmark the qutrit approach against qubit-based models on accuracy, scalability, and computational efficiency. Their stated aim is to establish whether qutrit architectures offer a real advantage for the computational and analytical demands of future collider experiments. In such settings, multi-level quantum systems may represent some physics, such as neutrino behavior, more naturally than binary ones.
arxiv-2510-14201:
Joshua Tomlin proves a formula describing how an invariant of families of four-dimensional shapes behaves when the shapes are glued together, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The invariant is the families Bauer-Furuta invariant, a refinement of the families Seiberg-Witten invariant built from an approximation of the Seiberg-Witten monopole map, a tool from gauge theory used to distinguish structures.

Tomlin's formula covers the fibrewise connected sum, the operation of cutting and gluing manifolds together along a shared piece, done simultaneously across a family. It extends Bauer's formula for a single manifold to the parameterized setting. In a subsequent paper, Tomlin plans to use the result to derive a general connected-sum formula for the families Seiberg-Witten invariant. It would incorporate both the families blow-up formula of Liu and the gluing formula of Baraglia and Konno. That unifies previously separate pieces of the theory.
arxiv-2510-14501:
Norihisa Namura, Riccardo Muolo, and Hiroya Nakao design interaction functions between oscillators so that their collective behavior is described by a higher-order Kuramoto model, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Kuramoto model of synchronization assumes purely sinusoidal coupling between phases. Real limit-cycle oscillators, from neurons to chemical reactors, reduced to phases by standard methods do not produce Kuramoto coupling exactly, except in one special case.

The authors invert the problem: they construct pairwise and higher-order interaction functions between the oscillators from which the higher-order Kuramoto dynamics follow exactly under phase reduction, for smooth limit-cycle oscillators. Simulations with FitzHugh-Nagumo oscillators, a standard neuron model, confirm that the collective synchronization predicted by the reduced models is realized. They demonstrate control of the oscillators' shared phase using a low-dimensional reduction of the higher-order Kuramoto model, turning an exactness result into a design tool.
arxiv-2510-14901:
Karan and Du ask, in a 2025 arXiv paper, whether the reasoning usually credited to reinforcement learning was inside base models all along. Frontier models gain reasoning from RL posttraining, and researchers debate which abilities RL truly creates. The authors approach from the opposite side: can sampling alone, at inference time, pull comparable reasoning out of a base model?

Their method borrows from Markov chain Monte Carlo. An iterative sampler proposes answers and reweights them using the base model's own likelihoods, sampling from a sharpened version of what the model believes. Across several base models, this power sampling delivered reasoning gains, nearly matching and sometimes beating RL posttraining on single-shot benchmarks including MATH500, HumanEval, and GPQA. It also avoided a known RL side effect, the collapse of answer diversity across samples. No training, curated data, or verifier is required, so it should travel where answers cannot be checked automatically.
arxiv-2510-15001:
The VaultGemma Team introduces VaultGemma 1B, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a language model trained from the start under a formal privacy guarantee. Differential privacy bounds what any training document can contribute to a model, protecting the people whose text it learned from. Fully training a model this way, rather than patching privacy on afterward, has been a challenge for the Gemma family and its peers.

VaultGemma has one billion parameters and was pre-trained on the same data mixture as the Gemma 2 series, so its utility can be compared against its non-private counterpart. Its guarantee is at sequence level: an epsilon of at most 2.0 in the stated bound, for sequences of about a thousand tokens after sampling and packing. The team evaluates the model across academic benchmarks against the non-private model, to quantify what the privacy costs. They release VaultGemma openly to accelerate research in private AI.
arxiv-2510-15601:
Models that design proteins need honest scoring, especially when they generate sequences under conditions. Pierre Glaser and five colleagues present evaluation tools for such models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their centerpiece is a discrepancy measure called ACMMD, which compares true and generated conditional distributions. The measure can be estimated from samples without bias, giving an absolute read on model fit. It also plugs into hypothesis tests and reliability checks for designed sequences.

The team applies the tools to ProteinMPNN, a well-known protein design model. They reject the idea that the model fits several protein families adequately. Tuning its temperature setting with their measure produces a visibly better fit.
arxiv-2510-15801:
Bonnie Rushing, Mac-Rufus Umeokolo, and Shouhuai Xu wrote a 2025 paper on cyber cognitive attacks. These attacks steer people's decisions. They exploit mental biases. New tools make them stronger, from AI-made disinformation to synthetic media. Most past work only catalogues current tricks. The authors argue defence should forecast what comes next.

They introduce a method for predicting new disruptive innovations. It also forecasts how attackers might misuse them. The team tracks trends in attacker tactics. From those trends they derive proactive defences. The aim is to prepare organisations early. Defences would be ready before a new manipulation technique spreads, not after.
arxiv-2510-16201:
Debatri Chattopadhyay and five co-authors model the futures of twenty-one star pairs found by the Gaia space mission. Each pair joins a neutron star with a normal star on an oval orbit. A neutron star is the dense core left by a dead star. The team runs them forward with the MESA code.

In every run the normal star ends as a white dwarf, but the path splits on how mass flows between the pair. If the flow keeps the orbit's oval shape, orbits widen and stretch, and the neutron star spins up mildly. If the orbit is rounded, the neutron star eats more and becomes a millisecond pulsar. Yet these Gaia pairs stay too wide to match the galaxy's tight pulsar-white dwarf pairs. The team concludes that pairs born with unlike mixes, prone to unstable flow, must make up the rest.
arxiv-2510-16301:
Amena Khatun and Muhammad Usman write a book chapter on making quantum machine learning practical and attack-resistant. Today's quantum hardware offers few, noisy qubits, so their hybrid design pairs classical convolutional networks, which extract image features, with quantum variational circuits that classify them, borrowing strength from transfer learning.

Across datasets including Ants and Bees, CIFAR-10, and road sign detection, their quantum transfer learning model beats both conventional models and quantum models trained from scratch. The chapter then probes the security angle: adversarial examples can fool the hybrid system, but adversarial training during learning restores much of its robustness. The authors pitch the combination as a realistic path for deploying quantum-enhanced classifiers in sensitive settings.
arxiv-2510-16401:
Ning Sun, Peng Zhang, and Pengfei Zhang built a toy model of strongly linked quantum matter in 2025. Their model mixes two known ones. One links all parts at random, and one adds strong on-site links. Toy models help labs study traits shared by many real materials. The mix lets them watch local and far links fight and blend.

As link strength grows, the model's energy spread shifts from one peak to two. That shift marks the onset of a stuck, Mott-like state. Other tests track how chaos grows with time in the system. One pace of chaos growth breaks a known bound. The model gives a rare case that can be solved yet still acts rich.
arxiv-2510-16501:
Tomasz Kania, the sole author, studies trace formulas in a 2025 maths paper. A trace adds up key values of a map on a space. His spaces have fixed size but any shape of distance rule. He looks at blown-up maps on wedge forms, which blend directions in a signed way. The question asks which chance weights on unit points make a mean-based trace formula hold.

He shows the formula holds just when a linked mean equals the identity map. One cone-based weight works for all distance rules. A skin-based weight works when the space has enough symmetry. He also gives sparse, point-based forms of the formula. One blocked form shows where the skin weight must fail.
arxiv-2510-16801:
Jingtao Zhu, Yuying Zhao, and Siqing Gan strengthen simulation math for interacting particles in a 2025 paper. Their equations are McKean-Vlasov equations, where each particle feels the whole crowd. Simulating them needs step-by-step numerical schemes. Standard schemes can break when growth terms rise faster than linearly.

The team builds one family of Milstein-type schemes covering those cases. Named variants tame the wild terms in different gentle ways. They prove the schemes still reach first-order accuracy overall. The proof needs only mild smoothness from the equation's coefficients. Earlier work had tested one such scheme without proof. Numerical experiments in the paper back the theory. The results give simulators a safer toolkit for crowded particle systems.
arxiv-2510-16901:
Shih-Yu Chang examines what polynomial changes do to matrices in a 2025 paper. Applying a function to a matrix extends ordinary function ideas. Every matrix splits into a spectral part and a nilpotent part. The spectral part carries the eigenvalues, the matrix's characteristic scaling values. The nilpotent part captures failure to be perfectly diagonal.

Chang asks two questions about polynomial-transformed matrices. When does the transformed matrix become nilpotent, meaning some power is zero? When does it become diagonalizable, meaning cleanly breakable into independent directions? He treats matrices with one eigenvalue and with several separately. Sparse polynomials call for root-counting tools like Descartes' rule. Dense ones need analytic tools from complex analysis. The results sort existence and counting of such matrices.
arxiv-2510-17401:
Automated negotiators usually rely on models of the other side or on machine learning tuned with care. David Aguilera-Luzon, Dave de Jonge, and Javier Larrosa start from MiCRO, a strikingly simple bargaining strategy that uses neither, yet matched or beat most leading methods in one to one talks. That success raised an open question: could the same plain idea handle talks among many parties at once?

Aguilera-Luzon and his co-authors build a many party version of MiCRO and test it against the winning agents from three past negotiation contests. Their version outperformed those winners. A game theory style analysis of many repeated match ups also suggests the new strategy settles into a stable balance where no side gains by switching away alone.
arxiv-2510-17601:
A random walk on a free product of graphs wanders through a combined landscape built from several simpler graphs glued together. Lorenz A Gilch, writing alone, studies the long run behaviour of a natural class of such walks, formed by mixing the walks on the separate pieces. Earlier work had already shown that these walks possess a definite drift, a steady average speed, and a definite entropy, which measures their randomness.

Gilch proves three central limit theorems for these walks, the bell curve style laws that describe how far a real walk typically strays from its average drift and entropy. He also shows how the spread of those curves changes smoothly when the walk depends on a few adjustable parameters. The results complete the statistical picture of drift and entropy for this class of walks.
arxiv-2510-17701:
Kristiana Mihali, with Dennis Wörthmüller and Pierre Sens, models how cell membranes can buckle from within in a 2025 arXiv paper. Cell shape is largely set by the actin cytoskeleton, a network of protein filaments under the membrane. Some cells grow free standing protrusions with no outside support. Proteins that sense membrane curvature help control how the actin network grows.

The team built a theory for a viscous actin layer growing on a wavy membrane. Uniform growth always steadies the membrane and reduces its deformation. Curvature sensitive proteins that recruit actin builders can flip that balance. Under the right interplay of membrane and actin dynamics, the flat state turns unstable. Spontaneous deformation then follows, which could start an extended free standing protrusion.
arxiv-2510-18101:
Vitor Pereira Matias, with six co-authors, surveys a fast-moving shift in three-dimensional graphics toward Gaussian splatting. Scenes are stored as clouds of soft three-dimensional blobs that render quickly and plug into normal graphics pipelines. The price is heavy memory use, lighting baked into the scene, and weak support for effects that need extra rays.

The tutorial walks the full pipeline from its math roots, then reviews fixes for those limits. Uses covered include surface rebuilding, avatars, animation, and content creation. Graphics readers get one concise tour of where this real-time method stands and what still holds it back.
arxiv-2510-18501:
Tung-Anh Nguyen and his five co-authors present FedSVD, a system for spotting intrusions in networks of small internet-connected devices. The devices learn together without pooling their raw data in one place, a pattern called federated learning, and the method needs no labeled examples of attacks. Its core tool is singular value decomposition, a matrix method run here through optimization on a special geometric space known as a Grassmann manifold.

The design targets low-power hardware such as the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, cutting both communication load and computing cost. In experiments, detection quality matched deep learning baselines for both known and unknown intrusions, while answers arrived more than ten times faster. That speed matters for security on live device networks, where a slow detector can miss the moment an attack is still stoppable.
arxiv-2510-18601:
Marco Alecci, with Jordan Samhi, Tegawendé Bissyandé, and Jacques Klein, tackles a common mobile security flaw: secret keys baked directly into Android apps. Developers hardcode passwords, tokens, and client identifiers to reach cloud services, and attackers can pull them out by reverse engineering the app. Older detectors rely on patterns, code analysis, or trained models, so each needs advance knowledge of what a secret looks like.

Their tool, SecretLoc, uses a large language model that reads context and structure to spot secrets without preset patterns or labeled training data. On a standard benchmark it found secrets every older method missed, including types never catalogued before, such as keys for AI services, access tokens, and private encryption keys. In total it uncovered 4,828 previously missed secrets and more than ten new types, and the team responsibly reported further finds in fresh apps from the Google Play store.
arxiv-2510-19001:
Seungjun Yu and three co-authors build a question-answering system for autonomous driving that explains scenes in words. The system answers high-level questions about perception, prediction, and planning, the three judgments a self-driving car must make from its cameras.

In a first phase, a large vision-language model reads six camera views, recent history, and worked examples, and checks itself by sampling several chains of reasoning. A second phase adds scene metadata, such as object labels and the car's own state, plus prompts tailored to each question type. On a driving benchmark, the setup clearly beats the base model.
arxiv-2510-19601:
Martín Matamala settles a graph case of a conjecture about lines in metric spaces. In 2008 Chen and Chvátal guessed that any metric space on n points determines at least n distinct lines, unless every point lies on a single line. Chvátal had already confirmed the guess for spaces whose distances take only the values zero, one, and two.

Matamala looks at metric spaces coming from graphs of diameter two, where the same distance restriction holds. He proves there is a family of exactly ten graphs with a clean property: such a space has fewer lines than points precisely when its graph belongs to that family. The result pins down all the exceptional cases for this class.
arxiv-2510-20001:
Yunpeng Xiao and four co-authors argue that medical question-answering benchmarks flatter language models, because real clinical decisions are far richer than picking an answer. They propose a unifying framework that grades clinical tasks along two dimensions: how complete the clinical background is, and how realistic the question is. As both approach the real clinic, difficulty rises.

Existing datasets and benchmarks are mapped onto these axes, and methods for improving clinical decision making, at training time and at test time, are reviewed with guidance on when each helps. The authors push evaluation beyond raw accuracy to efficiency and explainability. They close with open challenges, aiming to standardize comparisons and steer development toward models that are clinically meaningful rather than merely test-smart.
arxiv-2510-20201:
Masao Hirokawa, Fumio Hiroshima, and DongYun Lee study the strong-coupling limit of the anisotropic quantum Rabi model. That model interpolates continuously between the standard quantum Rabi model and the Jaynes-Cummings model, two central descriptions of light-matter interaction. The question is what the model becomes as the coupling strength grows without bound.

After subtracting an explicit quadratic renormalization term, the authors identify the limiting Hamiltonian in the norm-resolvent sense. That limit fixes the asymptotic spectral structure of the model at strong coupling. Their result gives one unified description linking the two endpoint models and shows that the counter-rotating interaction plays the dominant role in that extreme regime.
arxiv-2510-20701:
Marco Hoffmann and seven co-authors track in real time how magnetic tunnel junctions switch when voltage shifts the magnetic pull inside them. Such switching promises fast, low power memory, and voltage control is often treated as near instant in device models.

Live tests show that slow charging in each device and grain level unevenness in the magnetic film hold up switching when voltage sits near the threshold. Raising the voltage or the applied field cuts the delay, bringing total switch times down to a few billionths of a second. Simulations that include charging time and film grain match the tests well, pointing to clear design steps for faster memory and logic parts.
arxiv-2510-20901:
Oscar Bouverot-Dupuis leads two co-authors on a Monte Carlo algorithm for the Mott transition in one dimensional quantum systems, modeled through the sine Gordon theory with a tilt. Standard local sampling stalls because configurations split into topological sectors that local moves cannot cross, limiting sizes severely.

Their smooth worm algorithm enlarges the configuration space so moves pass smoothly between sectors, joining worm updates with event chain moves. Validity is proved and performance is measured, showing substantial speedup. Larger reachable sizes let the generic Mott transition be studied with far less finite size distortion.
arxiv-2510-21001:
Gert-Martin Greuel and one co-author extend Grauert approximation theorem to power series over fields of any characteristic, with uses. Grauert nineteen seventy two result solved nested formula based rules over the complex numbers and founded modern singularity deformation theory.

The original proof invented standard bases for ideals in power series rings and a generalized Weierstrass splitting theorem, all over the complex numbers. Extending splitting and approximation to arbitrary characteristic convergent series widens singularity theory to settings algebraic geometry now demands. The article revisits a classic engine and rebuilds it for broader ground fields.
arxiv-2510-21101:
Hui Han leads nine co-authors on a tunable one sided delay attack against quantum clock time sync, exposing a weakness in a tech that secures messaging and core systems. Quantum clock sync assumes the channel behaves the same in both directions, and an attacker who breaks that symmetry can skew the shared time.

Static delay attacks cannot aim at specific steadiness needs, so the proposed attack adjusts its delay pattern dynamically along tailored trajectories. Experiments show selective compromise of system steadiness across scenarios. Naming and demonstrating the tunable attack gives defenders concrete failure modes to design against before deployment.
arxiv-2510-21201:
Quan Mu proposes a new geometric model for ice crystals in high cirrus clouds, built from random convex polyhedra, meaning solid shapes with many flat faces. Knowing how such crystals scatter light matters for reading satellite data correctly and for calculations about Earth's energy balance.

Shapes are generated with a convex hull algorithm, and the full scattering matrix, which carries polarization information, is computed in the geometric optics approximation for crystals pointing in random directions. The method works for any convex polyhedron shape. Results for three example shapes are given, and the classic hexagonal column case agrees well with earlier published results. Diffraction and absorption are left out of the calculations.
arxiv-2510-21401:
Mojtaba Eshghie and four co-authors use fine-tuned language models to write safety guards for smart contracts, the self-running programs on blockchains whose flaws have cost billions of dollars. Existing tools mostly flag weak spots; they rarely produce a working defense a developer can drop into live code.

Their system, FLAMES, learns from real protective conditions mined out of more than half a million verified contracts, training by filling in missing middle pieces of code. The guards it writes are short require statements in the Solidity language. Nearly all of them compile, and on a hard test set of five thousand guards, about forty-four percent match the reference exactly or in meaning. Against 108 real attacks, the guards stop twenty-two while keeping contracts working, including one live incident the system blocks outright.
arxiv-2510-21601:
Emmanuel Dare Alalade and Ashraf Matrawy model privacy threats against Internet of Things systems by following the attackers, not just the weak points. Earlier analyses sorted threats by where they might occur and how likely they seemed, skipping who carries them out, what they do step by step, and why.

Their framework walks a threat through phases, borrowing tactics from the MITRE ATT&CK catalogue of attacker behavior and techniques from the LINDDUN privacy threat method. Twelve IoT privacy threats were put to security and privacy experts from industry and academia through a structured questionnaire. Mapping their answers exposes the actors behind each threat. For the threat of identifying IoT users, the top three actor types and the critical paths they use, giving defenders a concrete map for placing countermeasures.
arxiv-2510-21801:
Marouane Tliba and six co-authors, Mohamed Amine Kerkouri, Yassine Nasser, Nour Aburaed, Aladine Chetouani, Ulas Bagci, and Rachid Jennane, work on grading knee osteoarthritis from X-ray images. The damage signs are subtle shape details that ordinary image models often miss, so the team adds explicit information about the joint's anatomy.

A segmentation tool first outlines the bones, and those outlines become a graph describing the joint's structure. The graph description is then aligned with what a vision encoder sees in the X-ray, so shape knowledge guides the reading. On a large public osteoarthritis dataset, the combined system beat image-only baselines by up to ten percent in accuracy and also passed earlier leading methods on both accuracy and F1 score.
arxiv-2510-22001:
Jacob S. Palmer and Kaitlin N. Smith ask how defective a quantum computer's parts can get before error correction stops helping. Real superconducting qubits vary widely, so the tidy uniform noise used in most studies flatters the hardware. The team instead hunts for the boundary of acceptable defectiveness, the error level past which one bad qubit poisons the whole computation.

Using a fast stabilizer simulator, they generated rotated surface code circuits at many sizes, planted defective qubits at assorted error rates and locations, and measured how protection held up. Evidence points to real boundaries of that kind, thresholds separating a qubit that is merely weaker from one that should be cut out of the code's map entirely. Knowing the line lets hardware teams decide which qubits to retire rather than rebuild.
arxiv-2510-22201:
Minho Park leads an eight-author team smoothing the jerky habits that robot policies absorb from human teachers. Vision-language-action models built on diffusion and flow methods generalize well, but they learn from demonstrations full of pauses, jitters. Corrections, and that noise reappears as incoherent actions, unstable motion, and drifting trajectories when the robot runs for real.

Their remedy, Action Coherence Guidance, needs no retraining: it steers the model's outputs at test time toward more coherent action sequences. Across two simulation suites for household and dexterous tasks and a real desktop robot arm, the guidance consistently raised both measured coherence and task success rates. The gains matter most in fine-grained manipulation, where a single incoherent jerk can ruin an otherwise good trajectory, and the code is publicly available.
arxiv-2510-22501:
Online information spreads a bit like disease, but people often pause before passing it on. Tran Van Khanh, Do Xuan Cho, and Hoang Phi Dung model that pause in a 2025 paper, extending a classic epidemic framework for social networks.

Their SDIR model adds a delayable state for users who received a message, waited, and may never share it. Using a mean field approximation, which tracks group averages, they derive motion equations and study when the system settles. They also give an approximate method for deleting edges, meaning links, in a way that limits how far information can spread.
arxiv-2510-22801:
Solar flares can disturb Earth, so flare forecasts matter. Griffin T Goodwin leads a team with six co-authors. In 2025 they present FOXES, a frame for X-ray synthesis. Current catalogs use only Earth view X-ray data. That limits far side flare location and strength.

Their model uses a Vision Transformer. It turns extreme ultraviolet views into soft X-ray flux. EUV and X-ray are both high energy light bands. Flux predictions stay accurate across flare classes. The frame also sets up future location estimates. EUV based detection could extend beyond Earth line of sight. That would yield a more complete flare catalog.
arxiv-2510-22901:
Motion planning on wild one dimensional spaces can be surprisingly hard. Jeremy Brazas and Petar Pavesic study that topic in 2025. They examine Lusternik-Schnirelmann category and topological complexity. Both measure how hard navigation and covering are. Their spaces are one dimensional Peano continua.

They define both invariants via closed filtrations. Filtrations are nested chains of subspaces. Main results tie both invariants to wildness rank. Wildness captures how badly behaved the space is. A surprise follows from their formulas. Both invariants can be arbitrarily high in one dimension. That contrasts with results for nicer CW complexes. CW complexes are built from simple cells.
arxiv-2510-23001:
Sharada Sahoo and five co-authors report a lab search for dark matter particles through invisible decays in nuclear gamma cascades. Light, weakly coupled particles remain a strong lead for dark matter, yet large parts of their possible range are still untested. The team used about one hundred kilograms of cesium iodide detectors in Texas.

A high-activity scandium-46 source produced cascades of gamma rays, and the team hunted for a missing gamma that would signal an invisible decay. High counts gave the search strong reach. The method adds a tabletop route to probing particles that big detectors might miss.
arxiv-2510-23201:
E Benhamou, J J Ohana, B Guez, E Setrouk, and T Jacquot present an AI framework to replicate private equity performance with liquid assets, aimed at building trust in illiquid markets. Private equity has delivered strong returns, but lockups and low transparency worry investors, especially when markets turn volatile.

Their method uses graphical models to decode liquid proxies for private equity and adds asymmetric risk adjustments that mimic the asset class profile. The approach seeks resilient, transparent instruments with fund-like behavior. If sound, liquid replication could widen access while easing systemic concerns tied to hidden leverage.
arxiv-2510-23301:
Yingying Feng and five co-authors present MDReID, a framework for re-identifying objects across images from different sensors. In the real world a query may come from a color camera while the gallery holds near-infrared or thermal images. Most methods assume matched modalities, which limits robustness in practice.

MDReID decouples modality information into shared and specific parts, enabling any-to-any matching at image level. It works under both matched and mismatched conditions. Flexible re-identification matters for security and tracking systems that must fuse whatever cameras happen to be installed. The authors present their evidence and methods in full for readers to judge.
arxiv-2510-23501:
Spyros Rigas and three co-authors fix a training problem in physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, models that solve physics equations using flexible curve-based layers. The Chebyshev-based versions train fast and are now standard, but they grow unstable when stacked deep, which blocks many uses. Simply starting the weights the usual way does not keep deep versions on track.

The authors propose a Glorot-like starting scheme that keeps signal strength steady across layers, improving stability and accuracy. For the deepest cases they add a design called Residual-Gated Adaptive KANs, which borrows a gating idea from PirateNet. On nine standard equation benchmarks, their models beat matched rivals, often by orders of magnitude, and stayed stable where the others broke down. A study of how information flows during training helps explain why the gated design keeps learning.
arxiv-2510-23701:
Yitao Feng and three co-authors clarify when a higher-form symmetry on a lattice can be made onsite. Onsite means spread into independent local actions, with help from ancilla qubits and a shallow circuit. Folklore says onsiteable is the same as anomaly-free, and that holds for ordinary symmetries in one spatial dimension. For higher-form symmetries, which act on lines and surfaces rather than points, the two notions come apart.

The authors propose that onsiteability equals the possibility of a generalized gauging procedure. For a finite 1-form symmetry in two spatial dimensions, they prove it is onsiteable exactly when its anomaly obeys a set algebraic condition that permits 1-gauging. Such cases can always be turned into transversal Pauli operators this way. In general dimensions they derive needed conditions from lattice anomaly data and conjecture the same match holds throughout.
arxiv-2510-23901:
Cristobal Heredia and two co-authors present RS-ORT, an algorithm for training regression trees that are provably optimal rather than merely good. Mixed-integer programming can learn such trees, but existing methods choke on continuous features or large data. The naive fix — chopping continuous values into bins first — throws away global optimality and grows needlessly deep trees.

RS-ORT recasts training as a two-stage problem and branches only on the tree's structural choices, which guarantees convergence and makes the cost independent of sample count. Closed-form leaf predictions, smart threshold discretization, and exact parsing of depth-one subtrees tighten the bounds, and the branch-and-bound tree splits naturally across processors. On benchmarks with binary and continuous features, it beat leading methods in training and test performance. With two million samples it still delivered guaranteed results, with simpler trees, inside four hours.
arxiv-2510-24101:
Nam Tran and four co-authors build a traceable signature scheme from lattice problems, aiming for safety against quantum computers. Traceable signatures let a user sign without revealing identity, while an opening authority can trace a signature in set cases. All prior schemes rest on number theory or pairings, which quantum machines may break.

Their construction uses lattices instead and comes with a proof of security in the quantum random oracle model. The paper revisits the definition of traceable signatures and shows the lattice version keeps anonymity and tracing power. The result offers a path to keep this privacy tool usable if large quantum computers arrive.
arxiv-2510-24401:
Vaibhav Katyal and two co-authors tighten a limit on possible new physics using isotope shifts in calcium ions, measured through a King's plot. Nonlinearities in that plot can signal a hypothetical boson coupling electrons to neutrons. The team critically evaluates higher order nonlinear effects in the shifts of low lying transitions of singly charged calcium, which earlier analyses neglected.

Using relativistic coupled cluster theory with two complementary methods, finite field and analytic response, they extract the isotope shift parameters. Including the higher order effects changes the electron neutron coupling limit by an order of magnitude compared with the prior report. The work shows precision atomic physics can sharpen searches for physics beyond the Standard Model.
arxiv-2510-24601:
Jessica Doohan, Lucas Kook, and Kevin Burke review work that pits two kinds of model against each other. One kind is the neural net, which can fit hard patterns but is hard to read. The other is the additive model, which stays clear to read while still bending to fit data.

The team used a set guide to find studies that ran both models on real tables of data. They found 143 studies and 430 data sets in all. When they pooled the scores, neither model won in a steady way. Traits such as field, year, and size helped explain when each one did best.
arxiv-2510-24801:
Vladyslav Larin, Ihor Naumenko, Aleksei Ivashov, Ivan Nikitin, and Alexander Firsov present Fortytwo, a plan for AI work shared across a swarm of peer nodes. Big central AI runs face cost and scale caps, they argue. Their plan lets many unlike models each take a task, then rank each other's work in pairs.

A rank rule pools those pair ranks, weighted by each node's past score, kept on a public chain log. Nodes that prove more right gain more weight over time. In tests, swarm picks beat plain vote by a wide gap on a hard quiz set. Low grade nodes get screened out by the rank loop.
arxiv-2510-25601:
Rossana Facen, Federica Capellino, Eduardo Grossi, Andrea Dubla, and Silvia Masciocchi study charm hadrons. Their 2025 physics paper uses a fluid-dynamic method. Previous studies showed fluid descriptions suit charm quarks. Quark-gluon plasma is the hot medium involved. The present work extends that earlier approach.

Corrections arise from initial out-of-equilibrium charm distributions. A free-streaming phase precedes fluid actions there. Freeze-out surface effects within fluid changes also contribute. Results enable exact computation of integrated yields. Transverse momentum distributions of charm hadrons follow too. That gives basis for determining charm transport coefficients. Agreement holds within uncertainties of readings ready. Limits of applicability are identified by transverse momentum. A region gives well-defined positive distribution functions. Charm transport in heavy-ion collisions gains modeling precision.
arxiv-2510-25801:
Kun Chen led six co-authors presenting Metis-SPECS. Peng Shi, Haibo Qiu, and Zhixiong Zeng helped. Siqi Yang, Wenji Mao, and Lin Ma joined. Their 2025 paper decouples multimodal learning via cold start. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards drives multimodal models. Most methods begin with supervised fine-tuning cold start. That initializes policy before reinforcement learning begins. Supervised cold start intertwines thinking with output format.

Instruction-style overfitting may result from that intertwining. Direct preference tuning beats supervised methods in cold start. Their SPECS approach uses self-distilled preference data. No larger teachers or manual annotation are needed. Preference training learns transferable surface criteria, not content. Reinforcement learning then handles deep thinking. Consistent gains appear across benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-26001:
Xinhua Wang, Caibo Feng, Xiangjun Fu, and Chunxiao Liu improve a Mamba based method for brightening low light images by changing how it scans the picture. Mamba is a sequence model that reads an image in a scanning pattern to capture both fine detail and long range links. Their Hilbert Selective Scan follows a Hilbert curve, a space filling path whose fractal shape covers the plane more thoroughly, which raises the pattern Hausdorff dimension.

Wang and the team report that the richer scan captures fine scale detail and local interactions better, while reducing information mismatches across the image. On public benchmarks, existing Mamba based enhancers gained in both measured quality and visual fidelity, while using less compute and finishing faster. The idea may transfer to other Mamba based tasks.
arxiv-2510-26101:
Taku Mikuriya leads eleven co-authors in a benchmark for language models that write quantum programs. Code generation is usually judged by running Python, but quantum programming also interacts with hardware, even if simulated, and human coders write code that runs on a quantum computer. Their QCoder Benchmark judges models with feedback from a quantum simulator, beyond plain Python execution.

The simulator reports domain measures such as circuit depth, execution time, and error class, which can guide better generation. The benchmark also holds human written submissions from real programming contests for comparison. Even advanced models scored low, with GPT-4o at about nineteen percent accuracy in their experiments, which shows how much room remains in quantum coding.
arxiv-2510-26601:
Anirban Ray, Vera Galinova, and Florian Jug sharpen blurry microscope images with a new learning method. Computational super-resolution tries to recover fine detail that a microscope never recorded, which is only possible with a good prior, a learned sense of what real samples look like. Noise in fluorescence images makes that prior hard to learn.

Ray and his two co-authors present ResMatching, built on guided conditional flow matching, a technique that learns to turn noise into data step by step. On four kinds of biological structures from the BioSR data set, it beat or matched seven rival methods. It gave the best balance between fidelity to the data and realistic looks, and it shone most on noisy images. It can also sample many plausible answers, and its per-pixel uncertainty scores were well calibrated.
arxiv-2510-26701:
Akhila Kandivalasa and Marcos Netto speed up a basic check for power grid control. Observability analysis asks whether a system's state can be inferred from its measures. For dynamic state estimation, which tracks the grid's changing state, the established analysis method does not scale.

Kandivalasa and Netto build a graph from the power system model, using only which variables depend on which, and derive a numerical method that runs in linear time in the graph's size. It is, they note, the first graph approach for dynamic rather than static estimation. They test both decentralised and centralised settings. Against the established method in a centralised case, their approach cut computation time by a factor of about one thousand four hundred forty.
arxiv-2510-26901:
Barry T Chiang, Frank C van den Bosch, and Hsi-Yu Schive set universal rules for when simulated dark matter subhalos can be trusted. Subhalos and satellite galaxies in cosmological simulations suffer overmerging: weak resolution makes tides strip them too fast and destroys them early. Past studies of the problem covered few orbits and assumed round, isotropic subhalos.

Chiang and his two co-authors run the first extensive suite on anisotropic subhalos across resolutions and orbits. They report a universal criterion: a subhalo's tidal radius must always span at least twenty cells, or twenty softening lengths, for its evolution to converge. They also give a universal formula for the scatter from discreteness noise. By their estimate, as many as half of all subhalos in leading simulations may be unresolved in force or mass, and they advocate adaptive refinement tied to the tidal radius.
arxiv-2510-27001:
Elise Wolf tackles a quiet problem in bandit research, where an algorithm repeatedly picks among options to learn which pays best. Comparing such methods fairly is hard because results swing with test conditions. Variance-aware versions, which watch how spread out rewards are, look strong in some settings and weak in others, yet few studies use shared, repeatable setups.

Wolf offers a reproducible framework that tests eight classical and variance-aware methods side by side. Scores cover reward, regret, reward spread, value at risk, and how often the best option is chosen, all through an interactive tool. Variance-aware methods win when uncertainty is high and options differ subtly, while classical methods match or beat them when options separate clearly.
arxiv-2511-00001:
Paul Immanuel's thesis explores incarnations of the Fourier transform in algebraic and arithmetic geometry. A central topic is Banach-Colmez spaces, introduced through the theory of perfectoid spaces. The motivation builds from the l-adic Fourier transform and a related transform for perfect unipotent group schemes, following toward recent research.

The endpoint is the 2021 work of Anschutz and Le Bras on a Fourier transform for Banach-Colmez spaces. Graduate readers get a guided path from classical transforms to the p-adic frontier. Fourier ideas recur across geometry because they exchange local and global information, and this thesis traces that theme into modern perfectoid theory.
arxiv-2511-00301:
Ciaran Bench and nine co-authors compare ways for medical AI to say how unsure it is. Their test bed is photoplethysmography, the light-based pulse signal from wearables, used here to detect atrial fibrillation and to estimate blood pressure. A wrong but confident answer outside a clinic could harm a patient, so honest uncertainty matters as much as accuracy.

The team implements eight uncertainty methods, an unusually broad set, and scores them with a careful evaluation plan. No single method wins everywhere: the best choice depends on the task, the uncertainty measure, and the scale of reliability checked. Checking local calibration, patient by patient, revealed behavior that global scores missed. Evaluation, they argue, should match the model's real clinical use.
arxiv-2511-00401:
Mohammad Shirzadi, Emilio Cruciani, and Ahad Zehmakan survey opinion dynamics, the study of how opinions evolve as people interact. The topic matters for politics and marketing, but it is studied in scattered pieces across computer science, mathematics, social science, and physics, often with no shared language. Their overview reviews the well-known models inside one unified framework and sorts them into classes by their properties.

Key findings are organized in three parts. First come convergence properties: whether a model ends in consensus or polarization, and how long it takes. Next comes viral marketing, with its main algorithmic and complexity results. Last, node traits such as stubbornness, activeness, and neutrality are shown to shape how opinions diffuse. The survey aims to spur cross-disciplinary work on a shared foundation.
arxiv-2511-00501:
Nihan Acar-Denizli and Pedro Delicado model the curves from continuous glucose monitors, devices that track blood sugar over time in daily life and clinical trials. Each person yields repeated curves, and the shape of those curves carries health information. After rescaling each curve to a standard interval, the authors model it with a Beta distribution whose two parameters drift with time.

Their local linear likelihood smoothing handles both time-varying parameters at once, extending earlier local methods that managed only one. The approach needs far fewer observations than previous functional methods and can work with a single individual. Tests on synthetic data and a large clinical trial dataset show competitive fit and speed against spline-based rivals. Theory for estimation and for cross-validation error estimates completes the package.
arxiv-2511-00601:
Hokuto Konno, Jianfeng Lin, Anubhav Mukherjee, and Juan Muñoz-Echániz constrain the topology of Lefschetz fibrations whose fibers are four-dimensional, using Seiberg-Witten theory. Their tool is the family Bauer-Furuta invariant, computed by analyzing the framed bordism class of one-dimensional Seiberg-Witten moduli spaces through the Bismut-Freed local index theorem. The payoff lands in the mapping class groups of four-manifolds.

New obstructions show certain compositions of Dehn twists on special spheres cannot be smoothly deformed to the identity. Two firsts follow. Some closed, simply connected symplectic four-manifolds admit Torelli symplectomorphisms that are smoothly nontrivial, answering a question of Donaldson negatively: squared Dehn-Seidel twists do not generate the symplectic Torelli group. And irreducible four-manifolds, symplectic and not, admit exotic diffeomorphisms built from Seifert-fibered Dehn twists.
arxiv-2511-00701:
M Mustamin and M Demirci use dark matter detectors to bound a trait of neutrinos. Sterile neutrinos, proposed partners that barely interact, could arise when plain neutrinos scatter off electrons through a transition magnetic moment, a so-called dipole portal. Direct detection setups built to catch dark matter also record low-energy recoils, and solar neutrinos leave exactly such signals in them.

Using data from PandaX-4T and XENONnT, the authors model the up-scattering of solar neutrinos into sterile states. They derive robust exclusion limits on transition magnetic moments, both flavor-blind and flavor-dependent, for fixed sterile masses and across the mass-coupling plane. Because these detectors see solar neutrino events, they can probe all neutrino flavors at once, and the limits extend into new ground.
arxiv-2511-00801:
Zhihui Chen and colleagues present Med-Banana, a framework for editing medical images from text instructions. Good edits must add the requested feature while keeping anatomy, image style, and clinical sense intact. Earlier data sets kept only edits that succeeded, and threw the failures away.

Med-Banana instead learns from both. Its resource, Med-Banana-80K, stores success and failure editing paths with candidate images, checks, rejection reasons, and revised prompts. Three parts are trained together: an editor, a verifier, and a refiner, so new edits can be checked and fixed in a loop. Tests with model judges, blinded experts, and other probes show steady gains over open medical image editors.
arxiv-2511-00901:
Vincenzo De Martino and colleagues ask how the people who build machine learning systems handle sustainability on the job. Sustainability here spans environmental, social, and economic concerns, not just carbon emissions, and earlier research offered mostly high level principles with little evidence from practice.

The team interviewed eight seasoned machine learning engineers, then surveyed more than two hundred more of them. They asked how engineers define sustainability, what practices they use to support it, and what blocks adoption. The central finding is a gap: awareness of sustainability is widespread, but planned implementation is rare. The authors call for clearer guidelines, ways to measure progress, and regulatory support to close that gap.
arxiv-2511-01001:
Johansell Villalobos and colleagues test whether a GPU based shallow water solver runs well across very different supercomputers. The solver, SERGHEI-SWE, models water flow for hydrology, where climate change is driving demand for finer, faster simulations. It is built on the Kokkos framework, which promises code that ports between hardware vendors.

They run it on four leading machines with AMD, NVIDIA, and Intel accelerators, scaling to more than a thousand GPUs. Speedup and efficiency stay strong, and a roofline analysis shows memory bandwidth as the main bottleneck. Portability scores with tuned problem sizes reach under seventy percent, and the authors point to finer kernel control, through Kokkos teams and device specific settings, as the route to improvement.
arxiv-2511-01101:
Marek Strong and Andreas Vlachos introduce TSVer, a benchmark for checking factual claims against time series evidence. Fact checking often turns on temporal and numerical data, such as trends in official statistics, but existing data sets lack structured evidence, give thin justifications, or invent synthetic claims.

TSVer holds just over three hundred real world claims gathered from forty one fact checking organizations, matched against a curated database of four hundred time series from varied domains. Each claim is annotated with the relevant time frames, a verdict, and justifications showing how the evidence supports it, with strong agreement between annotators. Even a leading reasoning model scores modestly on verdicts and worse on justifications, showing how hard time series reasoning remains.
arxiv-2511-01501:
Yufeng Jin and six colleagues address a robot's basic uncertainty: from one camera view, where exactly is the object it wants to grab? Occlusions and symmetry often leave several poses that fit the image, yet most neural networks answer with a single confident guess. Their system, SE(3)-PoseFlow, instead estimates a whole distribution of possible six-dimensional poses.

The method uses flow matching on the manifold of rigid-body motions to sample likely poses, so downstream software can reason about doubt instead of ignoring it. It reaches state-of-the-art scores on the Real275, YCB-V, and LM-O benchmarks. The authors also show the samples helping real manipulation tasks, such as choosing a better viewpoint or planning a grasp that accounts for uncertainty.
arxiv-2511-01601:
Soheyla Feyzbakhsh and Aliaksandra Novik work at the meeting point of algebraic geometry and stability theory. Their stage is a smooth projective curve of positive genus, and their objects are coherent systems on it, bundles equipped with extra linear data, gathered into a bounded derived category.

Bridgeland stability conditions are a way of declaring which objects in such a category count as stable, organized into a geometric space called the stability manifold. The authors describe an open region of that manifold for coherent systems on the curve. Their main finding is that the stability manifold is sensitive enough to detect the curve's Brill-Noether theory, the classical study of what special divisors and bundles the curve carries. The result ties a modern homological tool back to concrete curve geometry.
arxiv-2511-01701:
Mirco Mannucci asks what kind of map should guide a tree search through a puzzle. Earlier work fed Monte Carlo tree search with features of the puzzle grid itself. Those features came from the grid's Laplacian spectrum. They gave no benefit. Mannucci's diagnosis is blunt: grid topology is the same for every instance. It cannot tell easy puzzles from hard ones.

His fix is to measure the topology of the solution space instead. The method finds pattern rules on its own. It then builds a compatibility graph. Its nodes are cell-color pairs, linked when the two can coexist. Features such as algebraic connectivity and rigidity vary with how hard a puzzle is. Fed into node choice, they guide the search. Tests that remove one piece at a time show connectivity is the strongest signal.
arxiv-2511-02101:
Arjun Rao, Marc Rußwurm, Konstantin Klemmer, and Esther Rolf measure how much information is packed into learned representations of the Earth. Geographic implicit neural representations turn simple longitude and latitude inputs into rich embeddings trained on satellite, image, or text data. The team asks how many degrees of freedom those embeddings actually use, a quantity called intrinsic dimension, regardless of how large the embedding space is.

For models with embedding sizes between 256 and 512, intrinsic dimensions landed roughly between two and ten, shifting with spatial resolution and the kinds of input data used in training. The measure tracked performance on downstream tasks and exposed spatial artefacts. The authors offer it as a label-free tool for evaluating and comparing Earth representation models.
arxiv-2511-02201:
F. F. Nascimento, V. B. Bezerra, J. M. Toledo, P. H. Morais, and J. C. Rocha derive exact solutions that generalise the Bardeen black hole, a regular black hole model without a central singularity. Their construction layers several physical ingredients onto the basic solution at once: electric charge, a cosmological constant, a surrounding quintessence field, and a cloud of strings threading the spacetime.

The most general member of the family combines all of these sources around the charged Bardeen core. The authors then discuss the Kretschmann scalar, which measures how strong the spacetime curvature is, and trace how it depends on the parameter attached to each source. The paper closes by analysing the geodesics, the paths available to particles and light, through the corresponding effective potential.
arxiv-2511-02301:
Kuan-Cheng Chen, Samuel Yen-Chi Chen, Chen-Yu Liu, and Kin Leung combine quantum computing with federated learning to watch for faults in industrial sensor networks. Factories generate high-dimensional time series from many machines, and spotting faults matters. The data cannot simply be pooled for privacy, scale, and bandwidth reasons. Classical federated learning keeps data local, yet it can miss the curved decision boundaries that separate normal operation from rare faults.

Their framework runs quantum feature maps on edge nodes, which compute compressed kernel summaries from their local data on quantum circuits. Only those summaries go to a central server, which assembles a global kernel matrix and trains the decision function. On synthetic industrial benchmarks the method generalised better than classical federated baselines at capturing complex time patterns, while notably reducing the communication overhead.
arxiv-2511-02501:
Mohan Liyanage, Eldiyar Zhantileuov, Ali Kadhum Idrees, and Rolf Schuster predict network delay for edge computing without pinging the network. Offloading tasks from a device to a nearby edge server only works in real time if the end-to-end latency is known in advance. The usual way to learn it, active probing, is itself intrusive. Their lightweight scheme instead builds a rational model, a ratio of polynomials, from passive features: frame size, arrival rate, and link utilisation.

Across extensive experiments with five-fold cross-validation, the model reached state-of-the-art prediction accuracy, reporting a mean absolute error of 0.0115 and an R-squared of 0.9847, while keeping inference fast. The authors frame the result as a strong trade-off between precision and efficiency against both traditional regression methods and neural networks, suitable for latency-sensitive edge applications that cannot afford heavyweight predictors.
arxiv-2511-02601:
Dakota Murray, Chaoqun Ni, Weiye Gu, and Trevor Hubbard study a small task with outsized influence on how scientists navigate the literature: naming clusters of papers. Bibliometric software groups documents into topics, and the old way of labelling a cluster, gluing together its most distinctive terms, produces terse, cryptic names. Generative language models can write fluent, human-like labels instead, and databases have adopted them quickly, ahead of any careful study of what makes such a label good.

The authors separate two label types, characteristic labels and descriptive labels, and give descriptive labelling a formal definition with its design decisions spelled out. They propose a structured generation workflow for bibliometric practice and an evaluation framework for judging the outputs. In their tests, model-written descriptive labels performed at or near the level of characteristic labels, and the paper closes with design guidance for using them responsibly.
arxiv-2511-02801:
L. Manchon, M. Deal, J. Marques, and Y. Lebreton describe Cesam2k20, the newest version of a code that simulates how stars evolve. The CESAM line began with P. Morel and co-workers and was refined over three decades. It was picked to compute the first grid of star models for the PLATO space mission, and is now public.

The 2025 paper reviews the code's numerical style, in which structure values are built from piecewise polynomials on a B-spline basis. It walks through the options for each physical process. Fresh strength lies in how the code moves chemical elements and angular momentum inside a star, shown with standard and non-standard solar models. Companion tools handle star oscillations, optimization, and Python access.
arxiv-2511-02901:
Zahar Sayapin, Daniil Rabinovich, Nikita Korolev, and Kirill Lakhmanskiy present a cheaper way to clean up results from noisy quantum computers. Their method, CLP-ZNE, extends zero-noise extrapolation, a trick that estimates the noiseless answer by watching how results degrade with added noise. The twist is to use the fact that gate errors vary across a chip's layout.

By cycling a circuit through different layouts and averaging, the method extrapolates to zero noise with far fewer layouts than older permutation schemes need. For twelve-qubit circuits modeled on IBM's Torino machine, typical errors in expected values fell by a factor of ten, beating standard unitary folding. The tests included both depolarizing noise and relaxation effects drawn from real hardware data.
arxiv-2511-03001:
Minseok Kang and five colleagues built LEGO, a benchmark that grades how faithfully a generated 3D scene follows a text description. A prompt like apples on the table hides many fine constraints: which objects, in what arrangement, in what manner. Older scores check only rough similarity or skip spatial checks entirely. Their 2025 benchmark pairs each description with human-written constraints and a reference scene.

The companion scorer, LEGO-Eval, splits a description into atomic constraints and checks each one with tools that locate objects in the scene and reason about their layout. It caught misalignments far more accurately than older metrics. Current scene generators did poorly: the best reached at most a 10 percent success rate, showing how far text-to-3D still is from following instructions closely.
arxiv-2511-03101: Shoumin Liu, Zhaohuan Peng, and Xumin Wang study faithful representations of Coxeter groups. These groups form a broad family of symmetry groups. The family includes the dihedral groups of regular polygons. Their 2025 paper analyzes those representations for the dihedral case. It then proves a clean identification result: a Coxeter group is fully determined by the proper joint spectrum of its faithful representations. In other words, that shared spectral fingerprint carries enough information to recover the group itself. The result is a rigidity statement in representation theory.
arxiv-2511-03401:
Kunrui Cao and co-authors analyze a wireless system where movable pinching antennas also deliver power to devices. Pinching antennas slide along a waveguide to build strong direct links and cut path loss. Powering devices from the same setup could free sensors from batteries in hard spots.

Exact formulas are derived for outage chance and average rate, covering both lossy real waveguides and ideal lossless ones. Guidance on where to place waveguides and users follows from those formulas. Heavier absorption in the guide hurts performance, as the analysis quantifies. The study weighs whether pinching designs keep their edge once energy harvesting joins communication duties.
arxiv-2511-03501:
Siyao Li examines how oscillons, long-lived lumps of a vibrating field, fall apart when coupled to a second field. Earlier work found decay through parametric resonance with a four-way coupling. Li asks whether a simpler three-way coupling shows the same behavior, testing how general the decay route is.

Growth rates for the second field are computed under the lump's steady pulsing, mapping which bands blow up for which couplings and shapes. Full simulations then watch the pair evolve. Resonance can stall before the lump dies, leaving a smaller lump that fades only slowly through plain radiation. Partial decay by resonance thus looks like a generic fate, not a quirk of one coupling choice.
arxiv-2511-03801:
Silvia P Nunes and three co-authors ask what happens to white dwarfs, the dense final stage of most stars, if dark matter collects inside them. Nunes, Jose D V Arbanil, Juan M Z Pretel, and Sergio B Duarte build a new equation of state that treats hot dense plasma and cold dark matter together.

The plasma part adds thermal and radiative effects, while the dark matter part is modeled as a simple fluid with a coupling set inside the star. A smooth mixing rule joins the two regimes. Adding dark matter raised the model radius by about twelve percent and total mass slightly. White dwarfs, the authors suggest, could serve as indirect probes of dark matter.
arxiv-2511-04001:
J Nathan Kutz is the lead author among fifteen authors arguing that machine learning for science needs a common task framework, a shared set of challenge datasets with agreed objectives. Learning methods now forecast, reconstruct, generalize, and control dynamic systems across engineering, physics, and biology, yet diverse goals and noisy, limited data make fair comparison hard.

Shared benchmarks helped speech, language, and vision advance quickly, and the authors want the same discipline for science and engineering. Their framework gathers datasets spanning practical objectives under limited-data and noisy conditions. Objective metrics would let users compare the many algorithms now appearing in practice and see which methods truly advance each scientific task.
arxiv-2511-04201:
Matteo Mio, writing alone, introduces compact quantitative equational theories, where every result of a theory can be derived by a finite proof. Such theories reason about distances and near equality, a setting used for chance-based and metric semantics, and compactness is the finiteness trait that makes such reasoning workable.

The theory of interpolative barycentric, or convex, quantitative algebras due to Mardare and co-authors is proved compact. That central example then yields other compact theories of convex algebras, each fixing some distance on finitely supported probability distributions. Convex combinations sit beneath mixture and averaging operations across semantics, so a compact axiom set has wide formal use.
arxiv-2511-04401:
Subeen Park and four colleagues address a quiet failure mode in deep learning. Models often lean on spurious cues, links that work in training but break for rare groups. Their method, called SCER, reshapes the learned features to cut that reliance.

The team proves that worst-group error depends on how much the classifier uses spurious traits. Their training rule then directly limits that use inside the embedding space. The goal is steady accuracy even for the group the model serves worst. The work matters for real deployments, where the rare group is often the one most in need of a correct answer.
arxiv-2511-04501:
Antonin Boisneault and three colleagues study spurious resonances in coupled FEM-BEM methods. Such couplings solve sound scattering from an obstacle in a mixed medium. Finite elements handle the varied inner zone, while boundary elements cover the open outer zone.

The team focuses on their newer formulation, called the Generalized Optimized Schwarz Method. Classical couplings can fail at certain wavenumbers even when the physical problem is sound. Those wavenumbers act like fake resonances inside the math alone. Pinpointing and removing them keeps large acoustic simulations trustworthy, which matters for noise control and sonar design alike.
arxiv-2511-04601:
Yicheng Xiao leads eight authors with PixCLIP, a method for fine-grained vision-language understanding. CLIP links images and text well at a broad level, but fine detail alignment lags. Most fixes add visual prompts that steer focus to chosen regions.

PixCLIP instead trains with pixel-level alignment at any chosen granularity. Long, detailed captions help, yet CLIP's text encoder has a strict token limit that blocks them. The authors work around that cap so detailed text can guide local image features. Sharper alignment should help tasks like grounding a phrase to the exact part of a picture.
arxiv-2511-05101:
Yu Mao and Mohamed Saïdi use Hoshi's mono-anabelian reconstruction to rebuild a number field from group data alone. Anabelian geometry asks how much of a field or curve is fixed by its Galois group, a group that tracks field symmetries.

Their result rebuilds both a field and its largest extension unramified outside a set of primes, for a density-one set of primes. The input is just a profinite group tied to that extension. Such pure group rules show how tight the bond is between a field and its symmetries at all.
arxiv-2511-05301:
Arthur Satouf and co-authors present QueStER, a method that turns a user query into a clear keyword search plan for a standard retriever. Generative retrieval stores relevance inside a model and can be brittle off its home domain, and costly to scale.

QueStER trains a light language model to write out the keyword query, which then runs on BM25, a classic search method. That mix keeps the broad skill of generated queries with the cheap, open run of classic search. Tests check how the bridge fares against both parent styles.
arxiv-2511-05401:
Alexandr Kostochka and co-authors settle the Turán number for four disjoint copies of a complete graph. The Turán number is the most edges a graph on a set count of vertices can have while it avoids a given pattern as a subgraph.

Here the banned pattern is four vertex-disjoint cliques, each of size at least three. Using ideas from the Hajnal-Szemerédi theorem plus a discharging count, they give the exact value for all sizes. Exact Turán values are prized since they close a counting task fully, with no gap between bound and build.
arxiv-2511-05601:
Cheng-Rong Xie, Hiroki Tsuchiura, and Manfred Sigrist study a superconducting device that lets current flow more easily one way than the other. Their setup joins two parallel chains of a special superconductor in a ladder shape. No magnetic field or spin-orbit coupling is used, so the one-way effect comes from geometry alone.

A phase gap between the two legs breaks time-reversal symmetry, and the lack of leg-exchange symmetry skews the current-phase relation. Splitting transport into two channels shows why: one channel is shifted by the leg phase while the other is not. Their interference, plus a channel tied to Majorana modes, yields a strong diode response that peaks at middle coupling strength.
arxiv-2511-05801:
Yue Fang and Geert Ridder work out the exact uncertainty of a treatment-effect estimate in trials where whole clusters, not individuals, are randomized. In such finite populations the exact variance of the standard estimator depends on outcomes nobody can observe, so it cannot be pinned down directly. Their study uses a common two-stage design: sample clusters, then sample units inside them.

First they derive the exact design-based variance, counting cluster sampling, unit sampling, and random assignment together. Then they extend earlier work to give a sharp upper bound on that variance, plus an estimator of the bound from observed data alone. In simulations and a real application, intervals from the bound stayed valid and were usually tighter than standard cluster errors.
arxiv-2511-06201:
Rodrigo Gallardo, Oz Fishman, and Alexander Htet Kyaw built a design assistant that suggests small changes to public spaces. The human-in-the-loop system uses generative tools to propose street-level interventions and invite more local participation in planning. It treats everyday patterns of objects in a place as evidence for what belongs there.

Object detection runs on a curated portion of the ADE20K dataset as a stand-in for real streets. Patterns of which objects appear together become embeddings, and a chosen anchor object earns five likely companions. A vision-language model then reasons over the scene and suggests a third object to complete the idea, while people keep control of choices and refinements.
arxiv-2511-06301:
Azzanzi Jiomekong and co-authors release Secu-Table, a dataset for testing how well systems interpret the meaning of security tables. Semantic table interpretation links table cells to knowledge graph entries, and progress depends on good test data. The security field lacked a public dataset of this kind until now.

Secu-Table holds more than fifteen hundred tables and over fifteen thousand entities drawn from public vulnerability and weakness databases. Entries were annotated with Wikidata and a cybersecurity knowledge graph, and all construction code is public. The dataset supports a shared challenge on table-to-graph matching, and the authors report baseline scores from two open language models and one closed model.
arxiv-2511-06501:
Antu Saha, Mehedi Sun, and Oscar Chaparro automate the hunt for solution talk inside software issue discussions. When a bug is debated, the thread mixes proposals, code changes, and evaluations, and finding the solution-bearing parts by hand is slow. Reopened bugs, regressions, and code reviews all depend on locating that content quickly.
