Maithri K and three co-authors study key traits of items in finite fields, and of the rules that make them. A finite field is a set with a fixed count of items, yet with full add and times rules. An item can be prime like, in that its powers span the set. It can be normal, in that its shifts span the set as a base.

Traits set for items can be set for rules too. Order for a rule tells how its roots act. The team proves traits of rules that are part prime or part normal. A reader in field work gets new links in a zoo of such items, used in codes and crypto.
arxiv-2601-09301:
Geng Liu and Masahito Hayashi give a check tool for a loop method in quantum facts work. The method, called QAB, builds up a best guess step by step with no slope sums. It is strong, but its past proofs rest on needs that are hard to test for a real task. A user may run it with no proof that it will settle true in their case.

Their frame checks a run past the fact. Give it the steps the run took, and it tells if those steps prove a near best end. That turns a hope into a check. A reader who runs QAB gets a seal they can test, case by case, not a broad claim.
arxiv-2601-09401:
G. Piccinini and five co-authors show how to weigh distant companions that orbit other stars. Their 2026 arXiv paper joins radial velocity data with astrometry from the Hipparcos and Gaia missions. Radial velocity surveys find long-period companions by watching a star wobble over many years.

A wobble alone gives only a lower bound on the companion's mass. Adding proper motion anomalies, small shifts in how the star moves across the sky, pins down the orbit's tilt. With the tilt known, the true mass follows. The method sharpens the line between giant planets and brown dwarfs in long-period systems.
arxiv-2601-09501:
Yubo Yuan, Ziye Zhu, Jiaming Hu, and Wenbin Li compute how charge carriers move in a promising layered semiconductor. Their 2026 arXiv paper is an ab initio study of carrier mobility in Bi2O2Se. The material is known for strong performance and good stability.

Experiments have mapped transport in this material across many doping levels, for both electron and hole conduction. A full theory of those results has lagged behind. The authors build that theory from first principles, with no fitted parameters. Knowing what limits mobility points to ways of making faster, cooler devices from the material.
arxiv-2601-09601:
Emmanuele Barberi, Felice Sfravara, and Filippo Cucinotta align pairs of 3D point clouds with a focus on the scoring metric. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents a method called IDEM, for iterative differential entropy minimization. Point cloud registration, lining up two scans of the same scene, is a core task in computer vision.

Common methods judge alignment by Euclidean distances and minimize scores such as root mean square error. The choice of metric shapes how robust the fit is to noise and outliers. IDEM instead works with differential entropy as its guide. A better metric could steady registration for scanning, robotics, and inspection tasks.
arxiv-2601-09701:
Fahimeh Orvati Nia, Shima Salehi, and Joshua Peeples test a hybrid network for spotting odd electricity use. Their 2026 arXiv paper evaluates a GAN-LSTM model for smart meter anomaly detection. Smart meters stream fine-grained consumption data that can improve monitoring and decisions in power systems.

Spotting anomalies in that stream is hard: usage is nonlinear, nonstationary, and varies across buildings and conditions. A GAN learns what normal use looks like while an LSTM tracks its rhythm over time. The authors judge how well the pairing works in practice. Reliable anomaly flags help utilities catch faults, theft, and failing equipment early.
arxiv-2601-09901:
Joshua Perlmutter works on a shape test for groups built from graphs. In curved spaces, paths that stay near the best route have a local to global trait. Short near best bits join into long near best paths. The Morse form of this trait fits a wider set of spaces.

Perlmutter shows that graph products keep this trait. If each part group has it, the joined group has it too. His proof grows a key max step from past work on ranked groups. The groups at hand have clean bins that make the step work. The result adds a firm case to the map of these traits.
arxiv-2601-10201:
Jiarui Yao, Ruida Wang, and Tong Zhang reward each step of a model's thought, not just the end. Most past work grades the full chain at the end. That gives a weak guide for where a chain went wrong. Step grades can guide more, but past plans were slow.

Some step plans need tree search or a whole new grade model. The team made Process Reward Learning, a leaner path. It learns step grades in the train run itself. The aim is a model that reasons more well. It should also reach past its old bounds, not just match them.
arxiv-2601-10601:
Reiko Liu and Wen-Jie Ma work in celestial holography, a program that recasts gravity in flat space as a theory on the sky at infinity. Soft current algebras are known to capture the low-energy, infrared side of scattering there. But no algebra had described the finite-energy side. The authors set out to close that gap.

They uncover an infinite-dimensional hard current algebra that encodes finite-energy scattering. It implies new Ward identities, rules that any scattering result must obey. The soft algebras turn out to arise from the hard ones, not to stand apart. The work gives the holography program a single frame that covers both soft and hard physics.
arxiv-2601-10701:
Chun Hei Michael Shiu and Chih Wei Ling design a federated learning scheme that saves bandwidth and bends to privacy needs. Federated learning lets many parties train one model together without pooling raw data. That fits rules that keep data in place. Two pain points remain: the cost of constant messages, and the level of privacy each party demands.

The authors propose a mechanism that is both communication-efficient and privacy-adaptable. They back it with a convergence analysis, a proof that the training still settles to a good model. Such proofs matter when methods leave the lab. The work targets hospitals, banks, and other groups that must learn together while keeping data home.
arxiv-2601-10901:
Honglian Wang, Sijing Tu, Lutz Oettershagen, and Aristides Gionis study streaming submodular maximization with on-demand requests. The setting mirrors news recommendation sites. Users can arrive at any time. At each visit, the site must show up to k news items, chosen from a stream it cannot store whole. Picks must be diverse yet relevant, the hallmark of submodular goals.

The on-demand twist breaks the usual one-pass setup: queries come when users come, not when the stream ends. Algorithms must keep a compact summary ready at all times. The work formalizes this problem and its trade-offs. It serves platform designers who must answer instantly from endless content with bounded memory.
arxiv-2601-11201:
Jan Rosenzweig writes on finance data in this 2026 preprint. Price series move on more than one clock at once. Fast swings mix with slow drifts in the same stream. He sets out a way to split those layers apart in a clean way.

His test for the split uses two traits of the data. One is how spread out the moves are. The other is how the tails of moves behave over time. He frames both tests as eigenvalue problems, a standard math form. The split finds slow parts and fast parts in returns and prices. Tests use exchange rates, stock funds, and bond yields to show its use.
arxiv-2601-11301:
A local tool for video segmentation is the subject of this 2026 preprint. The authors are not named in the record held here. The tool is called SAMannot and builds on SAM2. It lets users mark objects in video by interaction.

Workflows for fine video masks face a three-way bind today. Hand curation is slow and eats skilled time. Paid platforms cost much and hold the data. Cloud tools raise privacy risks for raw footage. SAMannot runs on the user's own machine, fully local. It is open-source and built to use memory with care. Research teams keep their video private and their costs down. That mix serves labs that mask much video by hand.
arxiv-2601-11501:
Frederik Walter, Maria Abu-Sini, Nils Weinhardt, and Antonia Wachter-Zeh code data for torn DNA. Their 2026 preprint treats DNA decay as a torn paper channel. DNA can store data for the long term in archives. Strands decay over time, and codes must survive that decay.

The channel model has two stages of damage in sequence. First, noise flips bits by substitution at random. Then the strand breaks into unordered, noisy substrings. Coders get a bag of torn scraps, like a ripped page. Schemes must rebuild the message from those scraps alone. The team designs coding schemes for that double damage. Sound codes are a must for DNA archives to work.
arxiv-2601-11601:
Daniil Bargman, Francesca Medda, and Akash Sedai Sharma rebuild the Phillips curve. Their 2026 preprint adds latent variables to the classic model. The Phillips curve links inflation to slack in the economy. Its use for medium-term inflation forecasts is re-examined here.

The team tests a latent variable Phillips curve hypothesis. They generate 3,968 random factor combinations for the test. US core PCE inflation is the data in scope. The window runs from early 1983 to early 2025. Latent models beat traditional ones six to eight quarters out. They also stand a better chance against a univariate benchmark. Hidden factors may carry the curve's lost signal.
arxiv-2601-11701:
Abhinav Chakraborty, Yuetian Luo, and Rina Foygel Barber weigh stability against accuracy. Their 2026 preprint deals with trade-offs in statistical estimation. Algorithmic stability measures how outputs react to data changes. Small changes in training data should not swing results wildly.

Stability is central to learning theory for good reason. It shapes generalization to new data from a sample. It also shapes robustness and replicability of findings. Many notions of stability have been proposed over time. Each fits a different learning setting in the literature. The team studies the trade-off with estimation accuracy. A stabler method may pay for calm with bias. Knowing that price helps statisticians choose wisely.
arxiv-2601-11801:
Nitish Sontakke, K. Niranjan Kumar, and Sehoon Ha build a tool that designs robots with the help of vision language models. Robot design is slow work by hand. A design must meet user needs, move in the right way, and look right, all at once.

Most past tools are rule based and need a set grammar of parts. Their tool, named RobotDesignGPT in the work, uses a model that reads both text and images. Such a tool could let non-experts sketch a robot brief and get a first design fast. Human skill would then refine the result.
arxiv-2601-12301:
Mingrui Liu, Sixiao Zhang, and Cheng Long improve sequential recommendation, which predicts a user's next pick from past acts. Most systems give each item one embedding vector. Models then merge those vectors into a sequence trait for user intent.

One vector per item can hide its many facets. Their facet-aware multi-head mixture model gives items a richer form. Text-enhanced pre-training adds item sense from words. Richer items could yield picks that fit user taste with more nuance.  Facet traits may also help cold start items a lot.  One trait per item is the weak point the new model aims to fix.
arxiv-2601-12601:
Metin Can Aydemir and Muhammet Boran improve a result in analytic number theory about a divisor function. The function d3 counts ways to write a number as a product of three factors. They study how its values spread across prime arithmetic progressions on average. The key yardstick is the exponent of distribution, a measure of how far the average stays well behaved.

Their title claims an improved exponent for this function. A higher exponent means the good average holds for larger moduli. Results of this type feed sieve methods, a core engine for prime number results. Even small gains in an exponent can unlock new theorems downstream. The work states its claims in the uniform form that sieve users need.
arxiv-2601-12801: Pranali Roy Chowdhury and four co authors, based largely at the University of Alberta, study how pollutants change fish. Their focus is pigmentation, the color patterns on fish bodies. They also track spatial patterns, how fish arrange and move in their habitat. Pigment shifts can signal stress or harm from contamination in the water.
arxiv-2601-13001:
Wenrui Yu, Jaron Skovsted Gundersen, and Richard Heusdens ask when shared sums can stay private. Their focus is on systems where many nodes each hold data and a joint result must be found. They study the case where the joint step is not a plain sum but a curved, nonlinear rule.

For plain sums, good tools can often hold back leaks well. For curved rules, the authors argue, the shape of the rule itself sets hard caps. Those caps bind even when the joint result must be exact. They seek the best such caps that pure theory allows. The work maps what privacy can and cannot promise in this setting.
arxiv-2601-13501:
Youness Diouane models how a mass shooter's fate sways the fate of the next such shooter in the United States. The team uses data from 1966 to 2024. Each case is tagged by if the actor died at the scene or lived past the act.

Their tool is a bivariate Hawkes process. Such a process lets each past event lift the rate of like events to come. With two fates as two streams, the model can say if a death at the scene lifts the odds the next actor dies too. Such a fate to fate spread, if real, bears on press guides and threat work. The model gives that ask a firm form.
arxiv-2601-13601:
Zhiwen Zhou and co-authors report lab work on tiny paired states of charge in thin films in 2026. These pairs, called indirect excitons, form in a stack of two crystal sheets, molybdenum selenide and tungsten selenide. The team placed the stack in strong magnetic fields, up to eight tesla. They tracked how the pairs move across the stack.

The group found that the pairs can travel long ranges in these fields. They also found long-range spin flow carried by the pairs. Spin is a small magnetic trait of each pair. Such results matter for new devices that move spin, not just charge, to carry signals.
arxiv-2601-13701:
Frédéric Marin and a large team report new polarization data on the active galaxy MCG-05-23-16 in 2026. They used the IXPE space telescope for its third look at this object. They also took optical spectro-polarimetry with the Very Large Telescope. Older data in ultraviolet, optical, and near-infrared light join the set.

Polarization shows how light waves align, which hints at the shape of gas near a black hole. The combined data challenge the object's Seyfert-1.9 class label. Class labels guide how teams read all data on a galaxy. A wrong label can skew years of work on its core.
arxiv-2601-14001:
Niall McGuire and Yashar Moshfeghi push brain-based search a step further with heard text in 2026. Forming a query from an internal need is hard in all search paradigms. Cognitive complexity and physical impairments both block typing or speaking a query. Brain Passage Retrieval maps EEG signals straight to passage representations.

Their Auditory Brain Passage Retrieval adds cross-sensory EEG training. EEG records electric signals from the brain through the scalp. The path skips intermediate text translation on the way to results. Such tools could give people with severe impairments a direct line to information.
arxiv-2601-14101:
Emily Kim, Allen Wu, and Jessica Hodgins help action recognition work from new camera angles in 2026. Human action recognition has made significant progress in recent years. Generalizing to diverse viewpoints remains a challenge, though. Most datasets are captured from ground-level perspectives.

Models trained on ground views struggle to transfer to aerial views. The team uses curriculum-based strategies for efficient cross-domain action recognition. A curriculum orders training from easy to hard cases. Drones and security cameras need models that read actions from above. A step-by-step plan keeps the task cheap to run. It also lets small labs train strong models with less data than a brute-force run.
arxiv-2601-14201:
Amy de Castro and Hyesuk Lee split a coupled fluid and porous solid problem into parts in 2026. The Stokes-Biot system models fluid flow interacting with a poroelastic structure. Their partitioned method starts from the monolithic formulation of the system. Lagrange multipliers enforce the interface conditions between fluid and solid.

The monolithic system is discretized using finite elements, with convergence established. A Schur complement algorithm decouples the subproblems at each time step. An efficient preconditioner keeps the split solves fast. Decoupled solves let teams use their best fluid and solid codes side by side. Each part can be solved with the tool that fits it best. That is the main gain of the split for day-to-day use.
arxiv-2601-14801:
Natsuki Terano and eight co-authors study a supernova remnant and a gamma-ray binary in this 2026 paper. The remnant is G284.3-1.8. It shows a radio shell and thermal X-ray emission. Located near its center is the gamma-ray binary 1FGL J1018.6-5856. That central placement raises the question the paper sets out to test. Whether the two systems are physically associated is not clear yet.

The team ran X-ray spectroscopy with the Suzaku satellite. Their abstract states that the spectra reveal a link between the remnant and the binary, though the abstract shown here ends before the full finding is stated. Readers get an X-ray test of whether a dead star's shell and a gamma-ray pair share one origin.
arxiv-2601-15001:
Rainer Backofen and Axel Voigt study a mix of two fluids, one active and one passive. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with phase separation, where the mix splits into regions of each fluid. The pattern that forms is mostly a two-way web, called bicontinuous.

The authors run two-dimensional simulations of the mix. The web that forms is not symmetric in shape or in how it links up. They show that flows the active region makes on its own can explain the full skew. No outside force is needed to break the symmetry.
arxiv-2601-15101:
Patrick Navez, Valentina Di Meo, and a large team study a network of superconducting qubits in a shared resonator. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with these qubit networks as a device for quantum work. The resonator that holds them loses very little energy.

That setup can show collective quantum dynamics at a large scale. It can also sharpen detectors of microwave photons a great deal. The paper treats Bose condensation in the network, where many qubits act as one. It also treats Bogoliubov excitation, the sound-like ripples of that shared state.
arxiv-2601-15301:
Jivnesh Sandhan, Harshit Jaiswal, Fei Cheng, and Yugo Murawaki ask whether AI text detectors can be trusted. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the tools meant to spot machine-written text. Demand for them has grown with the rapid spread of language models.

Yet detectors often fail outside tidy benchmarks. The authors evaluate the two dominant paradigms: training-free methods and supervised ones. Both prove brittle under distribution shift. New generators and even simple style changes can fool them. The sobering results warn against leaning too hard on these brittle detector scores in court or class.
arxiv-2601-15401:
Sajjad Akherati and Xinmiao Zhang extend a basic operation of encrypted computing. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with homomorphic encryption, a tool that lets math run on locked data. The data stays sealed while the sums are done. This serves machine learning, medical tests, and finance, where raw data must stay private and safe.

In popular schemes, ciphertext multiplication is defined for two inputs only. Many applications need to multiply several inputs at once. The authors tackle multi-input ciphertext multiplication. Their work aims to make that wider product a native operation, so programs that run on locked data need fewer clumsy workarounds in the end.
arxiv-2601-15601:
Amita Malik and Rishabh Sarma extend a line of partition theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. Partitions write a number as a sum of parts. Recent work by Andrews and Bachraoui studied partitions whose smallest part repeats exactly k times. The remaining parts in those partitions are distinct. Generating functions for them turned out to be linear combinations of q-Pochhammer symbols. Polynomial coefficients in q complete those formulas.

Malik and Sarma move the idea to overpartitions. In an overpartition, the first copy of a part may be overlined. Their focus is partitions with a repeated smallest non-overlined part. Such extensions test whether neat formulas survive richer counting rules. Partition theory thrives on this pattern. A small twist in the rules often yields deep new identities.
arxiv-2601-16201:
A maths note sets out broad Bassian modules over a class of prime rings. The 2026 preprint deals with rings of the Dedekind type that are not prime in the plain sense. A module counts as broad Bassian by a test with maps in. If a map sends the module in to a part of it, a split must hold. That split means the left part is a clean part of the whole.

The note asks which modules pass that test on such rings. Tests of this kind sort modules by how they split. Clean splits ease work with sums of modules. The work sits in pure ring and module theory. It builds on the known Bassian case with a wider test.
arxiv-2601-16701:
Przemysław Berk and Łukasz Kotlewski study how paths in a math system come back or drift off. Their systems swap chunks of a line in a set dance. A weight rule then bends each step's path. Some such rules make paths come back oft. Others make paths fade and not return. Their 2026 preprint proves a split of this sort.

For a broad class of weights, the paths tend to fade. The weight blows up near the ends of the line. That blow-up drives the drift in most cases. Sharp proofs of this sort test our grip on wild systems. They also feed work on flows, waves, and chance walks.
arxiv-2601-16801:
Ben Groom and a large team of co-authors bring wild life loss into state budgets. Species keep dying off due to human acts. Yet state spend plans oft price that loss at nil. Their 2026 preprint sets out a way to price it fair. The way starts from goals a state sets for wild life.

Costs to hit those goals then set the price tag. This flips the usual path, which asks what folks would pay. Goal-based prices can slot into real spend checks. That slot may save funds for woods, seas, and fields. It also makes loss in kind show up in pounds.
arxiv-2601-17101:
Xiaodong Jiang races a beam of paired hydrogen ions in big rings. The beam holds H2+ ions, each a pair bound as one. A past run pushed such a beam in a small ring. That run reached a set speed with clear success. His 2026 preprint asks if the big RHIC ring can push it far more. The goal is one hundred GeV per unit.

The ask is time-pressed, since RHIC nears shut-down. A yes would open rare tests with such beams. A no would spare teams a vain push. Paired-ion beams act unlike lone proton beams in rings. Firm calls here guide the ring's last runs.
arxiv-2601-17401:
Dušan Dragutinović studies links between number sequences and partitions. He looks at final types, certain non-decreasing integer sequences. Each such sequence pairs with partitions in a natural way. From that link, he proves an identity for n-nacci numbers. Those numbers extend the Fibonacci rule to longer sums. The identity writes them as sums of products of binomial coefficients.

The sums run over the partitions tied to final types. The result extends a classical identity to the full family. Such identities help counters check formulas in two ways at once. They also show hidden order in fast-growing sequences. Pure counters gain a new bridge between sequences and splits.
arxiv-2601-17601:
Fangping Lan, Abdullah Aljebreen, and Eduard Dragut study why people post links on social media. Links bridge platforms and the wider web. On Twitter, now X, about one in five tweets holds at least one URL. That rate shows how central links are to information flow. The authors build an intent taxonomy for link sharing.

Knowing intent helps sort news, ads, spam, and self-promotion. Platforms can rank and moderate with more care. Researchers can track how claims spread across sites. A taxonomy turns a mass of links into named motives. That clarity aids studies of influence and misinformation. It also helps users read their own feeds with sharper eyes.
arxiv-2601-17801:
Hongfu Zhang and Hui Tang test whether quantum methods can help control the flow of fluids. Their 2026 preprint joins quantum machine learning with reinforcement learning. Flow control is hard because fluid motion is both high in dimension and strongly nonlinear. Small inputs can have large and hard-to-guess effects. Classical methods strain under that load.

Quantum computing has shown an edge over classical computing on some tasks. The authors build on that hope and train a quantum reinforcement learning setup for flow control. In such a setup, an agent learns by trial and reward which actions calm or steer the flow. The study adds a new data point on where quantum tools may pay off.
arxiv-2601-18001:
Aqsa Yousaf, Sint Sint Win, Megan Coffee, and Habeeb Olufowobi build an explainable tool for finding parasites in blood samples. Their 2026 preprint presents MorphXAI. Parasitic infections remain a heavy health burden, above all in low-resource settings. Diagnosis there leans on slow hand checks of blood smears by scarce experts. Deep learning can spot parasites well, but doctors cannot use a tool they cannot interrogate.

MorphXAI adds morphological analysis, the study of the parasite's shape and form, to the detection. Explanations tied to shape features are ones a clinician can judge. That makes the tool's calls easier to trust and to challenge. The work aims at labs where expert time is the scarcest resource.
arxiv-2601-18901:
Christopher Kissling, Elena Merdjanovska, and Alan Akbik ask if a language model knows when its own facts are firm and when they are frail. Tests of fact stock in such models grade how oft the model's first call is right. That grade skips a key trait: does the model put high trust on its right calls and low trust on its wrong ones? A model that can't tell is a risk in use, since users lean on its tone of trust.

The team grade both the calls and the trust that rides with them. They use fact pairs of the form this links to that, a clean test of stored facts. A model that knows its own gaps could flag the facts it should not be asked to state. Such self-ware tools could make fact use safer in search and in school.
arxiv-2601-19001:
Haozheng Luo and six co-authors speed up the long reasoning chains of language models. Models that think step by step often wander down paths that add words but not value. The team calls the stray steps reasoning outliers and aims to prune them with a method named FROST.

FROST reads the model's own attention weights to spot which paths count and which do not. Cutting the weak paths leaves shorter chains that the authors find more reliable as well. Shorter, cleaner reasoning saves compute and may cut the slips that long chains invite along the way.
arxiv-2601-20201:
Sherry H. F. Yan works on permutation statistics, a classic topic in enumerative combinatorics that counts patterns in arrangements. In her study of the genus zeta function, Denert found a new Mahonian statistic for permutations, later called Denert's statistic by Foata and Zeilberger. Mahonian statistics are those that share the same count distribution as inversions.

The paper gives further refinements of Euler-Mahonian statistics for multipermutations, where entries may repeat. Refined counts track several statistics at once and still match known distributions. Such results deepen the map of how permutation patterns behave, a theory with links to sorting, probability, and algebra.
arxiv-2601-20601:
Zhuonan Wang and seven colleagues present CLEAR-Mamba, a method for classifying eye angiography across multiple image sequences. Medical image classification supports early detection, treatment planning, and prognosis. In eye care, fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography reveal blood flow and lesion structure that plain fundus photos cannot capture.

Using several sequences at once is harder: the scans arrive in series and must be read together. CLEAR-Mamba aims at accuracy, adaptability, and trustworthiness in that setting. In real clinics, the two scan types are often read side by side. A tool that reads them as one case fits that habit well. Reliable classification of retinal scans could speed up diagnosis of diseases that threaten sight.
arxiv-2601-21101:
Shaheda Begum Shaik and five co-authors measure how fast a comet's tail regrows after solar storms tear it off. Their 2026 paper studies comet C/2023 P1, called Nishimura. The Solar Orbiter imager watched the comet in September 2023. In that window, the comet's ion tail shifted without pause. It suffered four tail disconnection events. Each matched the passage of a coronal mass ejection.

A disconnection event severs the ion tail from the comet's head. The tail then regrows as the solar wind reshapes it. This is the first quantitative study of that regrowth. Timing it measures how comet plasma couples to the solar wind. Such events turn comets into free probes of solar storms. The paper gives space weather science a clean, counted case.
arxiv-2601-21401:
Ferdinand Buchner, David Jobst, Annette Möller, and Claudia Czado improve forecasts of wind as a full vector. Weather services run ensembles to capture forecast uncertainty. Those raw forecasts still carry steady biases and spread errors, so statistical fixes are applied afterward.

Wind has two linked parts, speed in each compass direction, and the parts must be fixed together. New methods build the link between the parts into the model itself. A joint fix gives forecasters honest odds for both direction and strength at once. That matters for aviation, shipping, and wind power, where the pair decides the risk.
arxiv-2601-21601:
Hoyeon Chang, Bálint Mucsányi, and Seong Joon Oh test whether gradient updates keep a network's logic coherent. Networks learn by small first-order steps in their parameters. It is often assumed that a small local step spreads sensibly to all its logical consequences.

The authors name that premise the linear propagation assumption and probe its limits. Using relation algebra, they track three basic operations: negation, converse, and composition of relations. The study shows where the premise breaks down as changes propagate. Knowing those limits helps explain odd failures where a model learns a fact but misses its obvious flip side.
arxiv-2601-21801:
Jing Yang, Satoya Imai, and Luca Pezzè address a central open problem in quantum sensing. When several unknown values must be measured at once, theory gives a best possible precision, called the multiparameter quantum Cramér-Rao bound. The hard question is when that bound can actually be reached with realistic single-copy measurements.

The authors establish an equivalence. The bound can be saturated exactly under one condition. A set of traceless operators tied to the model must be made hollow at the same time. Their 2026 preprint turns a vague feasibility question into a concrete geometric test. Quantum sensors that measure several fields at once, from magnetometers to imaging devices, stand to benefit from knowing when perfection is even possible.
arxiv-2601-22201:
Gabriela Juncosa and co-authors test the wisdom of crowds in content moderation. Platforms facing misinformation have adopted community-based systems: Community Notes on X, Footnotes on TikTok, and community features on Facebook. The hope is that collective intelligence beats any single moderator or algorithm.

The team's 2026 preprint finds that benefit limited by overt political factors. When content is politically charged, the crowd's judgment bends with the politics of the raters and readers. That finding matters for platform design today: community moderation still helps. But its limits need engineering around, not wishful thinking, especially during elections and crises when accuracy carries the highest stakes.
arxiv-2601-22701:
Emilien Biré, María Santos, and Kai Yuan rank a vision-language agent's next moves with a learned value score. Such agents run web and system tasks on their own. Their 2026 preprint notes that the base models adapt poorly to fast-changing screens, and retraining for each shift is dear.

Best-of-Q scores each candidate act at run time and picks the best, with no new training. A good ranker can rescue a weak base model. It can also cut wasted clicks in live tasks. The work is a light add-on with a clear job. It steers at the moment of choice.
arxiv-2601-22801:
Ömer Veysel Çağatan and three co-authors propose a new way to train large language models with rewards. The standard methods clip, or cap, each update to keep training stable. At large scale, clipping can stall learning, invite reward hacking, and make training shaky.

Their method, CFPO, drops clipping and uses a smooth penalty based on total variation distance instead. The penalty has no hard edges, so updates stay stable but never fully flat. They test it on reasoning and alignment tasks, two core uses of reward-based training.
arxiv-2601-23001:
Afrozah Nadeem and three co-authors measure political bias in language models across many languages. These models shape public discussion worldwide, so fairness and neutrality matter. Earlier work focused mostly on rich, Western languages, leaving cross-language consistency and safe fixes little studied.

The study both evaluates ideology in multilingual models and tests ways to steer it after training. A model that leans one way in English and another way elsewhere is hard to govern. Shared measures and gentle steering tools help builders keep global systems even-handed. Cross-lingual consistency is a central test, since a fair system should not change its leanings when the language changes.
arxiv-2601-23101:
Therese Biedl and Dinis Vitorino answer a question about order among bipartite graphs. A bipartite minor relation ranks these two-sided graphs in a way akin to the classic minor relation. Chudnovsky and co-authors had asked whether that ranking is a well-order, with no endless descending chains.

The answer is no: the authors give an endless family of highly connected bipartite graphs, none comparable to another. A negative answer closes one path in graph structure theory. It also shows bipartite minors behave quite differently from ordinary minors. The counterexample family is two-connected throughout, so the failure of well-ordering cannot be blamed on fragile, barely linked graphs.
arxiv-2601-23201:
Darshan Thaker and four co-authors sharpen medical images with scale-cascaded diffusion models. Diffusion models act as strong priors for inverse problems like super-resolution, which rebuilds fine detail from coarse scans. Standard approaches train the prior at a single scale, ignoring the layered scale structure of images.

Their cascade uses several scales in sequence, so coarse anatomy guides finer detail. That ordering matches how medical images are actually structured. Sharper scans from lower-dose or faster acquisitions would help patients and clinics alike. Hierarchical scale structure is the untapped signal, since anatomy organizes itself from whole organs down to fine tissue.
arxiv-2603-01601:
Large 3D models can build a scene from one image, but they sometimes invent odd holes or bumps. Xiwen Wang, Shichao Zhang, Ruowei Wang, and colleagues name and fight those flaws in this 2026 work. Fake parts hurt most when a model is printed or placed in a virtual scene.

The flaws often start when sparse views with wide gaps guide the rebuild. Their tool, Dehallu3D, forces smooth shifts across many close views while it guards sharp real edges. Two rules do the work: one keeps nearby views in geometric agreement, and one adapts smoothing to spare fine detail. A new score counts outlier risk, so gains can be measured, not just seen. Tests show cleaner meshes that keep true detail while stray parts vanish.
arxiv-2603-01901:
Hannah Selder, Charlotte Beylier, Nico Scherf, and Arthur Fleig test whether brightness tricks fake users in interface simulations. Their 2026 study trains simulated users with reinforcement learning on pointing and tracking tasks. If scores hinge on rendering artifacts, the simulation says little about real design quality.

The team trains hundreds of simulated users while varying luminance of targets, distractors, and background. Settings include no distractors, still distractors, and moving distractors around the task. With still distractors, luminance becomes decisive and both performance and robustness drop sharply. Motion cues soften that effect, which points to dynamics as a buffer against brightness bias. Robustness also tracks the ordering between luminance levels more than their exact values, a subtle rule for fair simulation design.
arxiv-2603-02001:
Johannes Wehrstein, Timo Eckmann, Matthias Jasny, and Carsten Binnig synthesize a database engine fitted to one fixed workload. Their 2026 work argues that general analytical engines pay for their flexibility in overhead. Runtime schema reading, indirection layers, and abstraction walls persist even in highly tuned systems.

A bespoke engine can drop those costs and use data structures shaped to the actual queries. Hand-building one was never worth the effort, but language-model code synthesis changes that math. Naive prompting fails, so their pipeline adds performance feedback, structured refinement, and validation loops. The autonomous system builds an engine from storage to query execution in minutes to hours. Order-of-magnitude speedups over a modern general engine show what workload-specific synthesis can win.
arxiv-2603-02101:
Anna Geisler, Mihyun Kang, Michail Sarantis, and Ronen Wdowinski study random sampling from a physics model in this 2026 paper. The model assigns weights to sets of graph points, with sets that contain many edges weighing less. They focus on split graphs where every node has the same number of links. Such graphs also spread out well, in a sense called expansion.

A standard random walk sampler turns out to mix far too slowly here. Across wide settings, it can take huge time to give a fair sample. The authors give a fast sampler built on cluster methods instead. Their method also estimates the model's total weight to high accuracy. The contrast shows sampler choice can matter more than the model itself.
arxiv-2603-02201:
Kilian Sandholzer, Ian Berkman, Peter Deák, and colleagues review single-photon sources in silicon in this 2026 paper. Single photons can carry quantum data over long distances. Solid chunks of matter that emit them one by one are handy and can be mass-produced. Add a spin, and the source can also store quantum states.

Silicon stands out for its fine chip making and very pure makeup. That purity lets spins hold their state for a long time. The review covers color centers and erbium atoms placed in tiny silicon light guides. It sums up what works now and what blocks coherent sources at scale. Such sources could anchor quantum networks and spread-out quantum computers.
arxiv-2603-02301:
J Kunc, B Morzhuk, V Stará, and colleagues study light-absorbing molecules layered on graphene in this 2026 paper. Clean interfaces are vital for devices that copy quantum behavior, yet factory steps often dirty them. The team presents a building protocol that restores graphene's atomic purity to vacuum-lab levels. Diffraction and microscopy checks confirm the clean surface.

On that surface, a molecular layer shows wide, coherent light effects. Its crystal symmetry splits one key light transition into bright and dark branches. Several light and vibration probes map the split pattern in detail. A fitted model quantifies coupling and energy terms behind the split. The dark branch dominates light emission, they find. The platform could support studies of dark states and molecular quantum memories.
arxiv-2603-02501:
Donggyu Kim, Rose McCarty, and Caleb McFarland answer a labeling question about graph trails in this 2026 mathematics paper. Edges carry labels from a group, and labels can be inverted along the way. An Eulerian trail uses every edge exactly once. The authors ask when every such trail between two fixed points earns the same total label.

Their answer is structural and precise. Each highly connected part of the graph must be labeled over a very specific group. That group is a power of the two-element group, for some exponent. They also show the decision problem reduces in fast time to the group's word problem. That link ties a graph question to a classic algebra computation.
arxiv-2603-02601:
Varun Pratap Bhardwaj argues that AI agents need a new kind of software testing, and his 2026 report AgentAssay supplies one. Agents built on large language models can act differently on each run, even with the same prompt and tools. Normal tests assume fixed outputs and simple pass or fail marks, so they miss real regressions.

AgentAssay replaces fixed verdicts with chance-based outcomes backed by confidence ranges and staged checks. It adds coverage measures for tools and choices, fault-injection tests, and gates for release pipelines. Trials across five models and three agent setups cut testing cost sharply while keeping the same statistical strength. Recorded traces also allow free re-checks of past runs.
arxiv-2603-03201:
Simone Betteti, Giacomo Baggio, and Sandro Zampieri build a mathematical theory of how associative memories move from one stored pattern to the next. Hopfield networks are classic models of memory that settle into stored patterns, and their still-frame retrieval is well understood. Chained retrieval, where one memory hands off to another like steps of reasoning, lacked theory.

Working with a recent input-driven plasticity variant, they analyze a two-timescale design: fast retrieval paired with slow reasoning dynamics. Explicit conditions emerge for self-sustained transitions between memories, including gain thresholds for switching, escape times, and regimes where the chain collapses. The results connect classical memory dynamics to the sequential reasoning that modern machine learning systems increasingly display.
arxiv-2603-03301:
Dvir David Biton and Roy Friedman study semantic caching, a speed trick for large language model services. Classic caches reuse exact repeats; a semantic cache reuses answers for new requests that merely mean something close to an old one, judged by embedding vectors. Their 2026 paper asks which requests such a cache should keep when space runs out.

The authors prove that even with full hindsight, picking the perfect offline policy is computationally intractable, then offer fast heuristics that run in reasonable time. They also design live policies mixing recency, frequency, and semantic closeness. Tests on varied datasets show frequency-based rules are strong, while their new variant improves semantic accuracy further. All of the code is open source.
arxiv-2603-03601:
Aida Abiad, Anuj Dawar, and Octavio B Zapata-Fonseca bring logic to two questions about when graphs count as the same. Controllable graphs and distance-regularized graphs are usually characterized algebraically, through spectra and eigenvalues. Whether two such graphs are isomorphic, or merely share a spectrum, had never been studied through definability in first-order logic. Their 2026 paper is the first to do so, extending and unifying earlier results.

The headline result: cospectral distance-regularized graphs cannot be told apart by counting first-order logic with three variables. The same holds for the broader pseudo-distance-regularized family. Earlier theorems of this kind covered only strongly regular graphs and distance-regular graphs separately. The new work subsumes both, giving logicians and graph theorists one common frame for these equivalence questions.
arxiv-2603-03701:
Tonmoy Dey, Lin Jiang, Zheng Dong, and Guang Wang let city services trade favors instead of competing. Smart city research usually optimizes one service at a time. Their 2026 framework, UrbanHuRo, jointly optimizes two: crowdsourced delivery and urban sensing. Human couriers can gather traffic and air quality data along their routes, while sensing robots can deliver packages at peak hours, each side covering the other's weakness.

Two designs make the joint optimization tractable in real time. A distributed MapReduce module handles order dispatch through a submodular maximization scheme. A deep reinforcement learning algorithm, also built on submodular rewards, plans the sensing routes. On real data from a food delivery platform, the system raised sensing coverage by about thirty percent and courier income by about forty percent on average, while significantly cutting overdue orders.
arxiv-2603-03801:
Reece Robertson and five colleagues prepare thermal quantum states on real trapped-ion hardware and catch the machine heating its own work. Gibbs states, the equilibrium states of statistical mechanics, are prime targets for quantum simulation. Their 2026 experiment runs a variational algorithm for the transverse-field Ising model on IonQ computers, training parameters classically and reading the prepared state back by tomography.

Fidelity falls as the target gets colder and as the system grows, though not monotonically. The telling result is a mismatch of identity: a state prepared for one temperature matches better the Gibbs state of a warmer temperature. Hardware fluctuations act as digital heating, silently raising the prepared state's temperature above intent. The finding sets a practical caution for near-term thermal state preparation.
arxiv-2605-00501:
Yan Lin, Yihong Su, and Yi Yang train financial prediction models on the very score they will be judged by. That score is Rank IC, the rank correlation between a model's predictions and the asset returns that actually follow. Most models instead train on regression losses or generic ranking goals, which can pull against the target metric.

Their method, LambdaRankIC, optimizes Rank IC directly. Ranking is not differentiable, so they derive closed-form expressions for the gradients created by swapping pairs of assets, letting standard gradient training proceed inside the LambdaRank framework. They implement it as a custom objective in a popular boosting library, and prove it optimizes an upper bound on the target. In simulations it recovered true rankings and beat rivals under noisy, heavy-tailed conditions. On real market data it led on Rank IC, stability, monthly return, and Sharpe ratio.
arxiv-2605-01001:
Ludwig Sidenmark and three co-authors present AnimationDiff, a visual tool for comparing generated 3D character animations. New methods now produce many animation variants easily, but choosing the best is hard because of timing misalignment and large amounts of spatial data. Classic creation took major animator effort, and comparing now becomes the bottleneck.

The tool supports side-by-side checks in the intended scene and camera angle. It combines established display methods with easy switching between overlaid and side-by-side views. Filtering handles information overload, and Temporal Lenses display whole animations over time for overview, alignment, and comparison. A user study shows the tool helps with such checks and yields design insights for comparing motion more generally.
arxiv-2605-01301:
Qingzhao Zhang and two co-authors present a stealthy fake-data attack on shared perception for connected and self-driving vehicles. Sharing sensory data improves it, but tampered inputs create security risks. Prior attacks spoof or remove objects, yet how practical they are in dynamic real-world driving was unclear. Many are easy to spot or tested only in hand-built scenarios.

Their attack subtly manipulates poses of existing objects in shared results, staying below detection thresholds. Small errors propagate through tracking and trajectory prediction, causing significant deviations and unsafe decisions such as unnecessary hard braking. An online scenario-aware framework adapts at runtime. Experiments show high success in inducing such errors and frequent safety-critical behavior while evading defenses. A localized mitigation cuts such errors markedly.
arxiv-2605-01701:
Jiahuan Wang and four co-authors bound how well decentralized learning generalizes when the data arrive as a Markov chain rather than as independent draws. Fleets of machines now train jointly, each seeing a stream with memory. Gradient methods, including the ascent-descent pairs used for minimax problems, inherit both the chain's dependence and the network's chatter.

Working through algorithmic stability, the lens that ties generalization to how much one data point can move the outcome, they separate the fingerprints of topology, chain mixing speed, and primal-dual dynamics. Both plain decentralized descent and its minimax sibling receive non-asymptotic generalization bounds. The results extend what was known for Markov sampling in one machine to the decentralized and minimax settings at once, which is where large-scale robust and adversarial training actually lives.
arxiv-2605-02001:
Cao-Vien Phung, Thomas Röthig, and Admela Jukan analyse low Earth orbit satellite networks that mix radio links with laser links. Lasers offer high speed and low delay between satellites, but weather can block optical paths to the ground, so radio remains needed. Traffic imbalance and changing capacity make scheduling and buffer size key design choices.

With finite buffers, interference-aware scheduling, and weather-based outage chances, their results show lasers bring large gains. Raising satellite power is not the best route to top throughput. Choosing the right scheduling priority can reach the maximum instead, while using less power. The work guides how large on-board buffers should be for hybrid networks.
arxiv-2605-02301:
Junhao Wei and colleagues present SAGA, a planner for agile drone navigation in cluttered spaces that must be fast and safe. SAGA casts local planning as a joint regression and ranking task over a fixed lattice of motion anchors. From a depth image and the drone's motion state, it predicts refined end states and scores for all anchors in one forward pass, then decodes the best into a feasible trajectory.

Anchor features become geometry-aware tokens, and self-attention reasons across anchors globally. A polar positional encoding, built from anchor yaw and pitch, preserves directional structure in that token space. The design aims to weigh many feasible motions at once without a slow search, a key need for autonomous flight among obstacles.
arxiv-2605-02701:
Davide Nobile and Philipp Grohs propose a robust way to train neural networks when gradient noise has heavy tails. Standard stochastic gradient methods can be thrown off by rare, huge gradients. Clipping gradients is a common guard, but it is usually applied to a whole batch at once, which can distort the update.

Their method clips each sample's gradient separately before averaging. Theory shows optimal convergence rates in expectation for non-convex problems under heavy-tailed noise, with high-probability bounds that match up to small factors. In experiments, the method beat both momentum-based training and batch clipping on a standard image task, even after counting its extra compute time. A further finding: with gradient accumulation, clipping at the mini-batch level can help at almost no cost.
arxiv-2605-03601:
Moritz Grillo and Guido Montúfar ask when the parameters of a deep ReLU neural network are determined by the function the network computes. Two networks can represent the same function with different weights, beyond the obvious rescalings and permutations of hidden units. The authors study the realization map that sends parameters to functions.

Using weighted polyhedral complexes, they prove that for every architecture whose input and hidden layers have width at least two, there is an open set of identifiable parameters. Hence the functional dimension equals the parameter count minus the hidden neuron count. They also show minimal representations can keep nontrivial redundancies, and they establish a generic depth hierarchy against shallower networks.
arxiv-2605-04401:
Wenxian Shen studies travelling waves in a chemotaxis model. A living population moves toward or away from a chemical it produces itself. It also grows toward a cap. Such waves, connecting a fully populated state to an empty one, describe how a species invades new territory as a moving front.

Earlier work established that these waves exist for the simplest parameter case, but their uniqueness, stability, and monotone shape were little studied. Shen addresses all four properties together for a general family. It allows repulsion as well as attraction. It also allows a range of growth and response powers. The results characterise when a single, stable invasion front is the whole story.
arxiv-2605-04801:
Dieter Horns, Niklas Knop, and Mohammad Mohammadidoust estimate how much of the local dark matter density might actually be ordinary matter. That matter would take the form of interstellar objects, the comets and asteroids wandering between stars. Three such visitors have now been detected passing through the solar system, implying a large unseen galactic population.

Combining the observed arrival rate with size and density estimates gives a local mass density for these objects. The result carries large uncertainty, though. Their nuclear sizes are hard to pin down. The apparently great age of the latest visitor motivates a thick-disk distribution model. Including this baryonic component in the galactic rotation curve would lower the inferred non-baryonic dark matter density.
arxiv-2605-04901:
Zhengyi Li and eight co-authors show that a shuffling defence used in secure transformer inference is weaker than previously claimed. Secure inference should let a client learn only the final output while the server learns nothing about the input. Revealing middle activations speeds things up, but shuffling them was meant to stop clients from stealing model weights.

The authors attack the defence by aligning differently shuffled activations to one common ordering, then using them to extract weights. On Pythia and GPT-2 models the alignment errors were tiny, and for about a dollar of queries the recovered weights came very close to the true ones. The result urges caution about this efficiency shortcut.
arxiv-2605-05201:
Manish Mishra constructs a pinned version of the local Langlands correspondence for a special family of representations of reductive groups over local fields. The correspondence matches representations with parameter data, and Mishra treats depth-zero supercuspidal representations, an important building block case. Fixing a pinned splitting of the inner form removes arbitrary choices and makes the matching canonical.

A depth-zero type splits naturally into a tame toral part and a finite cuspidal part, and each is matched separately. The toral part uses the known correspondence for elliptic tori, while the finite part uses a pinned Jordan decomposition that keeps extension data for possibly disconnected quotients. Combining these pieces with a known unipotent correspondence gives the enhanced parameter and its inverse map.
arxiv-2605-05401:
Every why-question hides a contrast: why this happened, rather than something else. Britt Besch and Tobias Gerstenberg study how people pick that hidden alternative, called the foil. Participants read short stories and judged what they expected before, what seemed closest, and what they thought could have happened instead.

Foil choices were best predicted by hindsight expectations, what people find surprising after knowing the outcome. The pair also ran language models on the same task. The models' foil choices did not line up with their own stated expectations in the consistent way human choices did.
arxiv-2605-05701:
Search agents spend two currencies at once: tool calls and tokens, both capped. Zhengru Fang and co-authors study how to budget those currencies during multi-hop question answering. Better answers need not only stronger models but decisions about which search action deserves the next unit of budget, and when the evidence is enough to stop.

Their controller scores each feasible action by value of information: marginal task value per unit budget, given the current state and what remains. A second stage decides when to commit a final answer. The formulation treats inference-time spending as an explicit optimization problem.
arxiv-2605-05801:
Gossip protocols spread information through a network by pairwise exchanges, and real exchanges sometimes garble the message. Giorgio Cignarale and five co-authors study protocols that correct their own transmission errors without any central coordinator. Earlier work treated faulty protocols in temporal epistemic logics; this team proposes a dynamic epistemic logic instead.

They show how agents can detect and repair faulty messages as the protocol runs. Self-correction changes what optimal means for such protocols. The authors also compare the approach against bounded-memory and full-information variants, mapping the trade-offs between resilience, memory, and speed of convergence.
arxiv-2605-06101:
Luis Colmenarez, Áron Márton, and Markus Müller introduce syndrome resampling, a method that raises quantum error correction thresholds without new hardware. Correction works only when physical error rates sit below a code dependent threshold, which current devices struggle to reach. Their idea works purely on the measurement records, called syndromes, that decoders already collect.

Unlikely syndromes are prone to logical failure, so biasing averages toward likely syndromes lifts logical fidelity. The authors tie this resampling to a known information measure and a family of optimal thresholds. In surface code simulations, thresholds rose for both optimal and weaker decoders, and logical error rates fell by up to four orders of magnitude. Tests on existing experimental data cut logical errors by up to two orders.
arxiv-2605-06201:
Ying Gu and five co-authors propose judging multimodal models by logical consistency instead of labeled accuracy alone. Accuracy scores can reward lucky guessing, and new tasks may have no ground truth labels for validation at all. Their metric checks whether a model's answers respect cause and effect logic in both directions, on sufficient and on necessary relations.

The Vision-Language Logical Consistency Metric works on standard multiple choice visual question tests and on newer natural benchmarks, with no ground truth needed. The team evaluated eleven open source models from four families on established benchmarks. Accuracy had improved markedly in recent models, but logical consistency lagged far behind it. Further checks support the metric's validity, and the authors suggest it for model selection and answer justification on unlabeled tasks.
arxiv-2605-06301:
Violeta Calleja-Solanas and four co-authors show that higher order interactions in ecosystems can hide behind ordinary pairwise models. Ecologists increasingly treat group interactions, where several species jointly shape each other's growth, as a key part of community dynamics. The natural hope is that rich abundance time series can reveal whether such higher order effects are at work in a given system.

The authors show that higher order Lotka-Volterra dynamics can often be reproduced accurately by an effective pairwise model fitted to the same data. Higher order structure therefore cannot, in general, be inferred from time series alone. Distinct mechanisms can generate nearly identical dynamics, a problem of mechanistic identifiability that risks accurate yet misleading readings. Time series need support from other ecological information before interaction structure can be trusted.
arxiv-2605-06501:
Chuanyang Zheng and eight co-authors propose Cubit, an architecture that replaces attention's token mixing with kernel ridge regression. Attention has stayed the core mixing step in Transformers since 2017 despite many changes elsewhere. The authors show attention can be read as Nadaraya-Watson regression, which averages values by similarity between tokens.

Cubit instead uses the closed-form solution of kernel ridge regression, adding normalization through the inverse kernel matrix. A limited-range rescale keeps training stable. Experiments suggest Cubit may model long sequences better than a standard Transformer, with its advantage growing as training sequence length increases. The work argues regression choice is a real design lever.
arxiv-2605-06601:
Isaac David and Arthur Gervais ask whether a language model agent can reconstruct the security meaning of a Linux update using only binary files. Defenders and attackers both diff patched packages, yet source patches and advisories are often unavailable. Their Patch2Vuln pipeline extracts old and new binary pairs, diffs them with Ghidra tools, and ranks changed functions for an offline agent.

On twenty-five Ubuntu package pairs, the agent localized a verified security patch function in half the security cases and assigned an accepted root cause in slightly more. Failures often came before reasoning, when the differ missed the right function. All negative controls stayed classified as unknown.
arxiv-2605-06801:
Domagoj Perković, Konstantinos Vasiliou, S. A. Parameswaran, and Steven H. Simon test a claim that fractional quantum Hall edges carry a protected intrinsic electric dipole moment. Earlier work by Park and Haldane predicted a universal value, and it was widely expected to hold. The authors find flaws in the earlier numerics and compute the ground-state dipole with care, using density matrix methods called DMRG.

Across three chosen systems, the expected intrinsic value appears only for the one-third filling edge. The two-thirds edge and the border between Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian phases do not show the claimed value. Composite fermion arguments suggest hierarchy states usually lack protected dipoles, changing thinking about Hall edge energy balance and structure.
arxiv-2605-07101:
Yuyang Zhang, Haldun Balim, and Na Li improve exploration when several learning agents must cooperate. A popular decentralized method uses energy-based policies, but in practice those are replaced by simple Gaussian policies. The authors show that this simplification badly limits exploration, and the problem grows as more agents join.

Their alternative gives each agent a diffusion-based policy, which can express several distinct action styles at once. A new training method with theoretical guarantees makes online training of such policies efficient. Across particle, robotics, and strategy-game benchmarks, the approach consistently improved performance over the Gaussian-based version.
arxiv-2605-07201:
Srikar Kashyap Pulipaka describes a system built for a shared task on detecting toxic behavior in gaming chat. Messages from the game World of Tanks had to be sorted into six categories, from non-toxic to insults, harassment, threats, and extremism. Pulipaka tried encoders, instruction-tuned models with light fine-tuning, layered classifiers, and ensembles.

The best setup paired a mid-size open language model with a small, carefully calibrated share of synthetic training data. It placed fourth among thirty-five teams on the test set. Analysis also exposed a validation trap in the data: doing well on the validation split predicted poor transfer to the real test.
arxiv-2605-07301:
Shiyue Cao and five co-authors model opponents for language-model agents by separating model building from prediction. Earlier approaches tangled the two, relying on implicit context reading that adapted poorly as interactions evolved. Their SOM framework first builds a structural causal model linking an opponent's observations to its actions.

That explicit graph then guides the language model's reasoning along clear pathways when predicting the opponent's next move. Across diverse multi-agent benchmarks, SOM consistently beat leading language-model reasoning baselines. The authors present the split design as a route to more accurate, adaptable strategy in complex, changing multi-agent settings.
arxiv-2605-07701:
Fan Zhou and Tim Van de Cruys argue that classifier-free guidance, the knob controlling how strongly a diffusion model follows a prompt, should not be frozen at one value. The best setting varies by task and by stage of generation, especially for language. Treating it as a fixed hyperparameter leaves quality and controllability on the table.

They recast guidance choice as sequential decision-making and train a policy with reinforcement learning to pick the guidance scale at each generation step from the current diffusion state. On three controlled text generation tasks with discrete diffusion language models, adaptive guidance beat fixed-scale strategies on the balance between control and quality. The learned policies followed distinct, interpretable patterns for different tasks.
arxiv-2605-07801:
Markus Walker and three co-authors bring trust regions to sampling-based model predictive control, the family that includes the popular MPPI algorithm. These controllers sample candidate action sequences, score their trajectories, and update the sampling distribution, but adjusting knobs like temperature or momentum has relied on heuristics and hand tuning.

Their setup bounds each update of the proposal distribution by a set divergence limit, with an entropy floor if wanted. The adaptation values then come out of the optimization rather than a rule of thumb. Deterministic local sampling further improves speed. On two benchmark environments the trust region version converged faster and used samples better in low-sample, low-iteration regimes, exactly where sampling controllers struggle.
arxiv-2605-07901:
Charul Gupta and four co-authors film what happens when a cavitation bubble collapses next to a confined air bubble inside a blind cylindrical hole. High-speed shadowgraphy shows a neat sequence: the growing cavitation bubble drives liquid down and squeezes the air bubble, which then rebounds and fires the liquid column upward as a slug. When the slug strikes the collapsing bubble's far side, a vortex ring is born.

Sweeping two dimensionless parameters mapped three regimes, and only the first, where impact lands during collapse at low stand-off and low fill fraction, makes a ring. Two simple one-dimensional models predict the impact point and speed, and a timing parameter comparing liquid travel time to the collapse half-period separates the regimes cleanly. The ring leaves at five meters per second before breaking up.
arxiv-2605-08201:
Sparsh Tiwari, Bettina Finzel, and Gesina Schwalbe cut the labeling cost of neurosymbolic vision systems. In two-stage designs, a neural network first perceives objects and a symbolic reasoner then applies rules, which keeps the system readable. The catch is that the perception stage normally needs expensive labels for its output symbols.

The authors pair a slot-based, object-centric architecture with a variational autoencoder for self-supervision, while concept guidance on selected latent dimensions steers the slots toward human-readable meanings. The grounded predictions become symbolic background knowledge for engines such as inductive logic programming and decision trees, so reasoning tasks can be learned from far fewer hand labels.
arxiv-2605-08801:
Peter Vanya, Katarína Šimková, and Rastislav Farkaš propose a data driven way to model traffic flows for planning roads and railways without the usual survey heavy machinery. Traditional macroscopic models need costly, bias prone surveys of how people live and travel, while earlier fitting frameworks are hard to interpret and prone to overfitting. Their protocol fits models to traffic counts, which are now cheap and reliable, with explainable weights and a controlled path for adding complexity.

Demonstrations on toy and realistic cases show the approach working end to end, with suggested extensions to systems mixing cars and public transport. Infrastructure planners gain forecasts they can explain to the public whose money builds the projects.
arxiv-2605-08901:
N. Semenova, V. Semenov, and A. Bukh study traveling waves in an ensemble of excitable FitzHugh-Nagumo units, a classic nerve pulse model, coupled weakly across distance and driven by extreme outside forcing. Three forcing types are compared: regular Gaussian pulses, pulses dirtied by white noise, and heavy tailed Lévy noise with tunable shape. Periodic forcing creates synchronization tongues with orderly collective motion, sometimes multiple waves or partial synchrony alongside propagation.

Lévy noise instead crushes regularity, producing counter propagating waves that melt into random walking behavior as intensity grows. The authors classify all observed regimes and map their layout across parameter space. Excitable media research gains a guide to how extreme environments reorganize signal travel.
arxiv-2605-09201: STT-MRAM stores bits in the magnetization of tiny magnets, flipped by spin-polarized currents. Afan Terko, George Lertzman-Lepofsky, Dieter Suess, and others study magnetization alignment in these memories. The 2026 paper is device physics for the next generation of RAM.
arxiv-2605-09301: Delivery trucks with limited capacity need routes planned in one shot, not endless re-optimization. Samuel J. K. Chin and Maximilian Schiffer cluster first with neural networks, then route second, via differentiable optimization. The 2026 paper is vehicle routing learned end to end.
arxiv-2605-09401: Chimera states — networks where order and chaos coexist — are as beautiful as they are baffling. Rommel Tchinda Djeudjo, Riccardo Muolo, Thierry Njougouo, and others classify them with Fourier analysis and unsupervised learning. The 2026 paper taxonomizes the half-ordered world of coupled oscillators.
arxiv-2605-09501: Active nematics — swirling fluids of self-driven rods, like bacterial soups — go unstable in beautiful patterns. I.K. Joseph, A.J.H. Houston, K.N. Kowal, and N.J. Mottram study how an orienting field steers that instability and selects the modes. The 2026 paper is soft-matter physics on living liquid crystals.
arxiv-2605-09701: Self-driving cars must imagine what happens next — pedestrians stepping out, cars swerving, sudden stops. Yufeng Hong, Xiaotian Zhou, Yingyan Li, and others build DriveFuture: future-aware latent world models for autonomous driving. The 2026 paper gives robot drivers an imagination.
arxiv-2605-10001: Hypergraphs capture higher-order relations beyond pairwise edges; condensing them with anchor guidance and dual-level discrimination preserves structure. Fan Li, Xiaoyang Wang, Chen Chen, and Wenjie Zhang develop the method. The 2026 paper is graph learning that compresses without losing the plot.
arxiv-2605-10201: Robot manipulation that generalizes across heterogeneous object mixings — HeteroGenManip. Zhenhao Shen, Zeming Yang, Yue Chen, and others build the generalizable system. The 2026 paper is robotics for diverse objects. It handles real object mixed results with true robotic grace. Diverse objects, one graceful policy.
arxiv-2606-00001:
Lican Huang proposes treating East Asian calligraphy as performance with a written score, much like music, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Image-based representations freeze a character as a static picture and lose the timing, pressure, and movement that define the craft. The Calligraphy Writing Score Representation instead encodes each brush stroke as an ordered, executable action. Characters sit within a structured grid, and strokes carry details such as type, execution order, and brush pressure.

The framework, Shu Dao, draws on Japanese Shodo and tea ceremony practice, where ritual matters. It organizes the score at three levels: strokes, character structure, and whole-composition layout, including rhythmic dynamics. The contributions are the notation system itself, the score-mediated view of calligraphy as scored performance, and a computational foundation for studying and generating such works. The author offers it as support for human-AI co-creation in computational art and digital humanities research.
arxiv-2606-00101:
Huidong Feng and co-authors build a benchmark of AI-generated videos good enough to fool existing detectors, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Detection datasets rely on open-source generators far weaker than commercial systems, and the few pro samples often carry watermarks that give them away. Their dataset, CoCoVideo-26K, covers thirteen mainstream pro systems and pairs fake videos with matched real ones. That pairing lets analysts isolate what differs between real footage and high-fidelity synthesis.

Their detector, CoCoDetect, pairs a spatio-temporal video network with contrastive learning, which teaches representations by comparing matched and mismatched pairs. A confidence gate sends uncertain cases to a multimodal language model that reasons about physical plausibility and scene fit. Experiments on the dataset and benchmarks reached state-of-the-art results in their comparisons. The authors release code and data, aiming to reset what forged video hunting must handle at pro grade.
