Within the paper, Al Rwaily proves basic facts about the family. She checks how it behaves under common operations. She also maps its links to better-known families, such as operators that preserve length in a broad sense. The work is theoretical, with no experiments or data. Its value lies in unifying scattered results and giving later researchers a cleaner framework for operator theory.
plos-pone-0355401:
Songyining Ding and co-authors analysed safety reports for heart assist devices used in children. Children's anatomy and blood clotting differ from adults', so adult device data cannot simply be borrowed. Their 2026 study pulled a decade of reports from the United States device reporting database and compared child and adult patterns.

Child reports numbered only a few hundred, against well over a thousand adult reports, and key fields were often missing. Because of those gaps, true complication rates cannot be calculated from the database. Ding and colleagues expose regulatory blind spots and call for a dedicated children's registry with live, multi-source monitoring to catch device risks earlier.
plos-pone-0355601:
Yasser Mohammad Al-Sharo and co-authors present a federated intrusion detector for networks of medical devices that learns without gathering private data. Hospitals cannot pool patient-linked traffic, yet shared learning catches more attack types. Heavy transformer models detect well but cost too much for small devices. Their 2026 design swaps them for state-space sequence blocks with linear cost.

Traffic features are reshaped into short token sequences for the stacked blocks. Formal privacy noise is added during training, and the merging step resists sabotage by rogue participants. Explanation tools operate at several levels so analysts can audit alerts. Al-Sharo and colleagues aim to square accuracy, privacy guarantees, and robustness in one framework.
plos-pone-0356001:
Maarten Niemantsverdriet and colleagues tested a tissue preserving method that avoids formalin, the toxic chemical standard in pathology labs. Their 2026 study used pressurised carbon dioxide to embed tissues without formalin or xylene. They then checked DNA and RNA quality in samples stored for days, two years, and seven years.

DNA from the new method was in better shape than DNA from formalin-fixed tissue. RNA quality was lower in fresher and two-year samples, but similar in the oldest ones. Even so, RNA from most samples still worked for gene sequencing, the main modern test. The results support a safer embedding route that keeps tissue usable for molecular diagnosis.
plos-pone-0356201:
Wajid Ullah, Fawad Khan, and Laila Al-Essa compare symmetry methods in general relativity in a 2026 PLOS ONE paper. General relativity describes gravity as curved spacetime shaped by matter and energy. Homothetic symmetries are scaling symmetries of a spacetime, and matter collineations are symmetries of its energy-momentum tensor, the object describing matter content.

The study works through static, plane-symmetric spacetimes using three written forms of that tensor. For non-degenerate cases, meaning tensors of full rank, one form gave finite symmetry algebras of several sizes, while the mixed form consistently gave infinite-dimensional ones. Degenerate cases gave infinite results for both forms checked. The three approaches, the authors show, do not agree, so representation choice matters.
plos-pone-0356501:
Xylena Reed and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE asking whether aging leaves a permanent mark on cells that have been reprogrammed back to stem cells. DNA methylation, chemical tags on DNA, accumulates age patterns so reliably that scientists use them as aging clocks. The team took blood cells from nearly one hundred healthy adults, reprogrammed them into induced pluripotent stem cells, and compared methylation in both states.

After reprogramming, the age-related signature was largely wiped away: epigenetic clocks read the stem cells as young regardless of donor age. Each cell type also carried its own set of sites where genetic variants influenced methylation, meaning the genetic control map changes with cell state. The reset, they say, supports using donor stem cells to model disease without donor age confounding results, though such cells cannot preserve what aging did to the original tissue.
plos-pone-0356601:
Hongjuan Bai and seven colleagues scan the brains of teenagers with depression, comparing those who injure themselves with those who do not, in this 2026 study. Non-suicidal self-injury is common in this group and poorly understood at the brain level. Just over one hundred thirty adolescents, including healthy controls, lay in a scanner at rest while researchers measured spontaneous activity across brain regions.

Teenagers who self-injured showed stronger activity in a region called the left precuneus, which sits toward the back of the brain and supports self-related thought. That activity, and the region's connection to a nearby visual area, tracked closely with self-injury behavior and with the urge to escape bad feelings. Prediction checks held up well, suggesting these measures could become markers to identify at-risk teenagers and targets for more precise treatment.
plos-pone-0356801:
Alon Tomashin, Ilanit Gordon, and Sebastian Wallot studied how heart signals couple over time, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Hearts do not beat in isolation; patterns in one signal relate to patterns in another, whether within a person or between people. Two analysis tools dominate this work, and the team compared them directly.

Tomashin and his colleagues evaluated multi-dimensional recurrence analysis against cross-correlation, weighing the analytic choices each demands. Their comparison guides researchers toward the right tool for their question, and warns where choices change the answer. Subtle heart coupling is used in studies of stress, bonding, and health, so method care is not a nicety; it decides what findings can be trusted.
plos-pone-0357101:
Zhongqiu Zhang and colleagues tested whether a pharmacist-led cleanup of stroke patients' drug lists could cut waste without slowing recovery. Their 2026 study ran at a Chinese hospital. It covered 416 people with acute ischemic stroke. Care before the change was compared with care after it. The new strategy capped extra brain-related drugs and traditional Chinese medicines. Pharmacists monitored and adjusted each list.

Patients under the strategy received far fewer add-on drugs. They also spent much less on medication and hospital care overall. Their neurological recovery matched the earlier group. Harmful drug events became less common. The results make a practical case that more medicine is not better medicine after stroke. They also show that pharmacists can safely trim crowded prescriptions.
plos-pone-0357301:
Fuchao Xu, Ao Liu, Zhen Liu, and Zinan Fang published a 2026 materials study in PLOS ONE on concrete made from red mud, the caustic waste of aluminum production. The study tests its survival under sulfate attack. Sulfate-rich wetting and drying cycles crack ordinary concrete over time. They added two short fibers, a synthetic polymer fiber and basalt fiber, alone and blended, then cycled the concrete through sulfate baths and examined strength, pores, and microstructure.

Basalt fiber helped more than the polymer fiber on its own, but a specific blend of the two performed best, keeping most of the concrete's sulfate resistance after sixty cycles. Under the microscope, fibers bridged and delayed cracks, gave corrosion products room without bursting the structure, and tightened the pore network. The blend also slowed breakdown of the glue-like gel holding concrete together, pointing to a tougher use for a usually stockpiled waste.
plos-pone-0357501:
Leonie Bourauel and fellow eye surgeons compare a tiny drainage implant for glaucoma across two forms of the disease. The implant lowers eye pressure by giving fluid a new exit, and the team matched patients with the common open-angle form against patients with a flaking form that clogs drainage further. Success was judged at several pressure targets one year after surgery.

Both groups reached far lower pressure than before surgery, but the common form did better on nearly every measure. Its patients needed fewer pressure drops afterward and hit strict targets more often. The flaking form brought more complications and follow-up procedures, though none threatened sight. Bourauel and colleagues support the implant for both forms while warning clinics to watch flaking cases closer.
plos-pone-0357601:
Jinyan Zhang led a team of five authors testing plant extracts against a stubborn fungus, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Malassezia furfur, a yeast linked to dandruff and skin disease, forms biofilms that resist standard treatment. The team tested combined extracts of Angelica dahurica and Ligusticum sinense, two plants used in traditional medicine.

Zhang's group measured how well the extracts inhibit the fungus and its biofilms, and checked their safety. A natural option that works on biofilms could reduce reliance on harsh antifungal chemicals. Biofilm testing matters because microbes in biofilms can survive doses that kill them when free-floating. The study gives product developers and clinicians a careful first look at a traditional pairing.
plos-pone-0357901:
Guanyi Liu, Xuewei Li, and Rui Yang published a 2026 safety study in PLOS ONE on finding the few risk factors that matter most in railway accidents. Modern rail operations are so interconnected that traditional checklists miss how causes chain together. From more than one hundred sixty accident reports, the team extracted risk factors and their causal links, building a directed, weighted network of how one failure triggers the next.

The resulting network had the hub-heavy shape of a scale-free network, where a few nodes matter enormously. Using a combined weighting and ranking method to score node importance. They then simulated attacks that knock out key nodes in different orders. The network stayed robust, and their score identified critical nodes better than standard measures. The practical claim is targeted: fix the highest-scoring risk factors first, and accident chains lose their favorite starting points.
plos-pone-0358701:
Song Jin and three colleagues trace how institutions shape China's energy deals with neighboring countries, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their account runs in two stages: officials form choices about cooperation, and those choices then steer actual energy trade and investment. To test whether choices truly carry the influence of the formal framework, they built a Bayesian model, a statistical approach that handles tangled paths between variables while stating uncertainty honestly.

The estimates supported the chain. Policy choices carried a real share of the influence running from formal frameworks to cooperation outcomes. The indirect effect was clearly positive. The authors also ran example analyses showing how this mediation approach behaves under differing data conditions, a methods contribution in its own right. For policy analysts, the message is that formal rules matter partly by moving the choices of the people who apply them.
plos-pone-0359001: de Oliveira and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on the personal cost of devotion to teaching. Based in schools, the study followed teachers over time with number-based methods. It tracked their habits and quality of life. Teaching is often praised as a calling, yet that praise can hide strain. Long-term data can show schools where support would protect both staff and students.
plos-pone-0359101:
Wang Hang and six colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on electric power safety. When extreme weather hits, a power system must keep supply and demand in balance or risk blackouts. The authors present a fast method for judging that risk before and during severe conditions.

Their approach uses deep reinforcement learning, software that learns decisions by trial and feedback, combined with a coupled attention mechanism that weighs which signals matter. Speed is the point: operators need risk answers quickly when storms strain the grid. Grid planners in regions facing harsher weather are the natural readers of this work.
plos-pone-0359301: Afassinou and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on heavy social media use among college students. They built a math model of how too much time on these platforms may drag down study results. A model lets them test how the parts link up before real-world trials. The work speaks to schools weighing phone rules, study support, and guidance on screen habits.
plos-pone-0360301:
Ezgi Şişman and colleagues surveyed clinical nurses in Türkiye in 2026 about sexual prejudice and the factors associated with it. Nurses care for patients of every background, and prejudice from a caregiver can quietly shape the quality and kindness of that care. Their cross-sectional study measured attitudes among working clinical nurses and tested which personal and professional factors tracked with stronger prejudice.

Studies like this give nursing schools and hospitals a factual starting point for training, rather than assumptions. If factors such as education or contact with diverse patients matter, programs can be designed around them. The work adds Turkish evidence to the wider effort to make health care welcoming to lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients.
pmc-13195201:
Joshua G Sanchez leads a 2026 large database study of social disadvantage and outcomes after Bankart repair, surgery to fix shoulder instability. Whether social determinants of health disparities, coding for social disadvantage, affect recovery was unclear. Patients were drawn from a national database covering two thousand and ten to two thousand and twenty-two.

Of over one hundred and forty thousand repair patients, about three and a half percent carried the disadvantage coding. After matching, disadvantage patients had similar rates of adverse events in the first ninety days. They did, however, use more physical therapy, visit emergency departments more, and cost more overall. At two years they also had more shoulder stiffness and more repeat shoulder surgery, the analysis found.
pmc-13197301:
Sergio Cornelio-Martínez and Francisco Alejandro Lagunas-Rangel wrote a 2026 review on oxygen sensing and new brain cells. HIF-1 is a switch that turns genes on when oxygen runs low. In adult brain niches, where new nerve cells form, small oxygen shifts help decide cell fate.

Early HIF-1 action after injury can worsen stress, swelling, and cell death. Later action instead aids defense, new vessel growth, and repair. The switch steers growth and sorting of stem cells through three linked signal paths. It also raises two growth signals that feed new vessels and red cells. The review frames how timed HIF-1 control might one day aid brain repair.
pmc-13197401:
Karan L Chohan and colleagues report 2026 outcomes for antibody therapy in lymphoma that reached the brain. Lymphoma is a cancer of the immune system. When it spreads to the brain or spinal cord, results are often poor, and new antibody drugs were untested in this group since trials shut them out.

The team gathered records from six United States centers in a joint consortium. They covered adults with active brain involvement or a past history of it who got CD3xCD20 bispecific antibodies, drugs that link immune cells to cancer cells. Treatment spanned from mid 2023 to mid 2025. The report fills a data gap for a group left out of the key trials.
pmc-13197801:
Min Dou and colleagues tested stool transplants in diabetic rats in a 2026 study. Brittle diabetes means blood sugar swings that are hard to control. Moving gut microbes from healthy donors had helped patients, yet the pathway was unclear, so the team used rats with induced diabetes.

Diabetic rats that got healthy stool showed smaller sugar swings than untreated diabetic rats. Their livers stored more glycogen, a stored form of sugar, than untreated rats did. One microbe group, Bifidobacteria, fell in diabetes but rose after transplant. Math checks tied that rise to part of the gain in liver storage. Healthy stool seems to steady sugar through liver storage.
pmc-13198501:
Monica Chacon de Vicente and colleagues report a 2026 case of drug poisoning in a dog, confirmed by earwax testing. Owners sometimes give pets human painkillers, which can poison them. Standard proof can be hard when signs are vague or samples are lacking, so the team tried earwax.

Their patient was a nine-year-old mixed-breed dog hurt in an accident. The owner then gave a drug holding acetaminophen and codeine. The dog arrived drowsy, drooling, and off food, with lab signs of liver injury. A lab method found drug traces in earwax, backing the exposure claim. With fluids, an antidote, and support care, the dog recovered fully. Earwax may widen testing options.
pmc-13200401:
Noha S El Baghdady and colleagues surveyed Egyptian pharmacists on probiotics in a 2026 study. Probiotics are live microbes sold for health gains. Use stays limited in Egypt, perhaps because pharmacists, a key advice source, know too little, so the team measured knowledge, attitude, and practice.

Only eleven percent showed good knowledge, while eighty-two percent held a positive view. Just three percent reported good practice in recommending them. Younger, newer staff scored worst on knowledge and outlook. Older, seasoned ones scored best. Women held more positive views than men. Barriers included unclear medical uses and thin knowledge. Training is the clear fix, the authors say.
pmc-13202301:
A vitamin made by engineered yeast for animal feed receives a formal safety verdict in a 2026 scientific opinion. The opinion comes from the EFSA Panel on Additives and Products or Substances used in Animal Feed. It assesses riboflavin at eighty percent strength, produced with a genetically modified yeast strain, for use in all animal species.

Although the production strain carries antimicrobial resistance genes, no living cells or its DNA were detected in the finished additive. The panel concluded the product raises no safety concern for target animals, consumers, or the environment, and that it meets animals' vitamin B2 needs through feed. It should still be handled as an irritant to skin, eyes, and airways.
pmc-13204301:
Precancer can turn invasive one cell population at a time, and a 2026 study headed by Yaomei Ma charts that shift in the cervix. Using single-cell sequencing, the research article compares cervical tissue at the CINIII precancer stage with cervical squamous cell carcinoma, tracking epithelial cells and their surrounding microenvironment.

The team found Sox2 signaling marking cervical cancer stem cells in the transformed tissue. Vessel-lining cells tied to cancer switched on genes including VWF, MMP2, and HTRA1, while fibroblasts converted toward a muscle-like myofibroblast state. Macrophages also grew more numerous, and the authors propose these changes as targets for non-surgical treatments that preserve fertility.
pmc-13211601:
Mental health apps sit unused when the phone itself is the barrier, and a 2026 study headed by Julie Lutz designs coaching for older veterans in that spot. The research article combines interviews with twelve older veterans about app interest and obstacles, then builds and pilots a support program from what they said.

Most veterans wanted to use the health system's mental health apps, but unfamiliarity with devices, awkward app design, fading motivation, and memory lapses got in the way. Their preferences shaped MoDAL, a two-session remote coaching program teaching device and app skills interactively. Thirteen veterans piloted it, and the team judged acceptability and feasibility while watching proficiency signals.
pmc-13212901:
Artur V. Trifonov and colleagues report in 2026 delicate quantum effects inside perovskite nanocrystals cooled to near absolute zero. Light-driven states in these crystals couple strongly to lattice vibrations, forming hybrid states called exciton-polarons.

Using pairs of laser pulses, the team watched rhythmic quantum beats between those hybrid states in crystals embedded in glass. Coherence lasted unusually long, while the beats faded over times set by vibration lifetimes. A four-level model let them measure coupling strengths for two low-energy vibration types. Both coupling and lifetimes depended strongly on crystal size, offering a tuning knob for future quantum light technologies.
pmc-13213601:
Ibrahim Ababtain and colleagues describe in 2026 the staged rebuilding of a young man's shoulder after a gunshot destroyed much of his upper arm bone and rotator cuff. Replacing the joint alone cannot restore length or rotation when so much bone is gone.

After wound cleaning and targeted antibiotics, the team first stabilised the arm with a rod and spacer. Twenty-one months after injury they fitted a reverse shoulder replacement joined to a donor bone segment, plated in place. A tendon from the back was transferred using the donor tissue's own attachments as an anchor. Two years on, the graft had fully incorporated and function had meaningfully improved.
pmc-13215501:
Qiuyu Li and co-authors report a 2026 longitudinal study of university students in southern China, testing whether computational thinking supports artificial intelligence literacy. Both skills are treated as core competencies for study and work in an AI-rich setting.

The authors tracked 216 undergraduates at two points in time and modelled the relationship with structural equation methods, alongside paired tests of change. Computational thinking had a significant positive effect on AI literacy, and both abilities improved over the study period. Their connection stayed stable across the two waves. The authors offer the results as a basis for course design that builds the two skills together.
pmc-13216101:
Carlos Noriega and co-authors present a 2026 study of acidification in two Amazonian city lakes that supply drinking water to Belém, Brazil. Tropical lakes acidify mostly through biology rather than acid rain, so pH alone can mislead managers.

Monthly sampling from September 2023 to August 2024 tracked 21 measures at the surface and bottom of Lakes Água Preta and Bolonha. An acidification sensitivity index stayed negative all year in both lakes, signalling thin alkaline reserves. Dry-season stress was driven by carbon dioxide build-up and oxygen loss at depth, while wet-season rain diluted alkalinity to critical levels. The authors recommend season-specific management rather than one year-round plan.
pmc-13216601:
Patrick Kraus and co-authors present a 2026 mouse study asking whether the anti-ageing protein Klotho, made locally in the brain's dentate gyrus, is required to keep producing new neurons there. Adding Klotho from outside boosts this neurogenesis, but the local supply's role was untested.

Deleting the Klotho gene only in dentate granule cells caused a temporary dip in immature neurons during a narrow window after their birth, roughly days seven to seventeen. Stem cell division, however, was untouched, and long-term survival of the new neurons was normal. The authors conclude that local Klotho fine-tunes early maturation but is not essential for building or keeping the adult-born neuron population.
pmc-13221501:
Ruizhe Ren, Xiao Liang, and Xiyang Wei review fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction, in a 2026 synthesis of causes and new treatments. The condition, now called MASLD, is the world's most common chronic liver disorder. It can advance to cirrhosis and liver cancer while raising heart and diabetes risk.

Three areas receive integrated coverage: disease mechanisms such as fat toxicity and mitochondrial failure, non-invasive diagnostic tools, and drugs targeting key pathways. One approved drug serves only a subset of patients with advanced scarring. By weighing late-stage trial successes against instructive failures, the review shows why turning mechanism knowledge into treatments that help patients remains hard.
pmc-13222001:
Hamad Yasin and co-authors audit inflammatory bowel disease care at a tertiary hospital in Islamabad, Pakistan, in a 2026 records study from 2019 to 2024. Records for 167 adults, mostly with ulcerative colitis, were checked against United Kingdom NICE guidelines. Drug use, surgery, diagnoses, and other conditions were taken from electronic files.

Steroids reached just over half of patients, while biologic drugs went to under one in eleven. Eighteen percent had surgery. Only a small share of the NICE recommendations was fully followed for either disease type. Diabetes and hypertension were common as well. The authors call for treatment protocols matched to local resources and stronger clinician training.
pmc-13222401:
Amy Beumer and colleagues run a patient-led survey on antibody-drug conjugate dosing in metastatic breast cancer, in a 2026 study of 170 patients who had received these targeted chemotherapy carriers. Side effects from the drugs can be severe, and dose cuts may ease them, yet patient experience with dosing was little known. Respondents described starting doses, changes, and barriers to supportive care.

Most began at the recommended dose and schedule. About one third later had dose reductions, mainly for experienced or feared side effects. Oncologists led side-effect management for most participants, though over two fifths reported money barriers to supportive care. The authors press for patient-centered dosing strategies.
pmc-13222601:
Isabel Ros González and colleagues describe nerve pain syndromes of the trigeminal nerve's end branches over fifteen years in a headache unit, in a 2026 retrospective series. Registry records from 2008 to 2023 covered 8,728 evaluated patients. Classification systems bury these branch neuralgias inside broader categories, leaving their frequency poorly mapped.

One hundred eight patients, about one in eighty, met the criteria, and two thirds were women. Average onset came in the late forties, while diagnosis trailed onset by nearly three years on average. Supraorbital neuralgia was commonest, followed by auriculotemporal. The authors argue that recognizing the pain's exact territory guides targeted peripheral treatment.
pmc-13223701:
Zhichao Lin and co-authors name the compounds behind the honey and sweet potato aroma of Wuyi black tea, in a 2026 flavor science study. This Fujian tea is prized for its warm, sweet scent, yet its active odor compounds were unmapped. Advanced 2D gas chromatography listed the volatiles, and aroma mixing tests checked which ones matter.

Nineteen key aroma-active compounds emerged. Five did the central work: 2-amylfuran, alpha-ionone, beta-cyclocitral, beta-damascenone, and benzeneacetaldehyde. Computer docking showed these molecules binding smell receptors through hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts, and simulations confirmed stable fits. Knowing the aroma's chemical core supports quality standards and process tuning for this regional specialty.
pmc-13230401:
Madiha Ajmal and colleagues model in 2026 how an electric field moves a blood-based nanofluid carrying swimming microbes through a hair-lined channel. The fluid holds graphene oxide particles and follows a model for blood that thins under shear. Tiny hairs on the channel wall help push fluid along, a setup linked to drug delivery devices.

Equations were solved with computer software using a collocation method. Raising one heat-related number lifted temperatures, and more particles improved heat spread while lowering microbe density. Faster microbe transport followed a higher Peclet number, which gauges flow against diffusion. Other settings made the self-steering microbes cluster more. Tuning electric forcing and wall motion could help control heat and cell placement in small devices.
pmc-13232601:
Martin Pursley and colleagues lay out in 2026 a plan to map digital health tools that serve pain patients and clinicians at once. Chronic pain touches about one adult in five worldwide, and guided self-management is a standard recommendation. Tools facing both sides of the clinic door may support that work better than patient-only apps.

Their scoping review will search six databases for studies since 2010 and chart system features, user groups, and guiding frameworks. Early screening already narrowed more than a thousand records to nineteen included studies. Signs point to patchy use of theory and weak links between the patient and clinician sides. Findings are meant to steer the design of stronger shared tools.
pmc-13235001:
Paniskaki and colleagues compare patterns of natural autoantibodies in adults whose bodies age unusually slowly. These antibodies bind the body's own G protein-coupled receptors, a huge family of cell-surface switches. Such antibodies normally rise with age, and some are tied to chronic inflammation and autoimmune disease in adults.

Adults with slowed biological aging, the team finds, carry antibody patterns that mirror those of children instead. That likeness hints that a youthful antibody profile may be part of what slowed aging looks like in the blood. The work adds a fresh marker to the study of healthy aging, and a clue to how inflammation and age may be uncoupled.
pmc-13240901:
Muhumuza and colleagues examined how climate stress, livelihoods, and gender collide in Uganda's Rukiga district. Gender-based violence surfaced repeatedly in fieldwork meant to study something else. The team ran twenty-eight focus groups and forty interviews with key informants. Narratives were coded thematically for violence pathways.

Two driver clusters stood out. Poverty, male drinking, and shifting gender roles destabilized households as women took on provider duties. Droughts, floods, and soil erosion then deepened economic strain and conflict. The authors call for climate and livelihood programs that also confront unequal gender norms.
pmc-13241301:
Cui and colleagues in Shijiazhuang tracked infants treated with noninvasive molding for misshapen ears over the long term. One hundred two cases from 2017 to 2022 were studied in hindsight. Deformities included prominent ear, cup ear, cryptotia, and lop ear. Every child was tracked for more than three years.

About eighty-five percent of corrections succeeded overall. Results did not differ meaningfully between deformity types. Starting within the first week of life predicted the best results, as did finishing within four weeks. One baby's eczema paused treatment briefly, the only notable complication recorded.
pmc-13241501:
Würfel's team at Munich asked whether CT and MRI contrast scans tell the same tumor story. Human studies favor CT; mouse studies favor MRI, muddying cross-species reads. A gene-edited pancreatic cancer mouse model had both scans. Laser mass spec later mapped the contrast agents inside cut tissue.

Both scans split sparse from densely packed tumor regions with excellent clarity. Local values tracked strongly across the two scans. Iodine and gadolinium stores tracked each other closely. Würfel holds the two scans swap freely as reads of tumor cell density in this mouse model. The finding eases cross-study reads.
pmc-13242501:
María Iñiguez and colleagues compared daily habits and diet in people with preclinical Alzheimer's disease and healthy peers. Their case-control study appeared in the European Journal of Nutrition in 2026. Fifty patients and forty-eight controls, aged fifty-five to seventy-five, reported activity, social and mental engagement, and eating patterns. The team also measured polyphenol breakdown products in urine as an objective check on plant food intake.

Diets richer in vegetables and nuts and lighter in processed foods tracked with better cognitive scores, echoing the MIND diet pattern. The advantage grew stronger in people who also kept up mentally stimulating activities. Urine markers, including compounds from berries and tea-like flavanols, rose with reported plant food intake, confirming the questionnaires. The authors suggest pairing plant-rich eating with cognitive activity to support resilience. They also offer the urine panel as a sharper tool for diet research.
pmc-13243301:
Mahadevaswamy M and Dean Fido wrote a letter questioning how a Hindi version of a grief questionnaire was validated. The letter appeared in the Indian Journal of Psychological Medicine in 2026. The study under discussion, by Mewani and colleagues, translated the PG-13-R prolonged grief scale for Hindi-speaking adults in the United States. The letter writers welcome the aim of closing language gaps but press on method.

They note the work used a single translator whose selection criteria were never documented, though guidance calls for two to four bilingual translators who know the subject. The back translation was done by a co-investigator, where best practice asks for someone blind to the original scale. Statistical gaps drew concern as well. Their recommendations include confirmatory factor analysis, measurement checks across gender and culture, and test-retest reliability. The goal, they stress, is a tool clinicians can trust in this community.
pmc-13245801:
Alak surveyed Turkish adults about how they view and interact with autistic people, in this 2026 PLOS One study. An online questionnaire reached five hundred seven adults, most of whom knew autistic individuals only indirectly. The survey measured what people knew about autism, what personal experience they had, and how comfortable they felt interacting in social and work settings.

Knowledge and comfort were fairly high overall, but comfort dropped in social settings compared with professional ones, and fell further when the autistic person needed more support. Statistical models showed knowledge was the bridge: experience raised comfort mainly when it built real understanding. The author argues for programs that create informed, meaningful contact, not awareness alone.
pmc-13246001:
Feddersen, Dyckmans, and Bramkamp dissected how a bacterial protein knows where a cell should split, in this 2026 eLife study. The Min system marks the future division site in bacteria. In Bacillus subtilis it works without the activator protein its E. coli cousin needs, raising the question of what switches its MinD motor on. Combining test-tube biochemistry with single-molecule imaging inside living cells, the team watched MinD meet the cell membrane.

Membrane binding itself activated MinD's energy-burning cycle, and ATP binding was required for the protein to let go again. Both single and paired forms of MinD could bind, but only the normal protein gathered at poles and division sites, helped by a partner protein. Locked variants spread uselessly along the membrane. The work rewrites how this division compass is regulated.
pmc-13247001:
Jin, Liu, Di, and co-authors identified a force-sensing protein pair that helps ovarian cancer spread, in this 2026 Molecular Biomedicine paper. High-grade serous ovarian cancer kills by scattering through the abdomen, which requires tumor cells to survive after detaching, a step many cancers fail. Searching gene data linked to tissue sugar metabolism, the team landed on a protein called CHP1 and its partner TMEM87A.

Removing either protein wrecked the tumor spheroids' structure in laboratory models and sharply reduced tumor growth and spread in mice, apparently by quieting a growth-signaling pathway. A repurposed compound, sodium gluconate, broke the pair apart and shrank tumors at low doses without obvious organ damage. The authors propose the complex as a druggable weak point in metastatic disease.
pmc-13247301:
Zai and co-authors propose a framework for governing artificial intelligence inside hospitals, in this 2026 Learning Health Systems article. A learning health system is one that continuously improves care from its own data, but classic models were not built for AI tools that drift, update, and need constant assurance. The authors combined learning-system theory with current AI governance frameworks in a structured conceptual exercise.

Their result is the HALO model, Health AI Learning and Oversight, which treats each AI tool as a living knowledge artifact passing through lifecycle stages inside the learning cycle. Five assurance dimensions, performance, safety, equity, transparency, and security, are monitored continuously rather than once at approval. Applying the model, the authors argue, lets health systems keep AI adaptive without losing control of it.
pmc-13249201:
Rutter and colleagues tracked mood and mental speed together in daily life, in a 2026 study of college students. Ninety-nine students answered morning and evening phone surveys for fourteen days, rating negative feelings and playing a reaction time task. The team focused on how much a person's mood swung from moment to moment, not just its average level.

On occasions when a student's negative feelings fluctuated more than usual, their reaction times also became more erratic. The link was strongest in the first few sessions, before practice smoothed performance. Men's reaction times were steadier than women's overall. The authors suggest steadying emotional swings as one route to steadier thinking in anxious or low-mood students.
pmc-13250001:
Morton and colleagues pooled oxygen fitness data for cross-country skiers, in a 2026 Sports Medicine Open review. Seventy-eight studies reported maximal oxygen uptake, the engine-size measure endurance coaches prize, alongside competitive level. The team re-scored every athlete group on a standard classification framework. They then asked whether the measure climbs with the tier of competition, separately by sex and by test mode.

Only treadmill running data were plentiful enough for firm statistics, and there the pattern was clear. Higher tiers showed higher oxygen uptake in both men and women. That held whether values were expressed absolutely or per kilogram. Even among elites the measure kept separating levels. The authors offer the pooled values as benchmarks for spotting and developing talent.
pmc-13250101:
Frkatovic and co-authors examine quantum generative adversarial networks, computer models that pit two quantum systems against each other to create images. Their 2026 paper in Scientific Reports asks a plain question: can these models learn new patterns, or do they only copy what they were shown? The team studied designs where both the generator and the judge run on quantum principles.

Through heavy numerical testing of the main current designs, the authors found the models failed to generalize across data sets. Instead, the generator settled on an average picture of its training data. They also derived a mathematical lower bound that explains this weakness when the generator outputs a pure quantum state. The result sets a clear limit for builders of quantum image generators.
pmc-13250701:
Emmet Norris and colleagues scope the evidence on dusty air in dry lands in this 2026 review. Fine particles in air are a top cause of heart and lung illness worldwide, yet dry regions, over 40 percent of the world's land, have been barely studied as a group.

The team found 102 studies from after 2012 across hot and cold dry zones. Pooled results showed raised risks of illness and death from short particle exposure, with hot dry regions about eight percent riskier than cold semi-dry ones for working-age adults. Studies in crowded dry regions were scarce, and none came from Africa, a gap the authors flag for urgent work.
pmc-13251101:
Zhang and co-authors map how the brain's wiring and activity drift apart in trigeminal neuralgia, a severe facial pain disorder. Their 2026 Journal of Headache and Pain study scans eighty-seven patients and forty-two healthy controls, then rescans many patients after treatment. A graph-based measure captures how tightly brain structure and function stay coupled.

Patients showed looser coupling than controls, especially in movement and attention networks, and looser coupling tracked with worse pain and longer illness. After successful treatment, coupling returned to healthy levels, and bigger rebounds meant bigger pain relief. Gene maps linked the loosening to energy, ion balance, and inflammation genes, while recovery tied to synapse and natural opioid genes. The authors offer coupling as a possible marker for treatment planning.
pmc-13251301:
Rattu and colleagues share lessons from involving patients and the public throughout three tic disorder studies at the University of Nottingham. Their 2026 Research Involvement and Engagement letter covers projects on care experiences, a new care pathway for young people, and an online behavioral treatment. Each study ran its own involvement panel.

Panels shaped design, recruitment, data collection, interpretation, and dissemination across all three projects. Key lessons include building panels with genuine lived experience, keeping spaces safe for honest views, and supporting communication around involuntary tics. Tracking each panel's impact and sustaining involvement through co-authorship also mattered. The authors offer the methods as transferable to other research areas working with underserved communities.
pmc-13252701:
Blanche Wright and colleagues pilot a co-designed mental health website for Latino adults in this 2026 study. Latino adults in the United States carry higher unmet mental health needs than other groups, and digital tools could help close the gap if people actually use them.

The bilingual Together for Wellness site was built with community partners during the COVID-19 pandemic and offered free coping resources. In the pilot, 131 Latino adults took a baseline survey and 68 a follow-up. Those preferring English felt far more comfortable using the site than Spanish-preferring users. Adults in their forties found it less easy to use than younger adults, a design warning the authors highlight.
pmc-13253001:
Ryan Serbin and a large team validate an online calculator for infected knee joints in this 2026 study. A hot, swollen knee may hide a joint infection that destroys cartilage fast if missed. Standard tests are unreliable, so a web tool that blends six clinical and lab values was put to the test.

The team reviewed 121 adult consults at a city trauma centre from 2018 to 2023. The calculator separated infected from clean joints with excellent accuracy; median risk scores were 80 percent for infected knees versus four percent for clean ones. They set two cut-offs: at or above 58 percent, operate; below about 25 percent, infection can be ruled out with confidence.
pmc-13253601:
Ross Walker and colleagues model how groups should spread out to share knowledge in this 2026 paper. From animal troops to robot swarms, collectives thrive on gathering information locally and passing it around, and their layout in space shapes how well that works.

Their mathematical model searches layouts, represented as rich network maps, for the arrangement that maximises group knowledge transfer. When members are equal in gathering skill, the amount of resources around favoured particular subgroup sizes. When skills vary, the model favours the population splitting into smaller subgroups that share space among themselves, not one mingled whole. The lessons span behavioural ecology and swarm robot design.
pmc-13253701:
Ahmet Alperen Palabiyik and Esra Palabiyik wrote a 2026 review of Wnt signaling, a cell message system that shapes the growing brain. They focus on two non-standard branches, Wnt/PCP and Wnt/Ca2+, rather than the best-known path. These branches guide cell polarity, meaning which way a cell faces, and calcium signals inside cells.

The review links these paths to nerve tube closure, neuron movement, axon guidance, and synapse change. When the paths fail, they may play a role in autism, spina bifida, Alzheimer's disease, and Parkinson's disease. The authors also note gene editing and lab-grown brain organoids, tiny brain-like tissues, as tools to study them.
pmc-13254501:
Yan-Ruide Li and a large team engineer off-the-shelf immune cells for a rare cancer in a 2026 study. Malignant pleural mesothelioma is an aggressive cancer of the chest lining with few options. The team reprogrammed blood stem cells to grow CAR-armored natural killer T cells aimed at mesothelin, boosted with interleukin-15.

The cells killed tumors in lab tests and in several mouse models, including lung spread models. They also reshaped the tumor surroundings by targeting certain macrophages. The cells showed few exhaustion markers and a strong safety profile, with no graft-versus-host disease or off-tumor effects seen.
pmc-13254701:
Gutiérrez-Villegas and colleagues tally what COPD costs patients, families, and societies worldwide. Their 2026 International Journal of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease review covers studies from 2020 to 2024 across fifteen countries. The disease is a leading cause of illness and death and a heavy drain on health systems.

Thirty studies qualified, and hospital care, driven by flare-ups, formed the biggest cost everywhere. Yearly costs per patient ran several thousand euros in Europe and well over ten thousand dollars in the United States. Lost productivity and unemployment costs rivaled medical bills in some middle-income countries. Anxiety, depression, caregiver strain, and financial toxicity were widespread, leading the authors to demand care that treats social and emotional burdens too.
pmc-13255001:
Giulia Senna and a large team record eagle rays in a mangrove bay in a 2026 study from the Maldives. Mangroves serve as nurseries for many sea species, but their role for rays and sharks is little documented. Using a consumer drone, the team flew over a 1.5 square kilometer bay at Baarah Island at high tide.

They observed four spotted eagle rays, including one juvenile, during about 50 minutes of flights. The authors say this first scientific record supports the idea that mangroves act as refuge or nursery habitat for young rays. They also praise cheap drones for spotting elusive species.
pmc-13255201:
Junhyun Hur and Sang-Tae Kim present a weed's chloroplast genome in a 2026 study. Persicaria pensylvanica, called Pennsylvania smartweed or pinkweed, is a yearly herb in the knotweed family that grows in many soil types. The team assembled its chloroplast genome and compared it with relatives in the same genus.

The genome runs 159,036 base pairs, with the classic four-part shape, and holds 131 working genes. A family tree built from the data placed it closest to Persicaria maculosa. The authors say the genome adds taxonomic insight, meaning help in sorting species, into how sections of the genus relate.
pmc-13255501:
Mai A. Wassel and colleagues study pufferfish gut microbes under salt and toxin stress in a 2026 experiment. Juvenile tiger pufferfish naturally carry tetrodotoxin, a nerve toxin. The team raised young fish at four salinity levels and fed them either a normal diet or one containing the toxin, then profiled gut bacteria with gene sequencing.

Salinity was the main driver of gut community structure, with only about five percent of bacterial variants shared across all salt levels. The toxin shifted specific bacteria and their functions instead, cutting some vitamin-making pathways while boosting others, yet fish growth was unaffected. The authors highlight how flexible the gut community is.
pmc-13260301:
Emilio D'Ignazio leads a 2026 review of musculoskeletal ultrasound in psoriatic arthritis, a chronic immune-driven joint disease linked to the skin condition psoriasis. Ultrasound uses sound waves to image joints and tendons. Because the disease varies widely and has no clear blood marker, early diagnosis is hard. The review assesses ultrasound across the disease path, from symptom-free psoriasis patients at risk, to established arthritis, including diagnosis, outlook, and treatment tracking.

Ultrasound can reveal hidden inflammation of joints, tendon attachments, and tendon sheaths, plus structural damage, before symptoms appear. That early detection could allow treatment before arthritis fully sets in. The review also covers telling immune-driven from other disease, predicting flares and future damage, and tracking response to treatment, including hard-to-treat cases. Standard scoring systems and new methods for small hand parts are discussed.
pmc-13261501:
Yinhuan Wang and Jiefang Guan review cancers that wander between the lungs and the urinary organs. Prostate, kidney, and bladder tumors trade metastatic ground with lung cancer often enough to confuse diagnosis and treatment. Their 2026 review gathers the molecular threads behind this two-way overlap.

The tumor types share escape toolkits, including a chemokine homing axis and a growth factor pathway that loosens cell identity. Each organ's immune neighborhood then shapes how arriving cells behave and respond to drugs. Blood-based biopsies and molecular profiling are sharpening the detective work. Even so, organ-specific soil keeps bending drug efficacy, demanding personalized plans.
pmc-13263101:
Makoto Mihara and colleagues survey staff on using ChatGPT in a specialist swelling clinic in Tokyo in a 2026 journal article. Lymphedema care, for limbs swollen by lymph fluid, needs heavy documentation and teamwork across facilities. The clinic had used the AI writing tool for two years when all twelve staff members answered an anonymous survey.

Every staff member had used ChatGPT, and most used it often. About 83 percent said efficiency improved, and everyone reported faster preparation of shared documents. Drafting documents and referral reports were the main uses. Staff also reported less stress and better outside communication. More than half raised privacy worries, and the authors stress human checking, safeguards, and training.
pmc-13263201:
Murat Aydın and colleagues measure how far a cut big-toe tendon pulls back in a 2026 cadaver study. The flexor hallucis longus tendon bends the big toe and is often cut by sharp objects, yet how much it retracts was little known. Using six donated feet, the team cut the tendon at toe level and applied measured pulling forces with a mechanical device.

Retraction grew gradually with force, averaging 7 millimeters under a light load and 21 millimeters at a mid-level load. Beyond that load, the other four toes also began to bend, owing to a link between this tendon and the toe-flexing tendon nearby. The authors conclude distal cuts retract only slightly, which may help surgical planning, though clinical checks are still needed.
pmc-13263301:
Kathrin Eller and co-authors present a 2026 consensus paper, written in German, on standardizing lab diagnosis of chronic kidney disease in Austria. Chronic kidney disease means the kidneys slowly lose function over time. The paper centers on two measures: filtration rate estimated from blood tests, and the urine albumin-creatinine ratio, which detects protein leaking into urine.

The authors recommend the EKFC formula for estimating filtration rate and note that the urine ratio test is still used far too little. They call for uniform lab methods and clear reporting so results match across sites. They also describe a risk equation that predicts kidney failure, and argue these tools must become routine in primary care.
pmc-13263701:
Sepideh Aarabi and Srijoni Sengupta present a 2026 case report of a blocked small intestine caused by a phytobezoar, a lump of undigested plant fiber. A 48-year-old woman came in with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and swelling. She had earlier lost part of her stomach to ulcer surgery and had recently eaten about five persimmons without chewing them well.

A CT scan showed a mottled, gas-containing mass in her jejunum, typical of this rare blockage. Surgeons opened the abdomen, cut into the bowel, and removed the mass. Her recovery was uneventful, and she received dietary counseling. The authors note surgery remains the main treatment for complete obstruction, with diet advice key to prevention.
pmc-13265001:
Ya-Chi Wu and colleagues wrote a 2026 study on predicting liver cancer return after surgery in patients with hepatitis B. Two markers were combined: a deletion flaw in the virus's pre-S2 gene, known to flag recurrence, and a tiny RNA in the tumor called miR-369-3p. The team looked for RNAs tied to both the virus flaw and recurrence.

They found miR-369-3p was lower in tumors of patients who carried the virus deletion or whose cancer returned. Low levels alone flagged higher recurrence risk. Patients with both the deletion and low RNA levels faced higher risk than those with either marker or none. The pair together predicted recurrence better than either alone. The authors call the combined marker exploratory and promising for guiding follow-up after curative surgery.
pmc-13267201:
Bruno Messias and colleagues issued a 2026 correction to their earlier study of blood sodium and appendicitis severity. The original paper appeared in BMC Surgery in 2023. After post-publication review, several claims were judged to overstate how useful sodium levels might be as a marker of severe appendicitis.

The correction softens the paper at several points. The title now calls sodium an adjunct, or supporting, marker rather than a novel predictor. The conclusions say sodium levels may help assess severity, not that they predict it. A new passage lists limits, including the single-center design, small sample, and factors like hydration that were not measured. The authors say firm claims must await stronger studies.
pmc-13267601:
Kenneth Cho and colleagues wrote a 2026 review of how doctors measure mitral valve leakage. In mitral regurgitation, blood flows backward through the heart's mitral valve. Ultrasound is the main measuring tool, but standard methods assume a round, steady leak and lean on single frames. Those guesses fail with off-center or multiple jets.

New machine learning tools measure the leak across the whole heartbeat instead. They handle odd jet shapes and uneven openings, and they match magnetic resonance scans well. Other AI tools can spot and grade leakage straight from ultrasound clips. The authors see value for screening where expert readers are scarce, such as low-resource settings. The review maps the move from hand measures to automated ones.
pmc-13267701:
Qi Pang and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of how carbon storage services flow across China's city clusters. Plants and soils absorb carbon in some places, while city life demands that service elsewhere. The team measured supply and demand across 19 urban agglomerations from 2000 to 2020, then modeled the flows using circuit theory, which treats movement like electric current.

Carbon supply grew only modestly while demand rose fast, leaving lasting gaps. Supply was higher in the west and south; demand clustered in big eastern city groups. More than half the clusters had surplus supply. Flow maps showed green supply areas ringing city demand centers, with strong links in central and western regions and broken links in the east. The authors offer the maps for fairer eco-payments between regions.
pmc-13267901:
Mahad Sadik Mukhtar and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a face infection that turned life-threatening. Their patient was a 20-year-old Somali man with no health problems. He came in with five days of growing swelling on the left side of his face from cellulitis, a skin infection, and three days of worsening breathlessness.

Scans showed infected clots had traveled to his lungs, a problem called septic pulmonary embolism. Both lungs had also collapsed from air leaks, worse on the left. Tubes were placed in both sides of his chest to drain the air. Blood cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus, a common skin bacterium. Targeted antibiotics and team care brought full recovery. The authors warn that chest problems in skin infection patients need fast imaging.
pmc-13268201:
Su D. Yang and colleagues present a 2026 study of COVID-19 infection among female sex workers in Nairobi, Kenya. The team expected high risk, given close contact with many partners and crowded venues. They followed a cohort enrolled in mid-2019, before the pandemic, and tested stored blood from 827 women about a year later for signs of past infection.

About 28 percent tested positive, and positivity climbed steadily the longer the pandemic had run. Infection linked to no behavior or background factor, only to time since the pandemic began. About half of infections caused no symptoms at all. HIV status made no difference to infection or symptoms. Antibodies found in pre-pandemic samples gave no protection. The authors conclude spread was extensive and untracked by the usual risk markers.
pmc-13269501:
Mugurel Constantin Rusu published a case report in 2026 describing a cluster of unusual blood vessel routes found on a scan of a 74-year-old woman. Five vessel variants appeared together in her neck and upper chest. Such variants matter because they can surprise surgeons operating near the windpipe and thyroid.

One main artery rode high across the front of the windpipe, and a small extra artery branched from it to feed both thyroid lobes. Another artery looped low in the chest before giving off the vessel to the brain. A tiny artery to the upper ribs arose in an uncommon pattern. A bone variant at the collarbones also placed several vessels in one narrow notch, raising the surgical stakes.
pmc-13270401:
Yuansi He and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 describing egg development in the crested ibis, an endangered bird with a long captive breeding history. Candling, shining light through the shell, lets keepers judge fertilization and embryo survival without breaking eggs. Ninety-eight eggs were documented in detail.

The study produced 1,422 candling images, averaging 14.52 per egg, and described both unfertilized eggs and normal embryo growth. Embryo deaths clustered in two windows: mid-incubation, days 7 to 15, held 60.0 percent of deaths, and days 23 to 29 before hatching held 35.0 percent. The authors offer the guide for breeding programs and field conservation of the species.
pmc-13271001:
Emily A. Erdmann is lead author of a 2026 journal article on RNA editing in the germline, the reproductive cell line, of the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Editing here means enzymes called ADARs change one RNA letter, adenosine, into another, inosine, altering the message a gene carries.

The authors profiled the active editing enzyme ADR-2 in the germline. They found many editing events differ from those in other tissues. The helper role of the inactive partner ADR-1 is preserved there. Losing editing barely changed the levels of edited messages, yet several unedited germline messages went astray. Extra checks suggested those changes are buffered when messages are turned into proteins.
pmc-13272201:
Felix Musabirema is lead author of a 2026 retrospective cohort study of hypoxemia management, care for low blood oxygen, in Rwandan public hospitals after national investment in medical oxygen systems. Good care depends on pulse oximetry, a fingertip oxygen check, and prompt oxygen therapy, and the team reviewed records from July to September 2022.

Across 39 hospitals and 5,731 admissions, oxygen checks on admission were documented for 87.7 percent, falling to 75.3 percent the next day. Among those screened, 9.4 percent had low oxygen, including 27.9 percent of newborns. Of patients found hypoxemic, 21.0 percent died, against 1.7 percent of others, and 93.4 percent received oxygen the same day.
pmc-13272601:
Dorian Peters leads a 2026 paper on making health chatbots fit the cultures where they are used, based on workshops in Latin America. Large language models often miss the lived experience of people in underserved regions. The team used hands-on workshops to gather local views rather than relying only on added training data.

Workshops showed that culture on the ground is tied up with money, politics, place, and daily logistics, not just language. The authors propose a framework they call Pluriversal Conversational AI for Health. It argues that health chatbots may need more room for different world views and closer ties to users, not just more data.
pmc-13272801:
Marc Augustin leads a 2026 review of delusions linked to artificial intelligence chatbots, where false beliefs are built up through long, personal chats. Unlike older technology delusions, AI may actively help construct the belief, the authors argue. They propose a framework called the amplification spiral to explain how this could happen.

Three chatbot traits are said to converge: mirroring a user's language, generating highly personal content, and agreeing without testing reality. Together these may deepen false beliefs in people who are vulnerable. The authors stress that the framework and its ideas need testing through case reports and empirical study, rather than being taken as proven.
pmc-13273101:
Vani Verma leads a 2026 scoping review of tools that measure outcomes in palliative care for children with cancer. Such care aims to improve quality of life for children and families, but measurement is fragmented. The team searched six databases from 2006 to 2025 for tools, their domains, validation, and fit for low- and middle-income settings.

They found 27 studies reporting 28 tools across six domains, including symptoms, quality of life, mental well-being, spiritual health, caregiver burden, and end-of-life care. Some tools performed strongly, but few were adapted for poorer settings. Mental and spiritual domains were underrepresented, and most tools relied on proxy reports from adults rather than children themselves.
pmc-13274601:
Lu Xia and a large team report a 2026 journal article on whether DNA tags inherited from mother versus father differ in autism. Chemical tags called methylation can be set differently on each parent's copy of a gene, an effect known as imprinting. The team used long-read sequencing to phase the tags by parent in 124 people from thirty-one families with an autistic child.

Comparing autistic children with their unaffected siblings turned up over two hundred parent-specific tag differences and thousands of outlier spots. Separate scans found 443 regions where the two parental copies are tagged unequally in general. These shifts clustered in known imprinted regions and in autism-linked genes, with mother's and father's copies showing distinct patterns.
pmc-13274901:
Pramita Shrestha and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on how dialysis patients in Nepal view the importance of sticking to treatment. Skipping sessions is dangerous, and patients' beliefs shape their behavior. The cross-sectional study ran from May to August 2025 in two tertiary care centers and included 283 patients aged eighteen and over, with a mean age of 50.6 years.

Good perception of adherence's importance was widespread overall. It ran higher among single patients than married ones, with an adjusted prevalence ratio of 1.12, and among patients accompanied by a parent, at 1.14, compared with those accompanied by others. The authors suggest family involvement, especially parents, may reinforce how seriously patients take their dialysis schedule.
pmc-13276501:
Michael Thomas and co-authors report a 2026 journal article recording a tree species in Rwanda for the first time. The Flora of Akagera National Park project is building a full checklist of the park's plants in the Eastern Province. Such checklists anchor conservation and planting choices.

Fieldwork in 2023 found Diospyros abyssinica, a member of the ebony family, growing in the province. The find extends the species' known range into Rwanda. The local stand is fragile: only fifteen trees survive in under twenty hectares, a relict of a once wider population. Because the tree has many uses for local people, managers have prioritized it for indigenous tree planting programs. The authors place the record within the park checklist effort, which blends field surveys, herbarium records, and literature review.
pmc-13277401:
Edson Marchiori and colleagues present a 2026 case report of an uncommon complication of tuberculosis in a 25-year-old man. He had five months of breathlessness, fever, productive cough, and weight loss. Scans showed lung infiltrates and a cavity in a swollen lymph node near the center of the chest, with a channel draining into an airway.

A scope exam of the airway found a matching defect with dead tissue and cheesy material draining in. Sputum tests confirmed the tuberculosis bacterium. Chest lymph node tuberculosis can erode into nearby structures and spread infection through the airways. The patient received a six-month course of anti-tuberculosis drugs and improved, with marked clearing on later scans.
pmc-13278401:
Xuehui Guo leads a 2026 study of what makes theme park visitors feel positive emotions in Shanghai, China. The team studied 106 theme parks, combining online reviews, map data on places, and geographic data to measure visitor emotion and park features. They also mapped how parks cluster across the city and how emotion varies by area.

Parks clustered strongly, but emotion levels inside hotspots were uneven. Brand strength of the park's theme, service quality, and green-space leisure were the features most tied to positive emotion. Only brand strength showed firm evidence of a nonlinear pattern, where gains level off or shift. The authors advise consistent theming, predictable service, restful green nodes, and better links to crowded hotspots.
pmc-13279201:
Chenchen Yang and colleagues offer a 2026 review of osteosarcoma, a harsh bone cancer seen most in the young. Care still leans on strong chemo drugs and surgery. Yet five year life rates for spread or returned disease have sat near forty percent for decades. The review maps gene change and the immune scene in tumours to guide more exact care.

Gene reads show big breaks and shuffles of DNA, not one single driver fault. Faults in guard genes TP53 and RB1 are common and fuel growth and drug escape. Marks that silence genes add more layers. Tumours also hold back immune attack, which the authors call immune cold. They chart how gene and immune clues could pair to shape custom drugs.
pmc-13280601:
Ilknur Aydin Teker and Fatma Mansur give a 2026 study of advice networks among family physicians, read with social network analysis. Peer interactions for information exchange are a powerful tool in the pursuit of solutions. Advice seeking is one such interaction. The whole network approach was used, with face to face research among one hundred thirty nine family physicians. Data were analysed in UCINET software and visualized in NETDRAW.

Advice acts were split in five dimensions. Frequency, density and reciprocity measures described each one, and a quadratic assignment procedure measured correlations between dimensions. A Girvan Newman algorithm checked clustering in the advice network. Density values in the dimensions were very low. The network was sparse, with limited interactions among family physicians in advice flow. Tie strength ran through validation first, then solutions, problem reformulation, meta information and legitimization.
pmc-13281301:
Mariana N Zavala Gómez and colleagues reported two lung transplant cases treated with a gas-clearing machine in a 2026 paper. After transplant, both patients built up too much carbon dioxide in the blood. High levels can force harsh settings on the breathing machine, which can harm new lungs. The device pulls blood out, strips the gas, and returns the blood. It was hooked into a kidney support machine already in wide use.

In both cases the device brought the gas level down. Breathing machine settings could then be eased to gentler levels. The authors call the method a useful add-on beside standard breathing support. They say it may guard the new lungs when gas buildup puts them at risk. They also call for larger studies to pin down who should get the device and how best to run it.
pmc-13281601:
Okello Malcom Mark and colleagues counted a stomach germ in Ugandan patients in a 2026 study. The germ, Helicobacter pylori, drives long-term stomach swelling. That swelling can be a first step toward stomach cancer. The team studied tissue from one hundred fifty patients with the swelling. Samples came from three labs and covered biopsies from 2018 to 2021. Special stains let them spot the germ under a microscope.

About three in ten patients carried the germ. Patients averaged forty-eight years old, and men outnumbered women. Germ carriers showed much worse stomach damage on every check. Their tissue had deeper long-term swelling and more active white cell attack. The stomach lining had also thinned more, and patches had shifted toward a bowel-like form, a known cancer warning sign. The authors say germ checks should guide care in Uganda, where tissue data have been scarce.
pmc-13281801:
Christine Yu and colleagues mapped a cell division machine in the silkmoth in a 2026 study. When cells divide, a grip called the kinetochore ties chromosomes to the pulling frame. Most species plant that grip at one spot on each chromosome, marked by a special protein. The silkmoth lacks that marker protein. Its grip runs along the whole chromosome instead. The team rebuilt the inner grip's shape from silkmoth parts.

Four new parts surfaced in the build, kin to a ring complex that grips the pulling ropes in other species. Here they act as scaffolding, not rope grips. Like its kin in yeast and humans, the silkmoth grip traps DNA in a closed chamber. Unlike them, it can pair up head to head on its own. The authors say a whole-chromosome grip may arise from many small grip units in a row.
pmc-13282301:
Wendy K Bragg and co-authors offer a 2026 framework to guide responses to environmental disasters that threaten natural resources. Two California case studies shaped it, both involving the endangered black abalone, a large sea snail. In one, a massive landslide buried abalone and their rocky habitat, then slowly spread along the coast. In the other, wildfire followed by heavy rain sent debris flows that buried abalone at stream mouths.

From those responses the team built a flexible decision framework, shortened to FRaMED. It is designed to fit many resources, from species to whole ecosystems, and many threats, from fires to oil spills. Managers can adjust actions during a disaster and between events. The materials also support planning for disasters that recur, not just one-off crises. The authors say climate extremes and human stressors make such ready guidance ever more necessary for protecting species at range edges.
pmc-13282401:
Valentina Pucino and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on nerve damage in the limbs and organs in Sjögren disease, an autoimmune disorder that mainly dries the eyes and mouth. Up to a fifth of patients develop nervous system problems, most often in the peripheral nerves, those outside brain and spinal cord. The patterns vary widely, which complicates diagnosis and treatment, and the underlying mechanism is often unclear.

The review summarises current knowledge of these neuropathies, meaning nerve disorders causing pain, numbness, or weakness, and details their disease mechanisms one by one. It argues for diagnosis and treatment targeted at the specific mechanism in each patient, rather than a single standard approach. Clearer mechanism-based frameworks should prevent severe disability, the authors say. They also stress trial design: grouping unlike neuropathies together may hide treatments that work for one type. Better patient selection could make future trials more informative.
pmc-13283401:
Right-heart load at admission triples three-year death risk after COPD flares, Aili Gao's eleven-hospital cohort finds in 2026. Extra load on the right heart may signal lung pressure problems. Its link to death after a flare was not well understood.

The study ran in 11 hospitals from 2017 to 2020 with heart scans on arrival. A total of 237 patients had high right heart load, and 415 had normal load. Three-year death rates were far higher in the high-load group in follow-up. Adjusted models kept high load as a separate predictor of death. A heart stress marker in blood also predicted worse outlook. Early heart checks may flag high-risk flare patients.
pmc-13283901:
Darkening palms alone pointed to vitamin B12 shortage in a 2026 case from Mukti Nath Sankhi and colleagues. Low B12 more often darkens knuckles or brings anemia and nerve symptoms. Palm-only darkening is a rare way for the shortage to appear.

The 45-year-old man, a strict vegetarian, noticed both palms darkening over four months. He had no breathlessness, gut symptoms, drug use, or chemical exposure in history. Blood tests showed low counts across cell types and large red cells. B12 levels sat far below the normal range given in the report. Shots of a B12 form formed the core treatment plan.
pmc-13284101:
Choosing general over spinal anesthesia kept a knee replacement safe for a woman with a tethered spinal cord, recount Lucas Alessi and colleagues in 2026. Her cord sat far lower than usual, ending near the bottom spine segments. Needle placement for spinal numbing risked direct cord injury.

The 65-year-old patient had prior spinal anesthesia for her other knee replacement. Apprehension about repeating it prompted deep review before this surgery. MRI review by imaging and brain surgery specialists confirmed minimal fluid around key levels. Team and patient jointly chose general anesthesia as the safest route. A thigh nerve block aided pain control after the operation.
pmc-13284501:
Hsin-Yi Yang and co-authors report a 2026 study on whether breast MRI before surgery improves long-term results after breast-conserving therapy. The value of pre-surgery MRI stays debated, even more so with modern risk-based radiation plans. Records for 613 patients treated at one center from 2014 to 2022 were split by MRI use and ASTRO risk class.

Overall return of cancer was lower in the MRI group than in the group without MRI in this single-center set. Gains centered on high-risk patients who got standard radiation, while low-risk patients showed no clear gain. Adjusted work still linked MRI to lower return risk. The authors suggest using risk class to target MRI to high-risk patients.
pmc-13285201:
Karol Marschollek and co-authors report a 2026 nationwide study of sleep quality and body clock type in Polish adults with headache disorders. Migraine and other primary headaches link closely to poor sleep, but large population data were lacking. The online study covered 5,311 adults, sorting headaches by standard criteria and scoring sleep and morningness with known questionnaires.

People with migraine had the worst sleep scores and the highest share of poor sleepers, well above headache-free adults in the survey results. Migraine also shifted people toward evening types. In the migraine group, poor sleep tracked with lower life quality and higher stress. The authors urge sleep checks as part of headache care.
pmc-13285401:
Emergency medicine in Asia needs a shared push on staff, standards, and digital tools, Arif Alper Cevik and co-authors argue in a 2026 conference report. The field grew from a new idea to a named specialty across much of Asia in four decades, yet growth is patchy. Shortages of trained staff, uneven teaching quality, and loss of doctors to richer systems persist.

Leaders at a 2025 Dubai conference panel weighed three linked fronts. They urged a clear training and leadership path from school through specialty years, society-led teamwork across borders to align standards, and digital change that widens access while keeping care human. The authors call for joint action to end scattered growth.
pmc-13285501:
Spotting which adults with severe short sight will keep stretching at the eyeball is the goal of a 2026 cohort study by Yuan Wang and co-authors in Wenzhou. Stretching raises the risk of sight-threatening harm. The team tracked 1,025 eyes from 532 adults aged eighteen to sixty for two years and tested nine candidate signs.

About a quarter of eyes stretched fast by the set mark. A six-sign model sorted risk well, and choroid thickness alone was the single best sign, with age next. Leaner models using just age and choroid thickness, with or without sex, lost little accuracy. The authors offer the pair as a handy clinic screen.
pmc-13286101:
Keyang Zhang and co-authors detail a ducts-first scope strategy for a tumor at the gut's bile opening in a 2026 technique report. A 51-year-old man had a growth on the papilla, the small nipple where bile and pancreatic juices enter the bowel. Cutting first can crush or bury those duct openings, so the team secured them before any tissue came off.

Doctors first threaded thin plastic tubes into both ducts to keep them open and draining, then waited three days. The tubes split the growth into upper and lower parts, each taken by a unlike scope method with careful work around the tubes. Strong clips sealed the raw area once the whole lesion was out. The man ate again on day six and went home on day nine, and tissue tests confirmed a neuroendocrine tumor, fully healed at one month.
pmc-13286201:
Yao-Hsiang Chen and colleagues test a simple breathing trainer against long COVID breathlessness in a 2026 trial at a hospital in northern Taiwan. The handheld device rewards deep, slow breaths with a rising float, giving patients visual proof of effort. Volunteers were split by how long ago they had recovered, from under three months to nearly a year, plus a waiting group that trained later.

Ninety people joined and 85 finished the six weeks of thrice-weekly sessions. Every training group reported easier breathing and better daily function at the end, while the waiting group barely moved on either scale. Walking distance gains showed mainly in the groups that started soonest after illness. Blood oxygen readings stayed flat throughout, and the authors ask for fuller lung testing to pin down what the trainer truly changes.
pmc-13287001:
Yuntao Zou and colleagues split-test language models on the two halves of evidence synthesis in a 2026 evaluation study. Two hepatology questions, a heart drug in cirrhosis and blood thinners for a portal vein clot, supplied the test bed. Models screened titles and abstracts against set criteria, then a retrieval-fed model drafted ten full reviews per topic for scoring against the PRISMA checklist by a separate judge model.

Screening shone: agreement with human reviewers ran high, catching most eligible studies while wrongly passing few. Hours of manual screening collapsed from 62 and 30 down to 3 and 2. Drafting lagged badly, acing titles and introductions but sagging below two-thirds compliance in abstracts and discussions. Judge scores tracked human scoring closely, and the authors conclude screening is ready for work while drafting still needs a human hand.
pmc-13287301:
Ziqing Zhou, Yifan Ren, Fei Yu, and Jie Ma report in 2026 on an electrode material for pulling chloride ions out of water using electricity. Treating copper phosphide with fluorine created both added atoms and missing spots in the crystal, shifting how electrons are shared inside the material.

According to the authors' summary, the paired defects sped up charge movement and ion travel.
