Electrodes carrying both defects removed more chloride per area and worked faster than comparison versions. The summary gives headline claims only, without the underlying figures. The work points toward compact electrical desalting units that target salt ions directly rather than filtering water through membranes.
pmc-13287801:
Mohamed I A Othman and co-authors work through the mathematics in 2026 of a spinning porous solid. The solid also generates heat inside itself. Their heat-flow theory allows a delayed response. Equations were scaled to unit-free form, solved by a standard wave method, and plotted with computing software.

Solutions give displacement, temperature, and stress at each point. Plots show how inner heating and spin interact to bend the material and move heat through its pores. Nonlocal effects, where each point feels its neighbours, are built into the model. The authors aim the results at engineers designing parts that face heat and rotation together.
pmc-13288701:
Selena T Lee and co-authors link the shape of village friendships to depression in a 2026 cross-sectional study from rural Honduras. Census-style surveys covered 25,605 adults in 176 villages in the Copan region between 2015 and 2019, capturing full social networks alongside symptoms of depression and postpartum depression.

About thirty-five percent reported depression symptoms, more often women than men, and nearly twenty-nine percent of recent parents reported postpartum symptoms. Women whose friends were less connected among themselves faced higher odds of depression, a pattern absent in men and in new parents. Splitting friendly from hostile ties narrowed the signal further. Where a person sits in the wider web matters beyond single friendships, the authors argue.
pmc-13288901:
Monica Lauridsen Kujabi leads a 2026 protocol for a pregnancy study in Somaliland. The PROMISE study will follow about 800 pregnant women in Hargeisa. Staff will recruit them before week 28. Visits will run through birth and past it. Women will answer surveys and get clinical checks.

The team will adapt a tool for near-miss events. A Delphi panel will shape that tool. The cohort will then test how well it works. Findings will guide new counseling aids. Local women will help create those aids. A small pilot will test if the aids work well.
pmc-13289101:
Peng Peng and colleagues plan a 2026 scoping review on families of cancer survivors. Cancer care weighs on kin as well as patients. Family strength may ease that weight. It may also spur growth after trauma. Past work uses mixed terms and tools.

The team will search ten databases. Grey sources and past reviews will also be checked. Work in English and Chinese will count. No nation will be barred. Two reviewers will screen each paper. A third will break any ties. Results will be shown in charts and text. Gaps will guide new studies and care.
pmc-13289201:
Gideon Victor and colleagues outline a 2026 cohort study plan in Islamabad, Pakistan. The study deals with self-care in coronary heart disease. Such disease is a top cause of death. Self-care can lift patient outcomes. Needs and drivers are still unclear there.

The study will enroll 354 patients in all. One tertiary hospital will host it. Data will be drawn at the start and at three months. Tools will gauge self-care and self-belief. Mood and other diseases will also be logged. Readmissions are a key outcome. ER visits and unplanned clinic visits count too. Models will hunt for traits that foretell each outcome.
pmc-13289301:
Weronika Grabowska and coauthors report 2026 baseline findings on traditional, complementary, and integrative medicine use in Berlin. Data came from the German National Cohort, known as NAKO, at its inner-city Berlin center for 2017 to 2019. Participants reported use in the prior year of seven non-drug approaches, from meditation to chiropractic care.

Among 1970 people, 1029 said they used at least one such approach in the past year. Meditation led at 26.8 percent, followed by chiropractic care and then yoga in use rates. Frequent users were more often women and reported more chronic pain, joint wear, back pain, and mental health problems than never users. Supplement use was also far more common among users, painting a picture of added care alongside usual medicine.
pmc-13289401:
Hevar Hamah Saed headed a 2026 cohort comparison on home-based drug titration for heart failure with reduced pumping strength. Guideline drugs help most when started fast and raised to target doses, yet routine care often stalls. The TELEFASTER-HF approach used a fixed home plan with remote monitoring to speed that process safely.

The home cohort held 60 patients, compared with 65 patients getting standard care at the same time. Weighting balanced the groups before outcome checks began. Time to best medical therapy was far shorter at home, with a median of 48 days versus 321 days for standard care in the results. Dose levels and target reach were higher at every check, and persistence stayed better through twelve months.
pmc-13289801:
Thibault Genissel, Alexandre Robert, Jane Lecomte, and François Sarrazin define a 2026 concept called evolutionary footprint for conservation science. Human-driven change now alters evolution itself, across fast and slow timescales, through genetics and other inheritance paths. Managers lack a single score for that impact, so the authors propose one that compares change against natural history baselines.

Metrics cover adaptive traits, genetic diversity, large-scale evolutionary processes, and family tree patterns for a species or group. Two cases illustrate scoring: a plant facing pollinator decline, and human effects across mammals as a whole. Mixing timescales, forecasting change, handling non-genetic paths, and building databases remain hard parts. A shared score could bring evolution into routine conservation choices.
pmc-13290601:
Research tying knee osteoarthritis to oxidative stress has boomed, and Yuhang Zhang and colleagues chart the field's shape in a 2026 bibliometric analysis. Pulling the literature from the Web of Science Core Collection, they mapped output, collaborations, and keyword clusters with CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and RStudio.

Publication volume climbed into rapid growth and peaked in 2024. China leads on raw output but sits loosely in the collaboration network, a pattern the authors call high-output and low-integration. Hubs such as Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine anchor the knowledge core. Keywords grouped into three themes: nutrition-based intervention, mechanism work such as cell senescence, and therapy studies such as ozone. The field's arc runs from basic validation through mechanism refinement toward clinical translation, now turning to whole-body interactions.
pmc-13290901:
Genes, a drug, and sex jointly tune fetal hemoglobin in sickle cell anemia, Manoel Ferreira de Magalhães Filho and colleagues report in a study from western Bahia, Brazil, in 2026. Fetal hemoglobin blunts red cell sickling, and both hydroxyurea therapy and variants near two genes are known to raise it; the team measured their combined hand.

DNA from 43 patients was typed for variants in BCL11A and the HBS1L-MYB region. Patients on hydroxyurea carried significantly higher fetal hemoglobin than untreated patients. A factorial analysis found the drug, beta-globin haplotype, and sex interacting to shape levels, and a regression model using the drug, sex, and three variants explained 46.5% of the variation. Several variants also traveled together in linkage blocks. The authors say such markers could guide individualized monitoring of therapy.
pmc-13291001:
Microbes inside digestive tumors get a full review by Huamin Zeng and colleagues in 2026. The cancers covered include stomach, pancreas, colon, liver, and esophagus. These cancers kill many patients each year. Inner microbes may shape how they grow and resist drugs.

The review traces where these microbes come from. It then maps how they affect tumor growth. Herbal medicine ideas to rebalance the tumor habitat get a close look. Drug paths that target microbes are weighed with care. Gaps that block clinic use are named plainly. A microbe-first view may guide future precision care.
pmc-13291601:
Noisy rhythms in nature carry a hidden energy cost. Daiki Sekizawa, Sosuke Ito, and Masafumi Oizumi break that cost apart in a 2026 study. Heartbeats, brain waves, and chemical pulses all oscillate. Each rhythm burns energy to persist.

A math tool called Koopman decomposition splits motion into modes. Total waste heat splits cleanly across those modes. Each mode’s cost grows with speed squared times strength. Fast modes thus face tight strength limits at fixed cost. One strong mode can drive most waste. Broad spectra can also share the burden. Bifurcation and resonance cases show both patterns. Frequency-level cost maps were invisible before.
pmc-13292301:
Yaakov Hoffman and co-authors offer a 2026 early study of trauma responses in older adults who survived captivity after the 7 October attack. Almost all captivity research covers young prisoners of war, not elderly civilians. The team assessed 26 Jewish Israeli adults from Gaza-envelope kibbutzim, mean age about 82, half of them released Hamas captives and half displaced survivors.

Apart from stronger prolonged grief among ex-captives, both groups reported similarly low levels of PTSD, complex PTSD, depression, and anxiety. Those treated cruelly on purpose while held fared worse. In the freed group alone, being lonely tracked with grief, and feeling unsafe tracked with PTSD symptoms. The authors read the overall pattern as late-life resilience, consistent with the inoculation hypothesis, while flagging captivity-specific risk factors.
pmc-13293601:
Wenjing Zhou and colleagues run, in a 2026 trial, an unguided online therapy course for major depression in Chinese adults, tracking effects for a full year. Online cognitive behavioral therapy is cheap and scalable, yet lasting benefit in China was unproven.

The eight-week trial in Shenzhen split 317 adults between instant access to a seven-module course plus usual care and a waitlist group. At course end, the instant group had eased depression more, with higher remission and response rates than controls, based on figures the authors report. Dropout was higher in the instant group. Gains were then tracked at three, six, and twelve months.
pmc-13294401:
Paolo Niccolò Franco and colleagues count the environmental savings of deep learning CT reconstruction in a 2026 single-center study. Eighteen months of data from four scanners, two with hybrid iterative methods and two with deep learning methods, covered 42,300 body scans. Deep learning protocols also ran lower tube voltage and trimmed contrast dye doses.

Electricity fell from 123,000 kWh in the older group to 66,927 kWh in the deep learning group, with matching carbon drops in the reported totals. Contrast savings reached 434 liters over the period, preserving water as well. Combined carbon from power and dye fell from 49.62 tons to 29.10 tons. Greener scanning need not mean weaker images.
pmc-13294501:
Wenyu Zhang and a large team train machine learners to screen for primary aldosteronism in a 2026 study. The hormone disorder drives much treatable high blood pressure, yet the standard ratio test falters when patients stay on blood pressure drugs. Three datasets totaling 1,380 patients supplied plasma steroids, potassium, and renin to several models, led by a feedforward neural network.

Renin-free models matched accuracy with or without drug washout, while ratio-style models sagged without washout. Three tuned renin-free models reached areas of 0.948–0.954 versus 0.839 for the standard ratio in the reported curves. At high sensitivity cutoffs, false alarms fell by 53–72% in the authors' figures.
pmc-13295001:
Petru Ifteni and colleagues survey Romanian psychiatrists about long-acting injectable antipsychotics in a 2026 study. Injections given every few weeks can improve adherence and cut relapse in schizophrenia, yet they remain underused. Views were gathered from doctors treating more than 1,000 patients in total.

Eighty psychiatrists rated the four products sold in Romania on benefit, safety, dosing, and monitoring needs. Aripiprazole injections scored best overall, while olanzapine scored lowest on most counts. Better adherence and fewer relapses most encouraged prescribing, named by almost all respondents. Patient distrust and patchy hospital supply were the leading barriers, pointing to fixes beyond the clinic room.
pmc-13295801:
Zachary Green and colleagues track bowel surgery in children as biologic drug use climbed in a 2026 study. A regional British centre followed young inflammatory bowel disease patients from 2007 to 2024. Anti-TNF drugs arrived earlier and reached far more children across three guideline eras.

The cohort held 1,538 children, mostly with Crohn's disease, as yearly patient numbers more than doubled. Treated shares rose from under six percent in the first era to over sixty percent in the latest. Resection rates fell steeply across the same span, driven by Crohn's cases, while ulcerative colitis trends stayed less certain.
pmc-13296301:
Mirko Sergio and a large veterinary team ask, in 2026, whether fat from around dogs' ovaries, taken during routine spaying, beats under-skin fat as a source of repair cells for worn joints. Cells from five healthy Labradors were grown and pushed toward cartilage making.

Ovary-area fat cells showed stronger cartilage-forming ability and built a richer cartilage-like matrix than skin fat cells from the same dogs. Since this tissue is normally thrown away, the authors call it an ethical, ready supply for regenerative work. They aim at future cartilage repair for dogs with osteoarthritis.
pmc-13297001:
Alexander C Campbell and colleagues review, in 2026, how accurately billing and records codes capture real health conditions. Pooling 280 studies that checked diagnosis codes against a trusted standard, mostly hospital charts in rich countries, they summarise hit and miss rates across many conditions.

Codes were strong at ruling conditions out and moderate to strong at confirming them, but accuracy for catching true cases swung widely between studies and disease groups. Only two studies came from poorer countries. The authors urge ongoing accuracy checks, since such data now steer population health research and policy.
pmc-13298001:
Honey pulled from the hive too soon sits in a gray zone in food law, and Anna Gajda and her team take that gray zone apart in a 2026 review. Some call such honey fake or low grade. The team finds the science and the rule books do not line up.

They read lab work on the microbes, make-up, and scent marks of honey. They also read world and EU food rules, from Codex Alimentarius to EU laws. Sugar-loving yeasts live in all honey, they note, so a yeast count alone should not fail a batch unless the honey is in fact souring. No rule sets a yeast cap today. Their fix is to judge ripe state by a set of signs at once, water level among them, and to test that set in many labs first.
pmc-13298601:
A cheap wireless fetal monitor reads heart tracings nearly as well as the hospital machine, found Pajaree Ruenpeng and co-authors in a 2026 prospective study. Four hundred four pregnant women underwent simultaneous monitoring with mobile and conventional cardiotocography, and blinded physician groups scored the paired tracings.

Agreement on baseline heart rate was excellent, with correlation above 0.95, and readings of accelerations and decelerations also matched closely. Judgments of variability and contractions agreed only moderately, and reviewers gave the conventional device slightly higher quality and satisfaction scores. Even so, the authors back mobile monitoring as a workable option for low-resource settings, given its cost and portability.
pmc-13299101:
A gut molecule better known as a tumor suppressor may help obesity open the door to colon cancer, argue Sidharth Prasad Mishra and colleagues in a 2026 review. They trace how diet and gut microbes push the microRNA miR-101a into overdrive in the obese colon.

Ethanolamine from food and microbes raises miR-101a, which then dismantles the messenger for ZO-1, a protein that seals the gut lining. The leakier barrier admits bacterial products, feeding chronic inflammation, oxidative damage, and growth signals that favor tumors. Because miR-101a can be measured in tissue, blood, or stool, the authors propose it as an early warning marker and a target for diet or microbiome interventions.
pmc-13300701:
Tiny fat bubbles secreted by cells can be turned into guided drug carriers, Sin Hye Park and colleagues demonstrate in a 2026 gastric cancer study. They fitted extracellular vesicles with the p51 peptide, which locks onto HER2, and loaded them with 17-DMAG, an HSP90-blocking drug. Tests ran in two cell lines and a mouse tumor model.

The guided vesicles entered HER2-positive cells far better than plain ones. Treated cells died by apoptosis, with cleaved PARP and caspase-3 up and growth signals such as c-Myc and VEGF down. In mice, the treatment slowed tumor growth without visible organ damage, marking the platform as a selective delivery route worth developing.
pmc-13302401:
Silencing four chitin-cutting genes could give farmers a greener weapon against the whitefly, Dejun Kong and colleagues report in a 2026 study of Bemisia tabaci. The pest drains plant sap and spreads viruses, and chemical sprays dominate current control. The team identified the whitefly's chitin deacetylase genes, which help build its cuticle and gut lining, then knocked them down with matching double-stranded RNA.

Two delivery routes worked: a nanomaterial carrier called SPc, and tomato plants engineered to produce the RNA themselves. Feeding whiteflies silenced the target genes in both cases. The authors present chitin deacetylases as promising targets for RNA-based pest control that leaves chemistry behind.
pmc-13303101:
Needling the spleen under ultrasound guidance cracked two diagnoses that safer routes could not, Zhuohang Zou and colleagues recount in a 2026 case report. Both patients arrived with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, a runaway inflammatory syndrome, driven by hidden B-cell lymphoma. Ravaged blood counts and clotting made standard biopsies too dangerous, and removing the spleen riskier still.

With disease centered in the spleen, the team sampled it percutaneously under imaging guidance. Both biopsies returned definitive lymphoma diagnoses and steered targeted therapy. The authors present the approach as a viable lifeline for carefully selected patients, provided a multidisciplinary team weighs the bleeding risk case by case.
pmc-13305501:
Song Gao and co-authors chart global colorectal cancer patterns from 1990 to 2021 in a 2026 multi-part study. Burden figures span 204 countries, split by a development index, to show where the disease grows and who bears it most.

New cases reached into the millions worldwide by 2021 while death rates fell, a split credited to better screening and care in richer regions. Aging drove most of the global rise, while population growth dominated in poorer regions. Inequality between regions widened over the span. Forecasts see case rates edging up but deaths falling, and gene analysis tied body mass to higher risk.
pmc-13307101:
Gabriela Adriany Lisboa Zilli shrank two citrus drugs with high press gas to fight chemo pain in a 2026 study. The pair ease pain in past work, but they mix poorly with water, which cuts their use by mouth.

Small bits made by the gas step melt fast in water, and a dock test checked fit to a pain switch called TRPV1. Swiss mice faced a hot spice pain test plus short and long pain from the chemo drug paclitaxel. Touch pain scores showed if the small bits gave more pain ease by mouth than plain drug.
pmc-13308701:
Alessandra Micozzi and co-authors compare in 2026 two ways to time antifungal care in febrile neutropenic patients with acute leukaemia whose fever defies antibiotics. In a GIMEMA trial, 92 patients were split between care started on test signs and care started for all at once, with mould cover split evenly.

Only 58 percent of the test led group ever started antifungals, versus every patient in the treat all group here. Deaths by discharge ran lower in the test led group, and no death was blamed on fungal disease in either arm. Mean cost per patient fell by more than half with the test led path, while harms stayed alike.
pmc-13308801:
Ruimin Gao and co-authors examine in 2026 whether the brain language network answers sentences in the same way across tasks, in 52 people who read sentences and nonword lists. Tasks spanned plain reading, memory probes, and deep meaning questions, while a broad demand network served as the foil.

The same person tuned spots lit for sentences over nonwords in every task, which shows that language maps hold steady across jobs. Those spots rose a bit more for deep meaning work, while the demand network fired for both kinds under any task. Word content was easier to read out of the language spots, and task content out of the demand spots.
pmc-13309201:
Mohammed Osman, Ammar Saed Aldien, and Elena Netchiporouk lay out in 2026 five key points on systemic sclerosis, a rare autoimmune disease. It brings vessel harm and organ scarring, and it touches about 4 per 100,000 person years in Canada. Women over 50 years are hit most, and work dusts like silica and solvents raise the risk.

The disease marks a top cause of secondary Raynaud attacks in adults, where fingers blanch and ache in the cold with pits or ulcers. Skin, gut, and lung harm follow, with lung states the deadliest part of the course in these patients. Yearly blood pressure, kidney, and urine checks, plus first lung and heart scans, anchor the watch. Early drugs and quit smoking pleas round out care.
pmc-13309601:
Yang Qiao surveys why many cancers stop responding to multiple drugs in a 2026 review. Drug resistance stays the chief barrier to lasting cancer control. Older accounts blamed pumps that push drugs out of cells, but the picture has widened a great deal since then.

Resistance now reads as a shifting survival plan across a mixed tumor under drug pressure. Inside cells, drugs get moved, trapped, or dodged by alternate death routes. Around cells, support tissue builds barriers, signals pass between cells, and immune attack gets muted. The review weighs current treatment dead ends against these layers. The author argues that durable control needs plans that hit several layers at once.
pmc-13309801:
Mercy Amo Aggrey and co-authors survey views on eating palm weevil larvae in Kumasi, Ghana, in a 2026 study. The larvae, locally called akokono, are a traditional food rich in protein, yet they rarely enter commercial processed foods. Gauging public openness is a first step toward such products.

A survey of 150 people in Ayeduase used street intercepts and referral chains to reach respondents. About 41.3 percent already ate the larvae, with taste the top reason given by eaters in the survey. Among non-eaters, 58.8 percent said they would try the larvae inside processed products, and sausage was the favorite form. The authors see a workable market if taste and trust are handled well.
pmc-13310501:
Yaxian Ma and co-authors report a hidden gene change behind malformed sperm tails in a 2026 case study. The condition, shortened to MMAF, twists, shortens, or removes sperm tails and causes male infertility. The gene CFAP44 helps build tails, and faults in it are a known cause.

Full exome sequencing of an infertile Chinese man with sperm that could not swim forward found a double dose of a deep intronic CFAP44 change. Family testing confirmed the pattern, and splicing predictions suggested the change disrupts message cutting. Lab splicing assays and RNA checks were run to test that effect. The authors add the variant to the catalog guiding genetic counseling for this condition.
pmc-13310701:
Gyuri Kim led a 2026 pilot study on lung testing in people with chronic airflow blockage. Standard breathing tests give a narrow view of lung health, so the team added two other tools. One tool sends small air pulses to sense airway response, and the other uses detailed chest scans to map lung change.

Sixty four adults were sorted into four groups by breathing test scores. Pulse test readings at low rates tracked closely with scan signs of tissue change, mainly in the lower lobes. Airway resistance showed weaker links. Pairing the pulse test with scans may give doctors a fuller picture than breathing tests alone.
pmc-13311101:
Ziwen Jiang and Xu Jiang study trust in smart finance tools inside a cruise ship economy in a 2026 survey. Mega cruise ships form dense closed economies with constant digital payments, where users must judge safety fast. Fit between tool and setting plus felt security may drive trust more than speed alone.

A field survey aboard a mega cruise vessel drew 329 valid replies, modeled with path methods. Good setting fit lifted felt safe contact and design quality. Design quality in turn updated safety hopes and confirmed reassurance. Reassurance and safe contact proved the main drivers of trust and satisfaction. Design for spatial safety may guide operators.
pmc-13311701:
Hanna Aberra and co-authors describe building a gastroenterology fellowship in Rwanda in a 2026 article. Gut and liver disease burden in sub-Saharan Africa nearly doubled between 1990 and 2019, while specialist supply stayed tiny.

The article sets out how partners at home and abroad built the training program step by step. Endoscopy rates in East Africa run under a tenth of those in rich countries, a gap the program attacks by training local specialists who stay. Rwanda's broad health coverage and stronger primary care give the program a base. The model is offered as a path other low-resource countries could adapt.
pmc-13312001:
Gihani Manodara and co-authors, in 2026, present a study building a cell-based test that reads total estrogenic activity in water, rather than hunting single chemicals. Hormone-disrupting pollutants spread widely through water sources.

The reporter assay, built on in vitro transcription, detected estradiol spikes down to 1.0 picogram per milliliter in trial waters. Applied to river, drinking, tank, rain, and bottled waters, it found estrogenic activity in most samples. Because chemical-by-chemical testing misses mixture effects, an activity test gives a truer picture of risk. The authors call for wider monitoring with tools of this kind.
pmc-13313001:
Angel Mancilla and co-authors document, in a 2026 study, the first solidly confirmed Antarctic sleeper shark from northern Chile. Sleeper sharks are big, slow deep-sea animals almost never recorded in the southeastern Pacific, and old Chilean reports lacked the proof to name the species. A gravid female hauled up by a deep-sea longline fishery off Antofagasta offered a rare chance.

During handling she released a late-stage male embryo, 90.5 centimeters long, whose body form, dermal denticles, and 40-turn spiral valve matched the large-bodied Antarctic species. A 639-letter stretch of mitochondrial DNA from mother and embryo came back identical, as inheritance predicts. Comparison with public sequences placed the pair inside the large southern sleeper complex, though this gene alone cannot fully part the closest species. The authors stress combining anatomy, internal counts, and DNA for bycatch records.
pmc-13313301:
Murat Olukman and co-workers test a blood-vessel peptide and its blockers on breast cancer cells in a 2026 lab study. Urotensin-II tightens vessels and acts in the brain, heart, and kidneys, and both it and its receptor GPR14 show up in breast tumors, with higher blood levels in patients.

No prior work had tested blockers of this receptor in breast cancer. So the team grew MCF-7 breast cancer cells and dosed them with the peptide and with blockers of unlike chemical shape. A WST-8 test gauged cell growth and its slowing. They also measured genes tied to spread and hormone response, named in the report as MTA-1, ESR1, Kiss1, and the genes for the peptide and its receptor. The study opens a fresh angle on whether this vessel path can be turned against breast tumors.
pmc-13313601:
Zeyu Fu and colleagues build a benchmark for single-cell data methods in their 2026 paper. Tools that compress data from millions of cells into maps often wobble. Random sampling adds noise, and each study uses its own test sets, which blocks fair comparison.

Their system, scCCVGBen, is anchored on a graph autoencoder that couples cell groups to centroids. Three choices define it. The steady mean of the learned spread serves as the cell embedding. A coupled bottleneck rebuilds the data two ways. A graph attention encoder runs over a nearest-neighbor cell graph. The benchmark varies the core method, encoder, graph build, data set, and scoring suite as free axes. That split design lets labs compare methods fairly on gene and chromatin data alike.
pmc-13314501:
Yangtian Ye and colleagues weigh a protein called LARP1 in breast cancer in work published in 2026. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women worldwide, and fresh markers that foretell outlook and guide therapy are still needed.

LARP1 binds RNA and sits downstream of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR path, with links to several cancers but a murky role in breast cancer. The team mined large databases such as TCGA, GTEx, and HPA, then mapped its partner networks and immune ties with web tools. Lab proof followed in two breast cancer cell lines with LARP1 silenced, using growth, spread, and flow tests, plus animal models and tissue arrays. LARP1 ran high in tumor tissue against normal tissue, as the authors report. The joined data cast it as both a warning sign and a lever on the immune setting of tumors.
pmc-13314801:
Jediah Grace Arellano and co-workers test whether a blood inflammation marker tracks depression severity in US adults, in work published in 2026. Body-wide inflammation may feed low mood, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein is a standard gauge of that state.

The team used national survey data from 2015 to 2023 covering 15,525 adults, as counted in the report. Depression was scored by the PHQ-9 questionnaire and split at a score of 10, while the marker was split at 3 mg per liter. Models that respect the survey design and adjust for social and health traits found high marker levels tied to high symptom severity. Those above the cut had odds higher by a margin the authors give as 26 percent, kept mid-sentence as reported. The link backs inflammation checks in mood care.
pmc-13315001:
Hamed Karami, Sifur Safuka Chowdhury, and Alexandra Smirnova model bird flu spread in US poultry on a network, in a study of 2026. The 2022 to 2025 outbreak hit millions of farm and backyard birds, cutting egg and meat output and costing farms dearly.

Their partly random network model treats farms and wild birds as nodes tied by contact and migration. Settings were fit from wild bird movement, past outbreak data, and farm counts by state, as the authors describe. Spread rides on wildlife motion, season, and farm-to-farm links. Unlike world models, theirs is tuned to US farm shape and current US control steps. Paired with optimization tools, the model can test which controls, from culls to movement bans, choke an outbreak fastest.
pmc-13315501:
Xin-yue Kong, Ya-nan Song, and Hai-rong Wang tracked a bacterial toxin in chickens in a 2026 study of necrotic enteritis, a costly gut disease of poultry. The NetB toxin from Clostridium perfringens is a key cause of the damage, yet where it goes in the body and what it targets were still unknown.

Using a custom antibody, the team built tissue staining and a sandwich ELISA test to follow the toxin after infection with type G bacteria. Toxin showed in heart, lungs, spleen, kidneys, liver, and small intestine by day three, strongest in the jejunum. By day fourteen only small amounts stayed in the gut.
pmc-13316201:
Andrea Tonelli and co-authors validated in animals in 2026 a pore-network model that predicts which scaffold designs let vessels grow through. What matters for vascular regrowth is not total empty space. It is continuous paths wider than a set size that cross the full scaffold thickness, a trait they call angio-permissivity.

Combining micro-CT scans, deep learning image sharpening, and network modeling, they compared three electrospun scaffold designs and checked predictions in rats at seven and twenty-one days. Modeling exposed a porosity paradox, where the airiest designs lacked through paths and integrated poorly, linking architecture to matrix remodeling and new vessels.
pmc-13316301:
A Lefevre and co-authors report a 2026 case of a rare graft infection in a 59-year-old man with a long vascular history. The germ found, Listeria monocytogenes, seldom attacks artificial blood vessel grafts, which makes the axillofemoral bypass case stand out in the surgical literature.

Doctors advised taking the infected graft out, the usual gold standard, paired with a new bypass route and targeted antibiotics. The patient refused surgery, so care shifted to long-term antibiotics alone. The report uses his course to show how hard choices get when a risky operation meets heavy other illness. It also reminds clinicians that late, focused graft infections can come from germs seeded through the blood.
pmc-13317001:
Jessiel Gonçalves de Souza and colleagues pooled, in a 2026 review, studies comparing two ways to fix a common childhood elbow break. The lateral condyle fracture of the upper arm bone was fixed with thin Kirschner wires or hollow screws. Surgeons debate which holds better with fewer harms.

Thirteen studies with 1,230 children fed the pooled math. Screw fixing cut infection risk sharply, with a risk ratio of 0.27 in the combined estimate, and gave slightly better function scores. Overall complications, overgrowth, stiffness, and failed healing did not differ clearly. Age and break severity did not change the picture. Screws look preferable, the authors say, though each child's case still guides the final choice.
pmc-13317201:
Sylvia B Khalil and Caitlin H Kowalski review, in a 2026 article, how skin microbes reshape the fatty landscape they live in, and how that landscape reshapes them back. Skin is rich in lipids, and resident microbes eat them, change them, and release new fats that steer rivals, immunity, and barrier strength.

Microbe-made fats, from short-chain acids to cell coat lipids, now count as part of the skin's own lipid map. They support balance in health and feed trouble in acne and eczema when balance slips. The review gathers fresh work on where these lipids come from and what they do, and argues they are an underused source of ideas for skin therapies.
pmc-13318501:
Harushi Ueno and colleagues give a 2026 case report of robot-assisted lung surgery. A 56-year-old woman had early lung cancer. She also had lymphangioleiomyomatosis linked to tuberous sclerosis. That rare disease leaves lung tissue extremely fragile, so air leaks are a major risk.

The team used a da Vinci Xi system and a no-touch method with rolled gauze. They avoided cutting through lung tissue where possible. An assistant used hand staplers lined with reinforcing material for key divisions. A tiny leak found on careful testing was sealed with sheets and glue. The patient left hospital on day five. Breathing function one year later was better than predicted.
pmc-13318701:
Jingge Miao and colleagues present a 2026 case report of two breast cancers at once. A 48-year-old woman had a primary breast carcinoma. She also had breast spread from a high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma. That combination is exceptionally uncommon and hard to tell apart.

She arrived with chest fluid, a swollen abdomen, masses on both ovaries, and several breast lumps. Biopsies showed two distinct adenocarcinoma patterns in the breast. Marker testing supported one primary breast tumour and one ovarian spread. Her ovarian cancer was staged IVB, with wide involvement. Treatment mixed chemotherapy, surgery, and maintenance drugs including bevacizumab and fluzoparib. At last follow-up on December 20, 2025, no progression was seen.
pmc-13318801:
Martina Pagliuca leads a large team reviewing, in 2026, the long road after breast cancer for young women. Better detection and treatment mean more young survivors live for decades. Their challenges extend far beyond active treatment. Life stage makes them distinct: careers, relationships, and family plans are still unfolding.

Physical effects include bone loss from early ovarian failure, thinking problems, and lasting fatigue. Hormone therapies add hot flushes, poor sleep, weight gain, and sexual difficulties. Anxiety, depression, trauma symptoms, and fear of recurrence are common. Fertility questions loom large, including pregnancy safety and pausing hormone therapy. Work return and money strain add social pressure. The authors urge tailored, team-based survivorship care with early counselling.
pmc-13318901:
Wiktoria Stasica and Alicja Anna Binkowska report a 2026 cross-sectional survey study of substance use and compulsive sexual behaviour in adults. Anonymous online questionnaires ran from May to October 2025. Standard scales measured alcohol use, cannabis use, compulsive sexual behaviour, and problematic pornography use. The sample was non-clinical.

In total, 158 adults aged 18 to 60 were analysed, and 61.4 percent were women. Heavier alcohol or cannabis use tracked with higher compulsive behaviour scores at first. After adjusting for age and gender, none of those links stayed significant. Effect sizes were small in the adjusted models reported. The authors suggest demographic differences may explain the raw associations. They call for long-term studies and methods that handle many zero scores better.
pmc-13319001:
Su Su and colleagues report a 2026 real-world cohort study of a blood-activating Chinese polyherbal preparation in older patients. Participants had ischaemic heart or brain vessel disease. Data came from the Beijing medical insurance database. The team compared herbal plus antiplatelet treatment against either one alone.

In total, 12,113 patients aged 65 or older were included, with a median age of 77. Most, 78.2 percent, received the combination in this cohort. Combined treatment linked to lower odds of major cardiac and cerebrovascular events. The odds ratio was 0.687 against antiplatelet treatment alone in their analysis. Bleeding risk did not rise significantly with the combination. Several statistical approaches gave consistent results, supporting the pairing as a possible add-on strategy.
pmc-13319101:
Lorrie Maccario and colleagues present a 2026 metagenomic study of microbes preserved in ancient waste heaps at Greenland settlements. Middens from Paleo-Inuit, Norse, and early colonial sites may hold old pathogens in cold, wet ground. The team took 78 midden samples across West and South Greenland. Another 143 soil samples from nearby ground gave a baseline.

Middens carried a distinct microbe signature rich in human-linked bacteria. Opportunistic pathogens such as Clostridium perfringens appeared among them. In some colonial layers, two Clostridium species together reached roughly 40 to 50 percent of counted abundance. Resistance genes from 17 classes were found at all sites. An eroding midden's bacteria stayed local, quickly replaced by marine microbes downslope. Spread into nearby ground looks limited so far.
pmc-13320101:
Xunuo Ma and co-authors review ways to help moved body fat survive in a 2026 article on stem cells from fat. Own fat is easy to take, kind to the body, and looks natural once placed, yet much of it melts away, with kept volume swinging widely across reports. Two cell boosts were built to fight that loss, one fresh mixed cell brew and one lab grown pure stem cell set.

Pooled proof shows the fresh brew lifts kept volume a bit, while lab grown cells lift it far more, at the cost of stricter making rules. Stem cells help through growth signals, calm of swelling, tiny parcel messages, and even sharing cell power parts. Uses span breast rebuilds, face refresh, scars, wounds, and hair, with gels and rich plasma as extra aids.
pmc-13320201:
Yu Zhang and co-authors build a forecast score for low blood oxygen during sleepy stomach scope checks in a 2026 study. Such checks are common and safe for most, yet oxygen dips strike often under sedation. Neck and throat measures taken by ultrasound before sedation were tested as early warning signs.

A total of 218 patients at one center had throat measures and body facts logged before their checks. Six measures stood out as solo warning signs, covering body weight index, skin to bone and skin to voice box spans, tongue depth, jaw span, and jaw glide. Joined in one score they sorted patients with near perfect sharpness in this group. The score could help teams plan airway care in advance.
pmc-13320401:
Hoc Le-Hieu and co-authors present a survey data set on job readiness among engineering students in Vietnam in a 2026 data article. Factories now run on digital tools, so new engineers must show both craft skill and ready to work habits from day one. Student views on their own readiness and its drivers were gathered to help schools tune their courses.

An online survey ran from late December 2025 to mid January 2026 and drew 439 valid replies from students at colleges across Vietnam, all joining by choice. Forty nine items span background facts, active study habits, school engagement, self belief, skill use, and job readiness itself. The set sits in a public store for reuse by schools and labor planners.
pmc-13320501:
Diana Kurmangali and co-authors publish a 2026 draft genome for a helpful bacterium taken from koumiss, a fermented milk drink, in the Akmola region of Kazakhstan. The strain, Levilactobacillus brevis 3LB, is held in the national collection under the code B-RKM 0546. Such strains matter for food making and for probiotic research.

Reading on an Illumina MiSeq machine and assembly with SPAdes gave a genome of about 2.3 million letters with 150 times coverage. The draft holds 63 pieces, 2260 coding genes, 61 transfer RNA genes, and 2 CRISPR regions. Gene sorting showed the largest groups tied to daily cell work, food use, and handling of stored information.
pmc-13321801:
Karim Tazibet and co-authors ask whether immune suppressing drugs before lung transplant worsen outcomes in scarred lung disease in a 2026 study. Fibrosing lung diseases are the leading reason for lung transplant and already fare worse than other groups. Records covered 209 adults transplanted at one centre from April 2011 to June 2024.

Seventy-six patients, or 36 percent, had received non-steroid immune drugs in the prior year. That group had worse one year transplant free survival, at 62 percent against 80 percent for others in adjusted analysis. Early graft failure, chest fistula, pneumonia, and resistant virus infection were all more common after such exposure. Pre-transplant drug history should weigh in planning.
pmc-13321901:
Rachel Weil and David M Loeb review immunotherapy for children's bone sarcomas in a 2026 article. In spread, relapsed, or resistant disease, outcomes have barely moved for decades despite combined standard care. These tumours suppress immunity, carry few mutations, and offer few targets, all of which blunt immune drugs.

Trials now span natural killer cell therapy, cytokine priming, CAR T cells, and a growing set of RNA based treatments. Checkpoint blockers are also being tested, often paired with other immune or targeted drugs. The authors weigh early promise against clear limits and argue that deeper grasp of sarcoma immune biology must guide the next, more effective wave of care.
pmc-13322901:
Erica Santaguida, Giuseppe Pagnoni and Massimo Bergamasco recast attachment as a joint modelling process between mother and infant, in a 2026 theory article. They use active inference, where the brain builds a model of the world and updates it through exchange with others.

In their account, a baby's internal working model forms through repeated exchanges with the mother, starting before birth. How steady and precise maternal care feels shapes how firm the baby's predictions become, which in turn organises secure or less secure attachment. The framework joins brain, gene and developmental views under one account, offers testable predictions, and points to early support and to how attachment patterns pass across generations.
pmc-13323301:
Jiacai Zuo and colleagues report emergency hybrid stenting for a carotid artery tear after major aortic surgery, in a 2026 case report. A 48-year-old man had full repair for acute type A aortic dissection, covering root, ascending aorta, arch and a descending stent graft.

About 26 hours later he developed severe right-sided weakness, and imaging showed the left common carotid artery nearly blocked with slow flow beyond. Normal catheter routes were barred by the rebuilt arch, so surgeons opened the neck and entered the artery backwards, placing three overlapping stents. Final imaging showed full reperfusion without stray clots, and recovery stayed strong with open stents at follow-up.
pmc-13324501:
Joanna Siuda and colleagues describe a hard treatment balance in a 2026 case report on Parkinson disease with bipolar disorder. Drugs that lift dopamine can unsettle mood, while mood drugs can worsen movement, which narrows choices for both illnesses.

Their patient, a 47-year-old man with bipolar disorder since age 18, developed Parkinson signs at 36 and later strong motor swings. Several mood drugs had failed or caused harm before lurasidone, quetiapine, and lamotrigine steadied him. A steady skin infusion of foslevodopa and foscarbidopa then eased his motor fluctuations. Mood stayed stable through treatment, with no psychiatric breakdown. The case hints this infusion may suit some patients once barred from advanced dopamine therapy.
pmc-13327401:
Mustafa Ozdemir describes a 2026 case linking a rare sexual symptom to later obsessive-compulsive illness. A 26-year-old single man first had ejaculation with no desire, arousal, or pleasure while seated at a barber shop. Shame followed, and he began avoiding barbers, then developed thoughts of being dirty or morally stained.

Washing habits, repeated religious rituals, and avoidance spread, and a second episode while driving led him to stop driving altogether. His Yale-Brown score was 28 at assessment, in the severe range. Treatment with fluoxetine brought marked improvement, the author reports. The sequence, not described before in this order, suggests clinicians should watch for obsessive symptoms after such episodes rather than treating the first event alone.
pmc-13328201:
Benoit Bertrand, Delphine Mieulet, and Jean-Christophe Breitler explain hybrid vigor in Arabica coffee in a 2026 review. Arabica is a self-pollinating allotetraploid with one of the narrowest gene bases of any major crop, yet structured crosses reliably give strong, predictable heterosis. Four decades of breeding and new genome work feed their account.

They propose two engines: blocks crossed in from the canephora parent create mosaics whose pairing restores balance, and rebalanced talks between the two ancestral subgenomes lift gene activity beyond simple addition. Together these buffer plants against stress even with little raw DNA variety. Chromosome-scale genomes and prediction models that count non-additive effects can now design hybrid groups on purpose rather than by trial.
pmc-13328401:
Wu Ling and co-authors test added continuing care after childbirth prolapse in a 2026 trial. One hundred women with postpartum uterine prolapse were randomized evenly between early pelvic floor training alone and the same training plus continuity of care, with blinded outcome checks. Muscle signals and mood were tracked to three months.

Both groups improved, yet the added-care group gained stronger pelvic floor muscles, with more women reaching grade 3 or better. Their resting muscle signal values also fell further at one and three months. Baseline mood scores differed slightly and were handled by adjustment in the analysis. Steady follow-up contact, not exercises alone, seems to carry part of the recovery, the authors suggest.
pmc-13328901:
Binayak Deb and co-authors present a 2026 case of a rare drug reaction in a young patient with a neck spine injury. The patient was treated in a trauma intensive care unit and developed a lasting high fever that did not settle with usual care. Doctors traced the fever to neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a dangerous response linked to drugs that block dopamine.

Core signs of the syndrome include very high temperature, stiff muscles, changed awareness, and unstable body control. Those signs can look like common problems after surgery or in intensive care, so diagnosis is hard. Quick suspicion and prompt treatment led to a good outcome here. The authors urge close watch when such drugs are used in intensive care.
pmc-13330401:
Yingcheng Qin and colleagues report a hard-to-treat Salmonella infection in a man with acute erythroid leukaemia in a 2026 case. The Kentucky strain resisted many drug classes, including carbapenems and ciprofloxacin, after chemotherapy left the patient vulnerable. Tests showed an NDM enzyme, and gene sequencing found blaNDM-5 plus two other resistance genes.

Lab synergy checks showed that aztreonam paired with ceftazidime-avibactam worked together against the strain. The patient was treated with that pair and recovered, the authors report. Layered testing, from drug response to immune assays to full gene reads, guided the choice. Mechanism-based pairing offers a path for such infections in blood cancer care.
pmc-13330501:
Hicran Uzun Karka and Songul Kesen study how harvest season changes tea leaf traits in a 2026 report. Leaves were compared from May through September for water content, acidity, ash, colour, minerals, chemical fingerprints, aroma, and antioxidant strength. Tea quality in Turkey's Black Sea region depends heavily on such seasonal shifts.

Water content fell from 75.3 percent in May to 70.5 percent in September across the season in the reported values. Leaf brightness dropped as green pigment broke down. Potassium fell while calcium rose late in the season, and early leaves held more manganese and iron. Total aroma compounds peaked in July. Antioxidant strength fell from spring to autumn, backing the view that early harvests are richest.
pmc-13333301:
Irene B Heijink and colleagues introduce EStiMapp in 2026, a free software tool that organizes what doctors learn when they stimulate electrodes inside the brains of epilepsy patients. Such mapping, done before surgery, reveals which areas drive seizures and which handle vital functions, but results were traditionally scribbled as free text and redrawn by hand.

The team defined shared categories for evoked symptoms from literature and expert consensus, then co-designed a graphical interface around them. Responses are annotated in a standard way inside the EEG software, and the tool renders them at once as a 2D electrode overview, a 3D brain view, and a per-electrode table. Usability testing gave a mean System Usability Scale score of 82.3, rated excellent. The authors say the open-source workflow cuts errors and makes stimulation findings easier to read uniformly.
pmc-13334401:
Laura J. Leighton and co-authors showed that systemically delivered messenger RNA nanoparticles can reach liver tumors in a 2026 preclinical study. mRNA drugs reliably enter healthy liver after intravenous dosing, but whether they enter primary and metastatic liver tumors was unclear.

The team gave mRNA lipid nanoparticles intravenously in mouse models. Nearly all liver cells took up the cargo in healthy, fibrotic, and cirrhotic livers, and many cells inside spontaneous liver cancers did too. Delivery also worked in xenograft models of primary and secondary liver cancer, though protein output ran lower than in normal liver tissue. The results support developing intravenous mRNA treatments for liver disease and for cancers growing in the liver, where options for advanced disease remain limited.
pmc-13335801:
Robert Zheng and co-authors reported a 2026 case of a congenital aortic defect first diagnosed in a 67-year-old woman with stubborn hypertension. Her blood pressure sat at 170/80 despite eight years of medication, with no murmur but faint foot pulses and an ankle-brachial index of 0.5 on both sides.

CT and aortography showed a type A interruption of the aortic arch beyond a dilated left subclavian artery. Rich collateral channels from the chest arteries kept her legs supplied, and high renin activity pointed to the interruption as the hypertension's cause. Surgeons placed a bypass graft from the left subclavian artery to the descending aorta. Her pressure normalized at once and stayed controlled through a year of follow-up. The authors urge doctors to consider this rare defect in unexplained hypertension with weak leg pulses.
pmc-13336901:
Yuanyuan Du and co-authors borrow a maize gene trick to supercharge yeast protein factories in a 2026 study. World protein demand rises while farm-based supply strains land and climate. Moving a nitrogen-handling enzyme, asparagine synthetase, into the yeast Pichia pastoris rewired its metabolism across the whole cell.

A strain with three copies of the gene reached a crude protein share of 62.48%, total amino acids of 47.86%, and branched-chain amino acids of 8.05% in the reported product, beating common protein sources on those measures. Modeling and gene data showed the enzyme couples two core cycles and switches on a nitrogen sensor circuit that feeds itself. Farm-free protein from microbes could ease pressure on agriculture.
pmc-13337401:
Wei Fan and co-authors compare brace care with surgery in simple Mason II radial head fractures in a 2026 study from Xi'an Honghui Hospital. Records covered 65 patients aged 18–65 years treated between January 2018 and January 2021: 36 had open surgery with internal fixation, and 29 were managed conservatively with braces.

Both groups healed in roughly ten weeks and regained similar elbow motion. Function scores landed close together, at 90.82 points for brace care and 91.44 points for surgery on the Broberg–Morrey scale used. One malunion occurred with braces, while surgery brought two infections and two fixation failures. With no clear edge for surgery, the authors support weighing patient factors case by case.
pmc-13337701:
Lillian C. Chen and colleagues explore views on digital care tools in a 2026 focus group study. Patients and clinicians from two fields took part: young adult mental health and prenatal care. Discussion centered on platforms for care delivery, with special attention to AI chatbots.

Both groups saw real benefits in chatbot tools, and both raised worries. Concerns included misuse, missed clinical context, and unclear accuracy. The authors call for plain and culturally fitting language, clear sourcing, and warnings to check with a clinician. They also urge rules that curb bias and misuse, so digital tools support care rather than quietly replacing judgment.
pmc-13339501:
Hemen Najar and a large team lay out the LAGOM trial protocol for heart-metabolic health in psychosis in a 2026 article. Heart disease, diabetes, and obesity shorten life greatly for people with psychotic disorders. Six outpatient clinics in Gothenburg, Sweden, host the program.

Clinics are grouped so whole sites deliver either the combined lifestyle program or usual care for 36 months. The program blends diet, activity, and medical follow-up inside regular psychiatric visits. Outcomes cover metabolic risk, lifestyle, and quality of life. A natural, clinic-based design tests whether integrated care works under real service conditions at scale.
pmc-13340101:
Sankar Prasad Chaki and a large team track coronavirus genomes across a university from 2020 to 2024 in a 2026 surveillance study. A large, globally mixed campus can mirror worldwide viral evolution. Clinical and screening samples supplied the sequences.

Genomes numbered 1,786 from clinical testing and 888 from surveillance as reported. Local patterns matched global trends: variants arrived in phases, lineages were introduced in bursts, and dominant clades shifted over time. Diversity peaked in fall terms and ran highest in undergraduate-aged groups. Tree analysis fit a semi-contained, high-contact setting, supporting campuses as early-warning sentinels.
pmc-13340201:
Wes Baumgartner leads a 2026 reference chapter on lesions of the fish nervous system for toxicology pathologists. Vertebrate brains share a three-part plan, yet fish brains stay simpler and laid along the body axis. Species variation in form and tissue detail complicates harm assessment.

Forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain parts are compared with mammals, rodents, and humans in standardized format. Microscopic findings are listed with shared diagnostic names under the INHAND series. Unlike mammals, the fish forebrain does not balloon into a cortex covering other parts as detailed. The guide helps labs separate normal species traits from true nervous injury.
pmc-13341301:
Arctigenin, a plant lignan from burdock, is reviewed as a candidate cancer drug by Deena Elsori and colleagues in 2026. The compound slows growth in liver, stomach, lung, and colon cancer cells and shows antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions in lab work.

Across tumor types it triggers cell-cycle arrest, caspase-driven cell death, and proteasome effects, and it lowers factors tied to spread and blood vessel growth such as VEGF and matrix metalloproteinases. Poor water solubility limits it, though amino acid ester forms may improve its behavior. The authors map shared targets across prostate, cervical, and other cancers while flagging how much evidence remains preclinical.
pmc-13341501:
Routine checkup data can flag hidden diabetes, in a 2026 modeling study by Hui Xiao's team. Records from 12 Chinese tertiary hospitals supplied 11,382 people for training an XGBoost model and 1,026 for testing, using only body and lifestyle data from standard exams.

The final model used 12 predictors, dominated by fasting blood glucose at 50.6% importance, followed by creatinine, triglycerides, age, and LDL cholesterol. On the test set it reached an AUC of 77.2%, a moderate performance. The authors propose embedding such scoring in health examinations to prompt confirmatory testing, while stressing that outside validation and prospective trials still lie ahead.
pmc-13341801:
Malnutrition, frailty, and muscle loss overlap heavily in cancer patients, in a 2026 survey by Lixue Cui and colleagues. The Ningxia study recruited 476 patients with comorbid cancer from two top-tier hospitals during 2025, screening nutrition risk, frailty, and sarcopenia with standard scales.

Malnutrition risk appeared in 31.3% and sarcopenia in 65.7%, while a quarter of patients, 122 people (25.6%), carried all three conditions at once. Frailty and sarcopenia overlapped most at 55.2%. Older age, advanced tumor stage, and rural residence raised the triple burden, while stronger socioeconomic support protected against it. Screening for one condition alone plainly misses the cluster.
pmc-13342001:
An immune sensor that both helps and harms in gynecologic cancers is reviewed by Yibo He and research partners in a 2026 mini-review. The NLRP3 inflammasome detects cellular danger, and the authors trace its opposing roles across ovarian, endometrial, and cervical cancers.

In ovarian cancer it can enforce immune suppression yet also raise chemotherapy sensitivity through cell-death signaling. Endometrial effects flip with molecular subtype. Cervical cancer viruses actively silence it to dodge surveillance. A tumor PD-L1 and NLRP3 axis drives resistance to checkpoint therapy broadly, while NLRP3-activating vaccines and agonists might thaw cold tumors, making the sensor a combination-therapy lever.
pmc-13349001:
Juyoung Jenna Yun and colleagues test room sensors that watch Parkinson walking without wearables, in a validation study from 2026. Fifteen patients with mild disease and fourteen matched healthy adults walked four metres in a living lab, patients repeating the walk in on and off medicine states. While depth cameras, radar, and a smart floor each timed stride length, stride time, and speed.

Stride time matched best across devices, while stride length matched less tightly yet still split off-state patients from healthy walkers for both camera and radar in the reported tests. Radar alone split on from off states, and on-state walking looked healthy, backing passive home watching for daily swings.
pmc-13349401:
Yula Salifu and colleagues track women empowerment gains and gaps in Ghana over two decades, in a survey study published in 2026. National health survey waves from 2003 to 2022 scored married women aged 15 to 49 on social independence, household decisions. The domains include views on violence. Fairness measures were split by region, wealth, schooling, age, and town or country living.

High empowerment rose in all three areas, with violence views jumping from 61.6 to 79.2 percent between 2008 and 2022. Yet decision power fell back after 2014 in the reported trend. Social independence stayed the most unequal area, with a 45-point regional gap and teen coverage under 5 percent, and schooling drove most of that split.
pmc-13350301:
Sayali S Dongare and colleagues compared a saliva marker across gum disease and liver scarring in a 2026 cross-sectional study of 40 people. Four groups of ten covered liver cirrhosis with gum disease, cirrhosis alone, gum disease alone, and healthy controls.

The marker, NGAL, spills from white blood cells during inflammation and tissue injury. Gum health was scored by standard criteria and saliva levels measured by a lab antibody test. Two long-lasting inflammatory diseases may reinforce each other, and a spit test is far easier than blood or tissue sampling. The study is the first to ask whether this marker behaves differently when the two conditions meet.
pmc-13351101:
Gaurav Singhal and Bernhard T. Baune reanalysed ageing behaviour data from mice in a 2026 computational study. Most ageing studies read each behaviour test alone, missing how abilities hang together.

Their workflow standardised features and built combined scores for six domains, from movement and anxiety to memory and sociability. Combined scores showed no broad age or sex split. Drilling into single features found modest movement differences and the clearest ageing signal in a maze efficiency measure. The mismatch warns that lumping tests into domains can hide real changes, while single tests can exaggerate them, a caution for designing ageing studies.
pmc-13352401:
Rong Liufu leads a 2026 Chinese validation study of the revised SOFA 2 organ failure score. The update aims to spot acute organ failure earlier, though sparse data in low-resource settings can limit scores. Records held 118,542 adults admitted to intensive care from 2014 to 2024, with scores computed over the first seven days.

Deaths in intensive care totalled 5,286 patients out of the full cohort studied. That death count equals 4.45 percent of all patients in the intensive care cohort. Higher SOFA 2 scores tracked with higher death rates across groups. The new score separated survivors from non-survivors better than the old score, reaching 80.9 percent accuracy against 76.7 percent for the older scoring system. Each added point raised the odds of death, with an odds ratio of 1.33 per point gained.
pmc-13352601:
Kajol Tonk leads a 2026 catalysis study that traps ruthenium particles at the closed ends of tiny silica pores to crack plastic chains. The design coats ruthenium on reduced graphene oxide with mesoporous silica, placing 2 nm particles solely at the bottoms of 2.9 nm pores. Mid-chain polyolefin hydrogenolysis was the test reaction.

Wax formed at rates up to 1700 grams per gram of ruthenium each hour, and bond-breaking turnover reached 130 per minute. Both values beat a nonporous twin by wide margins, at 23-fold and 16-fold. Methane waste fell to about 30 percent of the twin's level. Narrower 2.3 nm pores improved wax selectivity further, and rates peaked at a hydrogen pressure of 37 bar.
pmc-13353101:
Huanan Li and colleagues test belly massage for diarrhoea-led irritable bowel syndrome in rats in 2026. The common gut disorder has tangled causes and incomplete explanations. Rats were made ill through early maternal separation plus chronic stress, then treated with massage or with stool transfer from massaged rats.

Massage eased diarrhoea, gut sensitivity, transit speed, and anxiety-like behaviour. Gut microbe diversity recovered, short-chain fatty acid levels fell, and a key inflammatory chain through TLR4 and NF-kappaB was suppressed. Barrier damage also healed, with tighter cell junctions and lower leak. Stool transfer copied most gains, pointing to microbes as a main route of benefit.
pmc-13354701:
Andrea Leung and John Koo write in 2026 from a United States skin and mind clinic about delusional skin disorders. People with these illnesses firmly believe that bugs or bits of matter are in or on their skin, though no such cause is found. Many refuse mental health referral, so skin doctors often must lead the care.

Drugs such as pimozide and risperidone can ease symptoms, but strong proof on which drug works best is scarce. The authors stress a full workup, kind and honest talk, and close safety checks while drugs are used. They argue that trust built in the skin clinic often opens the door to real relief.
pmc-13354801:
Yiran Tao and co-authors report a 2026 plant study on moving RNA across graft joins to change traits without adding foreign genes. Grafting joins a shoot to a root stock, and some RNAs travel through the joined plant. The team built a live-image test to screen which RNAs move and to find the short parts that let them travel.

Of 100 RNAs screened, three moved reliably, and one moved best in both ways. The team found two short elements in that RNA and showed that doubling one made a strong delivery tag. With that tag, they sent three RNAs that do not move on their own across graft joins and saw effects in the tissue that got them.
pmc-13355001:
Marie-Paule Morin and co-authors interviewed teens with juvenile arthritis in 2025 about teaching medical students as patient-educators. Adult patients often help teach, but teens rarely do, even for child health topics. Nineteen patients aged 13 to 18 at two Canadian children's centers shared what would draw them in or hold them back.

Teens said they wanted to learn about their own illness, meet peers, help students learn, and raise awareness. School load, travel, and shyness about sharing in big groups were the main blocks. Parent support, volunteer hours, and having health staff in sessions would help. The findings guide how to build lasting teen educator programs.
pmc-13355201:
Kayla E Tate and Kristina S Petersen analyzed United States survey data in 2026 to link food choices with diet quality in adults. Diet quality was scored by the Healthy Eating Index-2020, and data came from a national health survey run from 2017 to early 2020. The team weighed habits people can change, such as reading food labels, against fixed traits.

Adults who rarely read labels scored about seven points lower than frequent label readers. Eating many meals away from home and rating one's own diet as poor also linked to lower scores. The authors suggest that programs should target several habits at once to lift diet quality in a real way.
pmc-13359001:
Francisco F Costa Filho and co-authors measure hospital deaths in two rare vessel diseases in a 2026 study. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis inflame small blood vessels and can wreck the lungs and kidneys. When patients with these diseases develop acute breathing failure, the stakes are high. The team used a national United States hospital database to count outcomes.

They found about 21,430 weighted hospital stays from 2016 to 2021 where the diseases paired with breathing failure. Most patients had the first disease, and the average age was about 64. Finding which factors during the stay predict death can help hospitals plan intensive care for this fragile group.
pmc-13359401:
Olaia Akesolo-Atutxa and co-authors study how a mother's diet echoes in her calves in a 2026 paper. Cows fed too little in late pregnancy bear smaller calves, which can cost beef farms money. The team asked whether hydroxytyrosol, a natural antioxidant from olive waste, could soften that harm when added to the feed of underfed cows.

Calves of underfed mothers started the fattening phase smaller but caught up once fed well. The antioxidant showed no broad effect, yet calves whose mothers received it ended about 31 kilograms heavier than those whose mothers did not. The hint of benefit supports more work on this cheap, sustainable supplement.
pmc-13361301:
Armando Cevenini and co-authors issued this 2026 correction to their 2025 paper on human cytomegalovirus infection. Their paper, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences, asked what flips this common virus between quiet latency and active growth, pointing to epigenetic triggers. The correction concerns one source the paper cited, a 2014 study on a gene called GFI1 and the virus's main switch promoter.

That cited study was retracted in January 2026. The authors note the retracted source was used only once in their paper, in a single section. Corrections like this keep the record honest when a building block of a paper falls away. Readers of the virus paper can now judge how much weight that one citation carried and treat the linked claim with care.
pmc-13362301:
Qinaer Beikan and co-authors tested a plant compound against heart rhythm risk in obese rats in a 2026 study. Obesity breeds oxidative stress and inflammation that remodel the heart and invite dangerous rhythms. Berberine, from medicinal plants, is known to calm rhythms, and an anti-aging protein called Klotho may carry its effect. Fat-fed rats received berberine for eight weeks.

Heart tracings showed the treatment shortened stretched electrical intervals linked to risk. In isolated hearts mapped with light, berberine wiped out arrhythmia susceptibility, which fell from 60 percent to zero. It steadied the heart's electrical wave, sped conduction back to normal, and fixed calcium handling in cells. The authors tie the gains to Klotho-driven cuts in oxidative stress and inflammation.
pmc-13363501:
Ting Zhao and colleagues report a 2026 trial of a structured diet for patients with gout, the painful joint disease driven by uric acid crystals. Ninety patients were split evenly: one group got standard nutrition advice, and the other followed a 42-day plan that was low in purines, cut calories, and kept nutrients balanced. Blood uric acid, urine handling of uric acid, weight, and belly fat were compared.

The diet group cut blood uric acid far more than controls and cleared more uric acid through the kidneys, while daily purine intake dropped sharply. Body mass index and deep belly fat also fell more in the diet group. The authors present the plan as drug-free support that tackles both gout and its metabolic risks.
pmc-13363901:
Xinyu Zhou and colleagues present a 2026 study on mepiquat chloride, a growth regulator, as a drought aid for soybean seedlings. Two varieties, one drought-tolerant and one sensitive, were stressed with a chemical that mimics dry soil, then sprayed with the regulator at five doses. The team tracked shoot and root growth, protective enzymes, and the sugars and amino acids plants use to hold water.

Mid doses worked best: shoots grew less, saving water loss, while roots grew more, reaching for water, and protective enzymes rose as cell damage markers fell. The best dose differed by variety, higher for the sensitive one. An overdose bent growth off course. The authors frame the regulator as a dose-tuned shield, not a blanket spray.
pmc-13364001:
Tue Minh Duong and colleagues present a 2026 study on the chemistry and healing potential of a Vietnamese variety of Crinum asiaticum, a lily-family plant. Screening found the leaves rich in polyphenols, flavonoids, and alkaloids, and instrument reads named nineteen main compounds in the fatty fraction. The team split the extract into solvent fractions. They tested each for antioxidant, antidiabetic, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer action in dishes, with computer checks on drug-likeness.

Different fractions led on different fronts. The chloroform part blocked a starch enzyme best and protected insulin cells. The fatty part calmed swollen immune cells. Cancer cell lines, above all cervical and liver, fell selectively, while key compounds passed drug-likeness rules. The authors flag the plant as a multitarget lead source.
pmc-13368601:

pmc-13369101:
Jiajia Deng and co-workers sum up in 2026 two needle routes for neck root pain from worn neck discs. One route, plasma coblation, shrinks the disc core to ease press. The next, pulse waves at the root knot, tunes pain calls with no flesh burn. Both dodge open knife work.

pmc-13372201:
Baby Sharma and co-authors follow one man's long sugar disease turnaround in a 2026 case report from India. At age 61 he had new type 2 sugar disease, high weight, and poor blood fats. He joined a three-month plan of plant meals, daily exercise, yoga, and calm mind work.

pmc-13373901:
Alexandria Smith Martin and Floyd Thompson review trauma stress in autistic youth in a 2026 paper. The search spanned three data banks and peer work in English from 2010 to 2025. Work on signs, tests, and care in autistic kids and teens was the core.

The review finds that trauma stress is often missed in this group. Signs can blur with autistic traits, speech gaps, sense strain, and the habit of staff to blame all on autism. Screens shaped for these youth, plus views from kin and teachers, help a lot. Fit care can then be built on a true read of the harm.
pmc-13375101:
Hadley Rahrig and co-authors argue for well-being in the act of research in a 2026 paper. Well-being is a top aim of much health work, yet those who do the work can fare poor. Rates of worry and sad mood run high in grad students and young fellows, the team notes.

Young staff bear much of the load of the science trade and feel that weight most. The paper sets key rules and hands-on steps to build well-being into lab life, not just lab aims. Steps span leads, work loads, and a tone that lets staff rest and speak. Care for staff, they hold, makes the science itself more sound.
pmc-13376201:
Khodjaeva and colleagues charted chronic hepatitis D in Uzbekistan in 2026, using records from the national virology institute for 2023 to 2024. Those patients were younger yet far sicker: about 78 percent had cirrhosis, liver scarring, against about 44 percent in hepatitis B alone. The authors call for wider access to hepatitis D therapy and screening.
pmc-13380201:
Muhammed Yusuf Afacan and a large team present a 2026 review of injuries to the ring of bones and joints that suspends the shoulder. Breaks at several points in that ring are uncommon and varied, and most published evidence comes from small case reports. That leaves surgeons with little guidance on when to operate.
