Patient factors such as age, bone quality, other illnesses, and physical demands are weighed at each step. Illustrative cases from the authors' own institution show how the framework works in practice.
pmc-13380601:
Veronika Boichenko and colleagues present a 2026 review of small RNA molecules that help control scarring in the liver and the heart. Scarring, called fibrosis, stiffens both organs and drives long-term failure. It involves activated support cells, excess scaffolding material, and inflammation in each organ.

The review compares three families of non-coding RNAs, which regulate genes without building proteins. Some of them act alike in liver and heart, switching the same scarring pathways up or down. Others behave differently depending on the organ. Because these molecules also circulate in the blood inside tiny parcels, they may serve as low-burden test markers. The comparison highlights shared drug targets across both organs.
pmc-13380801:
Thomas Roosdorp, Michael Fridén, Daniel B Ibsen, and Fredrik Rosqvist published a 2026 methods study on how nutrition researchers model swapping one food for another. When studies adjust for total energy, they are in effect estimating substitution, and earlier simulations showed the modelling choice can flip the apparent effect. Few studies had tested the approaches on real data.

The authors compared strategies using milk, fermented and not, against death from any cause in a Swedish group of 1,063 older men. Models differed in which foods they adjusted for and whether intake was counted in grams, energy, or a mix. Eighteen model versions were run. The comparison shows how much conclusions depend on choices that are often left unstated.
pmc-13382301:
Qingyi Wu and a large team present a 2026 study on adding riboflavin, a B vitamin, to duck feed to improve breast meat quality. Pekin ducks are a major meat breed. Ninety-six young ducks were fed for 28 days with either no added riboflavin or a supplemented diet, in groups with several replicates.

Supplemented ducks had firmer breast meat and thicker muscle fibres. Gene studies showed higher activity in genes that drive muscle development and contraction, and in genes for building and burning fats. Chemical profiling of the meat showed more fat-burning related compounds. The combined evidence, gathered with several large-scale methods, explains how a cheap vitamin can change meat texture and composition.
pmc-13382701:
Jack E Thirkell and colleagues present a 2026 study of resting energy use in naked mole-rats, social mammals that live underground in colonies with a single breeding female. Resting metabolic rate shapes how energy is divided between survival, breeding, and long life. Its drivers inside such a structured society were unclear.

The team measured 76 animals from five colonies, testing body mass, sex, breeding status, age, rank, and colony stability. Body mass predicted energy use most strongly, though rates were far below those expected for mammals of that size, confirming a suppressed metabolism. Breeding females ran slightly higher than non-breeders, while age and rank had no effect once mass was allowed for.
pmc-13383901:
Meixner and colleagues lay out a technique for revision repair of a ruptured quadriceps tendon, reinforced with a biocomposite scaffold, in a 2026 orthopedic technique paper. The quadriceps tendon, anchoring the thigh muscle to the kneecap, typically tears in middle-aged men, with systemic illness weakening the tissue. First-time repairs succeed. But revision surgery faces tissue quality and compromised blood supply at the failed repair site, raising rupture and weakness risk in straightening the knee.

The method combines transosseous fixation, sutures passed through tunnels in the kneecap, with a cerclage, a reinforcing loop that shares load across it. Over the scaffold the surgeons lay BioBrace, a biocomposite implant to support healing biologically while adding strength. Meixner presents the sequence, from exposure and tissue preparation to closure and rehabilitation logic, as a reproducible recipe for a problem with no standard solution. It aims to give the tendon mechanical and biological help.
pmc-13384501:
Bhakti Banerjee and co-authors reply to readers about their study of tissue oxygen during heart surgery in a 2026 response letter. The original work tracked kidney and muscle oxygen with near-infrared sensors during bypass surgery. Readers had raised points about early creatinine shifts and what they truly signal.

The authors agree that small early creatinine changes do not always mean real kidney injury. They explain design choices, including a depth rule for sensor placement and using thumb muscle as a stand-in site. Both sides converge on the view that global blood flow targets alone cannot capture local tissue supply.
pmc-13384901:
Dania Al-Qasrawi and co-authors name an early driver of pancreatic cancer growth in 2026 research. The protein ECT2, known for roles in cell division, rises early in pancreatic ductal tumors and stays high as disease advances. High levels also track with poorer patient survival in the datasets studied.

Removing ECT2 slowed transformed growth, invasion, and tumor formation in animals, with little effect on cell division itself. The protein proved needed to switch on two signaling arms that feed growth pathways. Blocking its signaling also made cancer cells more sensitive to MEK-targeted drugs, which marks a possible paired treatment route.
pmc-13386501:
Yuxiang Zhao and colleagues track antibiotic resistance genes in Chinese soils across 14 years in 2026 work. Their set of 2,243 soil metagenomes spans 2009 to 2022 and feeds an open interactive map platform. The study tests whether the national action plan period left a mark on farm soils.

After 2016, total resistance gene abundance in croplands fell markedly compared with earlier samples, with high-risk genes dropping even more steeply. Cropland profiles worldwide also grew more alike under similar farm pressures, a homogenization the authors flag. They call for global coordination joining pollution control with better farm practice.
pmc-13386601:
Ryo Kanda and colleagues use guided talking-aloud to rebuild self-monitoring after stroke in a 2026 report of two cases. Both patients had executive problems that hurt daily life despite standard tabletop cognitive training. Therapists prompted each patient to voice their thinking, catch errors, and reflect during the tasks.

After the program, both patients completed trail-making tests they could not finish before. One also stopped making medication errors, and daily goal-directed behavior improved in both cases. The authors present guided verbalization as a feasible bridge from clinic tasks to real life, while noting two cases cannot prove cause.
pmc-13387601:
Cui and colleagues trace premature ovarian insufficiency, early loss of ovarian function, to a metabolic switch thrown by a missing enzyme regulator, in 2026 reproductive biology research. In ovarian tissue from patients and a chemotherapy-induced mouse model, the NAD-dependent enzyme SIRT1 was reduced in the granulosa cells that nurse eggs. Its fall left the enzyme PKM2 over-tagged and hyperactive, flooding the cells with lactate, the end product of glycolysis, as follicles deteriorated.

Restoring SIRT1, by gene delivery or by giving nicotinamide mononucleotide, a NAD booster, reversed the picture in mice. Follicle development improved, granulosa cell death fell, and anti-Müllerian hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone normalized. The mechanism is direct: SIRT1 interacts with PKM2 and strips its acetyl tags, throttling lactate production. Cui names the SIRT1-PKM2-lactate axis a therapeutic target, with NAD-boosting compounds as the intervention for women facing early ovarian failure.
pmc-13392201:
Donald R Royall and Raymond F Palmer test, in 2026, whether being afflicted by several dementia biomarkers at once adds up to worse dementia. Their view is that dementia has many causes at once. Alzheimer's-linked markers form just one set among them.

The team used tested scoring rules on nearly a thousand scan-positive people from a national imaging pool. Each person was classed as hit by, or holding firm against, three harms. The harms were brain amyloid, blood fat signals, and nerve cell loss. Dementia severity scores rose with the number of afflicting markers, in both demented and non-demented groups, and conversion risk was also tracked. Brain doctors gain support for models with many markers. One-cause accounts of dementia look too thin in light of these data.
pmc-13392501:
Milad Noei and colleagues measured two linked molecules in breast tissue: a small regulatory RNA called miR-326, known to restrain tumours, and NOB1, a gene needed to build the cell's protein-shredding proteasome. Earlier work showed the RNA targets NOB1 messages and lowers its output. The study compared cancer tissue, tissue beside the tumour, and healthy breast tissue.

The small RNA ran markedly lower in cancer than in either comparison group, while NOB1 ran higher, and the two moved in opposite directions within samples. Test accuracy figures were fair for both markers. The authors read the pattern as support for a control link that loosens in cancer, and float both molecules as possible markers for diagnosis or treatment research.
pmc-13393801:
Li and co-authors compare, in 2026, how resident physicians fare after intensive care unit night shifts versus night shifts on other wards. Sixty-one residents at one teaching hospital completed the questionnaire after a non-ICU night shift and after a second ICU night shift, so each doctor served as their own comparison. The survey captured duty length, sleep during the shift, overnight calls and awakenings, recovery, and well-being.

ICU nights brought longer duties, less sleep during the shift, and more work-related awakenings than ward nights. Emotional exhaustion ran higher after ICU shifts, with a mean paired difference of 3.39 points on the study scale. Life satisfaction also dropped, by 8.90 points on average in the paired comparison. The authors frame night-shift burden as more than a shift count, urging residency programs to target sleep opportunity, interruptions, and recovery time in scheduling.
pmc-13394901:
Patrick Swain and colleagues test, in 2026, jumping in fake Moon gravity with tight leg cuffs as space exercise. Fourteen healthy adults jumped while hung from a tilted frame that left them at one fifth of their weight. On one visit, cuffs partly blocked leg blood flow during two-minute jump rounds. The team tracked heart rate, breath gases, muscle oxygen, and felt effort.

With cuffs, hearts beat faster and muscles held less oxygen. Breath output and the burn marker lactate also rose. Leg force dropped about the same with or without cuffs after the sets. Effort and discomfort felt higher with cuffs. The authors say the cheap setup could help crews keep fit on the Moon.
pmc-13395401:
Aikta Sharma and co-authors film, in 2026, tiny strains inside mouse knees to catch arthritis at its start. Healthy joints pass loads smoothly across their parts. The team loaded knee bones while scanning them with bright X-rays, then computed strain in three dimensions. They compared normal mice with a strain prone to joint disease.

In disease-prone knees, hot spots of strain bunched in the bone plate under cartilage at ten weeks of age. That was before any cartilage wear showed. Healthy knees, young or old, sent strain away from the surface instead. Models blamed local flaws in bone texture. The authors name misaligned micro-structure as an early driver worth watching.
pmc-13396301:
Barbara Poletti and colleagues compared rival scoring rules for sorting ALS patients by their thinking and behavior profile, in a 2026 study. ALS, the motor neuron disease that weakens muscles, also affects the mind in many patients, and clinics need a shared way to name those changes.

Records came from 901 patients with no formal dementia diagnosis, each screened with the Edinburgh Cognitive and Behavioural ALS Screen plus a carer interview. The team applied several published algorithms, including those of Abrahams and of Poletti's own group, under the standard Strong criteria. Where the rules disagree on the same person, the study shows which choices drive the clash.
pmc-13397701:
Shuai Ren and Jun Wen review how sepsis can flip the immune system from overdrive into shutdown. Their 2026 survey covers the damage across both arms of immunity, from worn-out front-line cells to depleted T and B cells and a tangled signal network. This weakened state helps explain why many sepsis patients later die from infections a healthy body would clear.

Clinicians track the shutdown by counting immune cells, checking HLA-DR markers on their surface and measuring signal proteins. Candidate treatments aim to wake the system back up, including IL-7, GM-CSF, checkpoint drugs and donated antibody preparations. The authors warn that none of these has yet proven itself in routine care, so careful trials remain the priority.
pmc-13398101:
Maria Grazia Cusi and co-authors report the first firm proof that Sindbis virus can invade the human brain and spinal cord. Family-tree analysis showed Clade D lineages circulating together in Italy, painting a tangled local picture. Sindbis, the authors conclude, should join the list of viruses doctors consider when the nervous system flares without a cause.
pmc-13398301:
Taylor C Johnson and co-authors test whether stronger local smoking bans bent cancer trends in Louisiana. Their 2026 study uses state tumour registry data from 2007 through 2022. A 2007 state law cleared smoke from many public places but left bars and casinos exempt, so Orleans Parish (2015) and Ouachita Parish (2017) later passed full local rules.

Orleans Parish declined steadily at an annual pace near 3.02 percent per year in its trend line. Ouachita's line bent in 2016, and the paper weighs whether local laws, rather than background drift, explain the gaps.
pmc-13399101:
Molecular Oncology issued this Expression of Concern in 2026 about a 2024 article by S. Prasad Gorantla and colleagues. The journal's editor-in-chief, the Federation of European Biochemical Societies, and Wiley agreed readers should be alerted.

The editors confirmed the duplication. The authors supplied data to support their findings. Yet much of the underlying material, from work done in 2010 to 2012, no longer exists. Because a correction could not settle the matter, the journal flags the reporting as doubtful.
pmc-13399301:

The team compared features across the stroke subtypes and searched for predictors of outcome. The study sits against a backdrop of disrupted stroke care in Brazil during the same period.
pmc-13399401: The notice is a correction only. pmc-13399701:

pmc-13399801:
Taidhgin J. Keel and co-authors, including senior surgeon Robert F. LaPrade, describe a combined operation that fixes three related knee problems in one sitting, in a 2026 technique paper. The authors argue that treating the rotational laxity and both tears together gives the meniscus its best chance to heal.
pmc-13400501:
Zhao and co-authors construct, in 2026, a signature for cutaneous melanoma from genes linking cuproptosis, a copper-driven form of cell death, with immune activity. Starting from cancer atlas data, they identified 474 cuproptosis-related immune genes by correlation, then found 194 of them dysregulated in melanoma against normal tissue. The training cohort held 406 patients, and an independent cohort of 208 patients validated the model. Low-risk tumors looked immune-inflamed, with higher mutational burden and checkpoint gene levels, suggesting better candidacy for checkpoint blockade. Drug response analysis hinted high-risk patients might benefit from other agents, making the signature a tool for therapy selection.
pmc-13400601:
Blanca Sánchez-Moreno and co-authors compare, in 2026, where a language-linked gene factor called Foxp2 appears in the mouse, rat and macaque thalamus. Foxp2 is essential for building brain circuits for language. Its pattern in the cortex is well known, but the thalamus, a relay hub deep in the brain, was poorly mapped.

Macaques showed broader and stronger expression in associative regions such as the pulvinar. The authors read this as a conserved role in circuits for attention, memory and sensorimotor integration, expanded in primates alongside more complex wiring.
pmc-13400701:
Lingke Jiang, Robbie M Parks, Yoshira Ornelas Van Horne and Xiao Wu study, in 2026, how social vulnerability in United States communities evolves for years after tropical cyclones. Most research stops days or months after a storm. Long-term shifts in who lives in exposed places matter for recovery and fairness.

By twelve years, though, it fell slightly below what would be expected without a storm. That late reversal may reflect gentrification, where poorer residents are displaced and replaced by wealthier newcomers.
pmc-13401201:
Qi Zhou and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of the high-intensity zone and its place in disc degeneration. The zone is a bright spot in the outer ring of a lumbar disc on T2-weighted MRI scans. They frame the zone as a dynamic inflammatory hub rather than a passive imaging curiosity.

After a tear in the disc's outer ring, granulation tissue full of small blood vessels grows in, and new nerves grow with it. That sets up a self-feeding cycle of inflammation and matrix breakdown. Signals such as TNF-alpha and IL-1beta and enzymes such as MMPs and ADAMTS drive the cycle. The review also covers artificial intelligence and multimodal imaging for spotting the zone. pmc-13401301:
Ahmed Abdellatif and colleagues ran a 2026 double-blinded randomized trial of computer-guided jaw fracture repair against the conventional plate method. The injury in question is a parasymphyseal mandibular fracture, a break near the chin, where standard open reduction and plate fixing depend heavily on surgeon experience and take considerable time.

The intervention group received a full virtual surgical planning protocol using a screw-holes locator guide and patient-specific custom plates. The comparison group had conventional plate osteosynthesis. The trial's central question is overall precision: whether the guided workflow reproduces the planned bone position more accurately and reproducibly than the experience-based routine, which the authors describe as labor-intensive and variable.
pmc-13401401:

Carriers borrowing from cell membranes, extracellular vesicles, or natural targeting molecules can circulate longer, dodge the immune system, and home in on damaged tissue. The review weighs design principles and animal evidence against translation hurdles: safety and immune concerns, uncertain drug behaviour in the body, hard-to-scale manufacturing, and quality control. Regulation counts too, plus the trade-off between loading more drug and releasing it well.
pmc-13401701:
Mehdi Safarabadi and co-authors ran a 2026 randomized trial of progressive muscle relaxation for people with hypothyroidism whose fatigue and low mood persist despite standard hormone replacement. The training group practised the technique twice daily for four weeks, and everyone completed tested fatigue and depression forms at the start and end. All 68 members stayed to the end, and the groups began largely alike. The control group showed no real change over the month. The relaxation group, by contrast, recorded clear drops in fatigue, and depression and quality-of-life results were also scored.
pmc-13402001:
Ravi Sharma and colleagues followed 282 adults after fracture surgery to test whether cheap blood markers can warn of early trouble. Patients were 18 to 65 years old and had fixation surgery at a large care center between December 2022 and June 2024. The team tracked ESR, C-reactive protein, D-dimer, and white cell counts from admission through day 14 after surgery.

Fifty patients, or 17.7 percent of the group, developed problems that included fracture-related infection, low oxygen, or low blood pressure needing support drugs. C-reactive protein gave the clearest warning for infection, especially when it stayed high near day 5 after surgery. High D-dimer flagged patients more likely to develop breathing or blood pressure problems. The authors suggest serial testing of both markers as a low-cost watch system where resources are tight.
pmc-13402101:
Samuel Novais and colleagues studied how beetles that live in dead wood, and the enemies that eat or parasitize them, answered the wreckage left by Hurricane Patricia. The first year brought more life: 133 species and 22,797 insects, against 82 species and 11,165 insects a year later. Fast-growing bark beetles and parasitoid wasps peaked early, while long-developing longhorn beetles and predatory beetles peaked in year two. The authors read the shift as a race set by life history: quick species feast first, then rivals and predators press them down as the wood ages.
pmc-13402301:
Heyi Wang and colleagues challenge a textbook strength rule by pulling layered crystals apart between their sheets. Wang and the team stretched graphite and hexagonal boron nitride along the layer direction in place, pairing the tests with first-principles math.

Both crystals failed far early, by local splitting at roughly 3 percent strain for graphite and 2 percent for boron nitride, well below what flaws alone would explain. Other layered solids such as molybdenum disulfide and gallium selenide showed no such local split. The authors trace the failure to a flexural phonon instability, a bending vibration that runs away and opens repeating nanogaps to dump stored energy. The finding resets the true elastic limits of these layered solids and hints at strain tricks for tuning them.
pmc-13402501:

Hospital and intensive care admission rates, Celegen notes, reflect local practice and bed supply as much as poisoning depth, and no scores such as the Poisoning Severity Score were used.

Outcomes such as ventilator need, blood pressure drugs, or death went unreported. Celegen asks future studies to record severity, dose, timing, and mental health context from the start.
pmc-13402801:
Sophie Seidel and colleagues present SciPhy, a Bayesian tool that rebuilds cell family trees from CRISPR lineage tracing records, using not only which edits happened but their order. A second test on mouse gastruloids, lab models of early embryos, showed it handling population sizes that change over time. The code is public. The authors pitch the framework as the quantitative backbone lineage tracing has lacked.
pmc-13404001:
Taieb Iheb and co-authors reported in 2026 a wrist bone break that healed on its own after years of staying unjoined. A 23-year-old manual worker hurt his wrist in 2017, then again in 2023. Scans showed a lasting break in the scaphoid bone with hardened edges and signs of poor blood supply.

Surgeons planned a bone graft fed by its own blood vessel. Films taken 13 months later, right before the operation, showed the break fully bridged instead. A CT scan confirmed solid new bone across the gap. The planned surgery was called off. Repeat imaging before surgery is the clear takeaway.
pmc-13404501:
Yueying Chen and co-authors lay out a 2026 protocol asking how much music therapy children with autism need for it to help. Two reviewers will select studies, extract data and judge bias risk on their own. Effects will be pooled with a random-effects model, graded with the GRADE approach, and split by dose in subgroup analyses. Funnel plots and Egger testing will check for publication bias.
pmc-13407701:
Leena Ghrayeb and co-authors simulate, in 2026, what happens when prenatal care stops giving every pregnancy the same visit schedule. National stakeholders now propose tailoring visit pathways to each patient instead.
