pmc-13408501:
Arata Takiguchi and co-authors built in 2026 a switch that can freeze and restart cargo traffic leaving the Golgi apparatus on command. The drug brefeldin A supplies the brake, letting the team watch membrane proteins begin their journey in synchrony under live imaging, electron microscopy, and biochemistry. Their test cargo was a class of proteins anchored to membranes by a lipid tail.

Cargo leaving the Golgi's exit station entered attached recycling compartments that swelled as they loaded, matured, and then pinched off as free recycling endosomes. Tube-like and beaded structures marked the handover points. In cells missing a sorting adaptor, the compartments still matured but failed to detach, stalling delivery to the cell surface. The system gives cell biologists a general tool for dissecting post-Golgi routes step by step.
pmc-13410801:
Ze Liu and colleagues design in 2026 a sponge-like gel that pulls uranium out of acidic nuclear wastewater within minutes. Cleaning such water is urgent, yet many sorbents crumble or work slowly in strong acid. Their gel copies reinforced concrete, with long nanowires as the steel bars.

Directional freezing carved straight channels that let water rush through the gel. The nanowire padding made the gel about seventy times stronger than the plain version. Most uranium was captured within two minutes, and treated groundwater fell to levels meeting drinking water discharge standards. Performance held in salty water and among rival metal ions. Surface studies explain the grip, which rests on friendly chemical groups along the channels.
pmc-13411101:
Gopika Gopinathan and co-authors refine in 2026 how to screen barley for covered smut, a fungal disease that ruins grain in the ear. The fungus hits organic growers hardest, yet testing breeding lines for resistance has proved unreliable. Plants often escape infection by chance, which hides true resistance.

A first trial under fast-breeding conditions gave low infection, likely from such escapes. Power calculations then set bigger plant numbers and better conditions for the fungus under a normal greenhouse setup. The revised method separated varieties clearly and needed fewer plants to spot at least one infected head. Infection also cut germination and stunted the most susceptible lines. Four varieties emerged as resistance candidates.
pmc-13412301:
Lena Lagally and co-authors examine in 2026 whether a sensitive inflammation marker rises with asthma severity across childhood and adult life. High-sensitivity C-reactive protein, or hsCRP, detects the low-grade inflammation standard tests miss. Within the ALLIANCE all-age asthma cohort, the team measured hsCRP in 944 participants, 728 of them children, and related levels to a validated severity score and its parts.

Adults with asthma carried higher hsCRP than healthy controls, and levels climbed with clinical severity at every age. The severity score correlated with hsCRP in patients aged six and older. Inhaled steroid use linked to lower hsCRP in preschool wheezers yet higher levels in adults, a split the authors read as reflecting disease course rather than drug effect alone.
pmc-13414801:
Ashna Talwar and co-authors link the total load of anticholinergic drugs to delirium risk in older adults with Alzheimer's disease, using 2026 analysis of Medicare claims. The cohort held 143,320 people aged 65 or older who started a cholinesterase inhibitor between 2013 and 2017. Burden was grouped as low, moderate, or high.

Delirium appeared in about 19 percent of the cohort during follow-up. Weighted risk models gave hazard ratios near 1.56 for moderate burden and 1.45 for high burden, each versus the low group. Those figures held after statistical balancing of group differences. Cutting dose, duration, or choosing other drugs could lower that extra risk.
pmc-13416201:
Eman Hajr and colleagues track electrical impedance in cochlear implants across the inner ear's regions over six months, in a 2026 retrospective study. Three hundred sixty implanted ears with one device type were analyzed. Activation happened either one day after surgery or about a month later, and age and sex were tested for influence.

Sex showed no link to impedance anywhere. Age mattered most at the apical electrodes near the cochlea's tip. Younger patients began with higher apical impedance, a relation that flipped positive by six months. Early activation softened the midterm rise in impedance. Middle and basal regions changed less with age.
pmc-13416401:
Eyuel Welelaw and colleagues compare royal jelly harvested at two times after larval grafting, in a 2026 food science study. Royal jelly, the secretion that feeds queen bees, was collected at seventy-two and one hundred forty-four hours. Protein content, the signature fatty acid 10-HDA, digestion access, and antibacterial plus antidiabetic activity were measured by standard methods.

Earlier harvest jelly held more protein, about thirteen percent, and more 10-HDA, about 3.4 percent by the reported values. Its components also became more accessible during simulated intestinal digestion than gastric digestion. Enzyme blocking tied to diabetes was strongest at seventy-two hours, near seventy-five percent for two enzymes. Antibacterial potency varied by bacterial species.
pmc-13416901:
Jeffrey Warner and co-authors test whether smart software can speed drug safety work, in a 2026 pilot study. Safety teams read case reports one by one to judge if a drug may have caused a harm. That work is slow and results vary by reader. Their tool uses a large language model to pull key facts from case text.

Human experts still checked each output. In five past safety reviews, scores for the facts sought ranged from weak to perfect. Even with the checks, the team saw clear time savings. The set up is machine first and human checked, and it stays within strict drug safety rules.
pmc-13418201:
Yuichi Saito and co-authors review risk scoring across heart and vessel medicine, in a 2026 article. Scores guide diagnosis, treatment choice, and prognosis in conditions from atrial fibrillation to acute coronary syndrome. The review traces how major scores were built, where guidelines use them, and how their roles keep evolving as care changes.

Good prediction alone does not guarantee better outcomes, the authors caution. Trials that test score guided care directly are examined for proof of benefit. Artificial intelligence is discussed as the next step, promising dynamic personal prediction tied to clear actions, provided it is validated in real clinics rather than only on past data.
pmc-13418701:
Mael Gagnon-Mailhot and colleagues explore pain beliefs taught in Canadian military basic training, in a 2026 qualitative study. Two focus groups with active instructors were analysed for themes on how pain is framed in training and wider military culture. Chronic pain burdens service members and veterans heavily, making early beliefs about pain consequential.

Instructors said recruits learn to push through pain for mission and team, while separating pain from true injury. Getting hurt often feels like personal failure, creating stigma around seeking care. Instructors themselves called the culture double edged, useful for endurance yet harmful when real injuries are endured silently. Training reform ideas follow.
pmc-13418901:
Chenhe Zhao and colleagues isolate two bacterial strains that can break down a short-chain industrial chemical found in coastal mud. The compound serves as a stand-in for a banned older pollutant in chip making and fire fighting, yet it leaks into water and mud and can disturb hormones. One strain came from estuary sediment and the other from sea sediment.

Gene matching placed the strains close to known harmless soil and plant bacteria. Neither strain could touch the two classic forever chemicals tested beside the target, showing a narrow taste for this compound. Their genomes held gene sets for stripping nitrogen, sulfur, and fluorine from molecules, steps that fit the breakdown seen. Such strains could one day help clean sites where this chemical builds up.
pmc-13420301:
Laurent Elisaut Marishamu and colleagues survey final-year students of clinical medicine in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, on their knowledge and attitudes toward trachoma. The eye infection remains a leading cause of blindness where water and hygiene are scarce. The survey ran from October to November 2021 at colleges of health and allied sciences in the region.

Each college in the area takes in roughly 200 or more students per intake, so the final-year pool reflects the near-future workforce. Knowledge level tracked with age and with sex in the statistical tests reported. Students close to practice will soon be the ones spotting and treating this blinding disease in clinics. Gaps found at this stage can still be closed by teaching before graduation, which is the practical use of the audit.
pmc-13421301:
Oliveira and a large team built an antibody-drug conjugate aimed at T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. A conjugate pairs a guiding antibody with a drug payload. This blood cancer is aggressive, and adult survival with chemotherapy stays below 50 percent. Their design steers a BCL-XL blocker straight into leukemia cells through the CD7 surface marker. The blocker disables a protein that keeps cancer cells alive.

In laboratory tests the conjugate killed most T-ALL cell lines. In mice carrying patient-derived leukemia it showed strong anti-leukemic activity, without damaging platelets. That platelet sparing matters. Free BCL-XL blockers cause severe platelet loss, the dose-limiting harm of this drug class. Combined with venetoclax, a related drug, it extended remission and mouse survival. Adding chemotherapy produced cures in some animals. The results support trials in patients.
pmc-13421601:
E V Mikhaylets leads a seven-author team recording brain waves, in a 2026 study, during Buddhist Highest Yoga Tantra meditation. The practice is an advanced one, said to unfold through eight dissolution stages toward a 'clear light' state. The recordings came from monasteries and hermitages, with 51 sessions from 36 experienced male practitioners.

An algorithm combining spectral power and synchrony carved each session into discrete brain states, and six reproducible types emerged, arranged in symmetric pairs. Written as symbol sequences, the sessions formed six clusters of meditation style. Greater expertise meant longer, more varied states, with more of the alpha-theta and beta-gamma patterns. The authors show that even a single canonical protocol produces systematically different neural journeys.
pmc-13421801:
Julio Humberto Fernandez and three colleagues report, in a 2026 case study, the surgical treatment of a 78-year-old man whose mouth cancer returned after earlier care. Oral squamous cell carcinoma is the commonest cancer of the mouth, and removing it with a safe margin leaves a defect that must be rebuilt for speech and swallowing.

The team resected the tumour with ten-millimetre margins and rebuilt the area with an island flap of tongue tissue, also removing selected neck lymph nodes on both sides. Free flaps are the gold standard for large defects, yet the tongue flap suited this moderate, rearward hole and the tissue at hand. Healing was clean, tongue movement and oral function were preserved, and at fourteen months the patient remained well.
pmc-13422801:
Katja Reuter, David R Freyer, Joel Milam and Erin M Mobley expose, in a 2026 brief communication, a reporting flaw that quietly hobbles cancer research on adolescents and young adults. This group, diagnosed between fifteen and thirty-nine, has distinct needs. Yet studies often report age at enrolment rather than age at diagnosis. That makes it impossible to tell who actually belongs.

The team reviewed 734 non-interventional cancer studies from 2018 to 2022. A third failed to report age at diagnosis well enough to show whether young patients were included. There was no improvement over the period. They recommend that guidelines require the full picture: mean, median, range and the count diagnosed in the window. Where numbers allow, results should also be split by this group.
pmc-13423301:
This 2026 article shows how schools can teach hands-on microbiology without a sterile laboratory, using Halobacterium salinarum, a salt-loving archaeon, a member of the third domain of life. The microbe is not known to cause disease.

The organism grows on media loaded with salt, up to 290 grams per liter, which keeps contaminants out. Ordinary school labs can therefore handle it with common consumer products. One activity has students grow colonies and note their pink color and violet glow under ultraviolet light. A second activity stains the cells with crystal violet for microscope viewing, revealing flexible rods that reflect the lack of a rigid cell wall. A short questionnaire and discussion of extremophiles, life forms that thrive in harsh settings, close the lesson.
pmc-13423801:
Bala and colleagues reviewed 77 infants born before 32 weeks of pregnancy to learn how feeding milestones relate to growth after birth in the neonatal unit. Growth was scored against age- and sex-specific standards, and postnatal growth faltering meant a steep drop in weight score, or simultaneous drops across weight, length, and head size.

Severe growth faltering affected 11.7 percent of the infants, while the broader complex pattern affected 22 percent overall. Babies born before 28 weeks fared worst, with severe faltering in 22.2 percent and complex faltering in 33.3 percent of that youngest group. Older age at first feeding, older age at full feeding, and a longer transition between them each tracked with slower growth. Feeding delays also came with longer hospital stays, leading the authors to argue that earlier feeding progress may support better growth.
pmc-13425001:
Gerd R Burmester opens a new viewpoint series on the global reach of rheumatology research in the journal EULAR Rheumatology Open. He argues that both the science and the diseases it treats ignore borders. The series will tour regions of the world, following an earlier landmark account of Japanese rheumatology, and it begins with China.

The opening article, by Wenwen Xu and Shuang Ye of Shanghai, traces Chinese rheumatology's move from follow-on validation studies toward improved and genuinely novel strategies. It shows researchers repurposing existing tools for unmet clinical needs. Burmester previews its highlights: landmark trials of JAK inhibitor drugs, biosimilars, and digital health tools in rheumatoid arthritis, and lupus work that has influenced international treatment guidance.
pmc-13425601:
Liu and colleagues link a sugar burning enzyme, pyruvate kinase M2, to Guillain-Barré syndrome, a sudden autoimmune attack on peripheral nerves that can paralyze. Their 2026 study starts with Mendelian randomization, a genetic method for causal hints, tying higher enzyme levels in the tibial nerve to raised disease risk. The team then checks a mouse model of autoimmune neuritis, the animal mirror of the disease, across its onset and peak.

In the mice, the enzyme climbed over time in the sciatic nerve, concentrated where immune cells had invaded. In helper T cells the enzyme's rise pushed the balance toward Th17 cells, attackers that make a fiery signal, and away from regulatory T cells, the peacekeepers. A methylation site, a chemical dimmer on the enzyme's gene, also tied to risk and sat unusually bare in adaptive immune cells. Calming this metabolic switch, the authors propose, deserves tests as a treatment idea.
pmc-13426101:
Zhang and colleagues reported in 2026 that slow-moving charge carriers in semiconductors are lost first at surfaces. They turned that loss into a feature that shapes which colors of light a detector sees. When light frees charges inside a material, the slow ones drift weakly and get caught by surface defects. Most engineers treat this as a flaw to suppress. This study treats it as a design tool.

Using a wide low-field region, the team generated charges at spots with different electric pull and watched how many survived to be collected. Across bare surfaces, surfaces with added defects, and faulty organic contacts, charges born where the pull was weak were lost first. By tuning that loss, the group built a silicon detector answering only a narrow band of colors.
pmc-13426201:
Parth Patel and coauthors describe lymphoma spreading to the breast in a 2026 case of peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified. A 74-year-old woman had one month of worsening left breast pain, redness, swelling, and fever and was first treated for stubborn mastitis. Mammography showed diffuse skin and tissue thickening, ultrasound found a fluid collection, and scans revealed widespread lymph node enlargement across neck, chest, and abdomen.

Biopsies of armpit and groin nodes confirmed the lymphoma diagnosis. Because breast involvement can imitate inflammatory breast cancer or infection, the authors urge early biopsy when presumed mastitis fails to resolve. One month of pain and heat in the breast that does not yield to drugs is a red flag staff should act on with a test of the tissue.
pmc-13426501:
Shinde and colleagues engineered catalysts in 2026 that turn carbon dioxide and hydrogen into methane, a way to recycle a greenhouse gas into fuel and store renewable energy. How well the reaction runs depends on the catalyst's defects and surface chemistry. The team varied how its cobalt-nickel catalyst was made, then compared the results.

The best recipe used fast solution combustion with cobalt swapped directly into the crystal structure. It converted about seven in ten carbon dioxide molecules fed to it, and nearly all the product was methane, at a moderate reaction heat. Analysis tied the win to many oxygen vacancies, empty spots in the crystal that grip carbon dioxide. The catalyst held its performance over a full day of running, and spectroscopy showed two middle compounds on the reaction path.
pmc-13427101:
Zhou and colleagues report an iron-driven reaction that turns simple carboxylic acids into chiral alpha,beta-diamino acids. It adds nitrogen groups on two next-door carbon atoms in a single pot. Building such 1,2-diamines with control over handedness and position has been a long-standing challenge in lab chemistry.

The team used a chiral iron catalyst with four nitrogen binding arms, plus a shielded nitrogen source. They reached selectivity up to better than 20 to 1 in diastereomer ratio. Enantiomeric excess topped 99 percent in the best runs. Aromatic and aliphatic starting compounds both reacted under mild setups. The path ran through two nitrogen insertion steps, each led by the iron center. Follow-up tests showed the first insertion site sets the order of events. It is beta for aromatic starting compounds and alpha for aliphatic ones. Several racemic starting compounds ended as a single handed product.
pmc-13427801:
Ricardo Antonio Gonzalez Jaramillo and colleagues pooled studies on adding a mesh patch when closing emergency belly surgery, to stop later hernias. A hernia here means the wound bulging open months later through the weakened scar.

Five studies with 617 patients compared mesh closure with plain stitches, including four randomised trials. Mesh cut the odds of later hernia sharply, to roughly a third of the risk seen with stitches alone. The benefit looked similar in clean wounds and in dirty, infected wounds, though that comparison rested on thin data. Fluid pockets under the skin rose about fourfold with mesh, and proof quality rated low, so the authors urge a bigger trial.
pmc-13429901:
Liangchao Sun and colleagues probe, in a 2026 study, why esophageal cancers shrug off radiation therapy. The cancer type studied, squamous cell carcinoma of the food pipe, dominates in Asia and often resists the chemoradiation used when surgery is impossible. An RNA-editing enzyme called ADAR1, which rewrites letters in RNA copies of genes, ran high in these tumors. High levels tracked with poor response to treatment given before surgery.

Removing ADAR1 slowed tumor growth and made cancer cells far more sensitive to radiation in dishes and in mice. Part of the effect ran through a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis. An editing target gene named C16orf46 proved central: when its editing fell, radiation worked better. A survival signaling chain offered a second route. Blocking ADAR1 could become a way to resensitize stubborn tumors.
pmc-13430201:
Feiroz Humayara and colleagues solve, in a 2026 methods study, a soggy lab problem: pulling clean RNA from cells grown on a birth membrane scaffold. Human amniotic membrane, the inner lining of the placenta, makes an attractive scaffold for regrowing gum ligament tissue. Its matrix gums up standard RNA extraction, leaving low yields and dirty samples that ruin gene readouts. The team tuned a phenol-based kit protocol through several optimization rounds.

Purity scores leapt from unusable to excellent ranges, and RNA concentration rose markedly. Half the samples now met strict quality bars, up from none under the standard method. On the selected measures, quality matched cells grown the ordinary flat way. Gene expression checks confirmed the extracted RNA actually works downstream. Tissue engineers using natural scaffolds gain a protocol that rescues molecular analysis from the scaffold itself.
pmc-13430301:
Yun Wang and co-authors reported a 2026 study linking how well older adults move and function with signs of depression. The group drew on full health checks from a Beijing hospital clinic between late 2021 and late 2023. After records with gaps were removed, 443 people aged 65 or older remained for review.

Tests covered grip strength, timed walking, sit-to-stand speed, balance, and a short battery that sums these skills into one score. People with low mood scored far lower on that battery, and higher scores went with lower odds of depression. Slower timed walking and higher worry scores went with higher odds. The authors suggest that adding the short battery to routine checks could help flag older adults who need support sooner.
pmc-13430701:
Bernhard-Skala and Steinweg ask in 2026 what skills medical students need when they teach fellow students, a practice called peer-to-peer teaching. No shared, evidence-based list of those teaching skills existed across medical subjects.

The pair ran a systematic mapping review, screening database results down from 322 records to 18 peer-reviewed studies from across North America, Europe, and Australia. From the training programs described, they extracted three medical competencies and twelve teaching competencies, and assembled them into one profile for student teachers. The profile overlaps with existing frameworks for medical teachers. They also found the underlying research weakly tied to learning theory and mostly low in evidence level, and they invite schools to debate and refine the profile.
pmc-13430901:
Seda Tecik and Nursan Çınar studied new mothers in Turkey in 2026 to untangle links among low mood, how content a mother feels in her role, and tender bonding with her baby. The cross-check survey enrolled 231 mothers whose infants were one to four months old at clinics in two hospitals. Mothers rated mood, role contentment, and bonding on standard forms.

Mood scores and role contentment moved together in a mid-strength link. Contentment moved against bonding scores, also at mid strength, while mood linked to bonding only weakly. A model of the paths found that contentment carried a clear direct tie to bonding, while mood showed no direct path once contentment was in place. Mood did tie to lower contentment. The authors stress backing a mother's felt sense of her role in the first months.
pmc-13431501:
Richard García Domínguez and co-authors weighed proof in 2026 on how the chemical worth of pollen shapes a wing-deforming virus in honey bees. Pollen feeds bees their protein, fats, and key minerals, yet its makeup shifts with plant source, place, and season. Those shifts can sway body defense and the strain a virus inflicts.

Rich, mixed pollen diets tend to go with longer colony life and better health in the studies surveyed. Effects on virus load split by study: some found lower loads, while others found flat or higher loads even as bees thrived. The split hints that good food may help bees bear the harm more than beat the virus back. Plant compounds in pollen draw interest as shield agents, yet proof of direct virus killing in bees stays thin.
pmc-13432601:
Harshal A Deshmukh and co-authors mined a large UK birth cohort in 2026 for the joint effect of a hormone-linked ovarian syndrome and pregnancy diabetes on newborn size. The Bradford cohort held more than nine thousand single births from 2007 to 2011. Mothers split into four sets: neither fault, each fault alone, or both at once.

Babies of mothers with either fault weighed less at birth than babies of clear mothers, despite the mothers' own higher body weight. Babies of mothers with both faults weighed least of all and carried the thinnest arms and skin folds. Tuned math that weighed age, body mass, and roots still tied each fault to lower birth weight on its own. The two faults stacked, which marks a group that may need closer watch in pregnancy.
pmc-13434601:
Lee analyzed in 2026 national health survey data from about seventeen hundred Korean adolescents, aged ten to eighteen, to map how asthma ties to body shape and blood fats. Asthma, obesity, and abnormal blood fats often travel together, but the pattern in teens was unclear. The data came from a national examination survey run in 2019 to 2021 across the country.

Asthma odds rose with body mass index and, much more steeply, with waist size, pointing to belly fat as the stronger signal. Higher levels of the protective cholesterol fraction went with lower asthma odds, and girls showed lower odds than boys. Smoking stood out sharply: teens who smoked had over four times the odds. Lee recommends activity, diet, and lipid checks in teen asthma care.
pmc-13434801:
Jiuya He and coauthors map how the human ATP synthase, the turbine that makes cell fuel, is built in 2026. The machine has 28 parts of 17 kinds, split between rotor and stator. Deleting parts or helpers in human cells traps half built forms for study.

Trapped forms reveal build paths for the rotor and for the fuel making head. Each path can now be tested by imaging the trapped forms. Part lists support the idea that three modules evolved apart, then joined. Assembly faults may explain some rare diseases of the power system. The map gives structural teams clear targets.
pmc-13436101:
Kathrin Julia Pann and colleagues lay out a study plan to judge how advanced practice nurse roles are growing at an Austrian university hospital. Advanced practice nurses are nurses with extra training who take on wider clinical duties.

The University Hospital Salzburg hired its first such nurses in 2017 and spread the roles across many fields from 2020. The study mixes surveys first, then interviews and group talks shaped by what the surveys show. Nurses, assistants, managers, and doctors will all give views on results for patients, staff, and the hospital. Running from June 2025 to November 2027, the work should show what helps or blocks these roles.
pmc-13436401:
Marin Delaunay and coauthors compare seventy six Staphylococcus lugdunensis strains from nine French hospitals in 2026. The skin germ turns virulent in joint, heart, and soft tissue infections. Strains date from 2001 to 2016 and sort into six clan groups.

Heart infection strains grip a clotting factor more strongly than other strains. Film growth runs higher in the three most common clans and in heart strains. Rival killing power varies by clan through changes in one gene cluster. A moth larva model ranks one clan as most virulent. Trait maps may help doctors judge which skin germ isolate threatens most.
pmc-13437401:
Zheyan Chen and colleagues review how gut bacteria may shape healing of diabetic foot ulcers, wounds that strike up to a third of people with diabetes and often return within a year. Standard care often fails to close these ulcers. Their 2026 review, centered on type 2 diabetes, traces a path from the gut to the skin through immune balance and inflammation.

Certain gut microbes make short-chain fatty acids, small molecules that calm inflammatory pathways and help balance two rival classes of immune cells. Through this gut-immune-skin link, a disturbed gut mix can keep a foot wound inflamed and slow to close. The authors sort the fixes under study: helpful live bacteria, fibers that feed them, stool transfers from healthy donors, and plain diet change. They present this as a working base for microbe-based therapies and call for trials testing whether gut care can cut amputations.
pmc-13437801:
Olga Vershinina and co-authors propose aggressive brain tumors called gliomas cannot be read apart from the biology of aging. Genes known to mark glioma type and patient survival also track age, and their activity shifts with age in the direction that worsens outlook. Their 2026 study adds biological clocks, math models reading aging from chemical marks on DNA, and finds sped-up aging inside many gliomas.

Its meaning changes with tumor subtype and with which clock does the measuring, and it does not always spell aggression. The review side weighs cell senescence, where worn cells stop dividing, as both a brake on tumors and a source of trouble. One question hangs: does age-linked inflammation feed gliomas, or do the tumors themselves age the body faster? Either way, the authors argue, profiling cellular aging could sharpen treatment choices, moving care toward personal plans rather than the label.
pmc-13438401:
Hanane Houmaid and colleagues reviewed seven years of uterine rupture, a tearing of the womb during pregnancy or labor, at a large Marrakesh hospital. Their 2026 study gathered every confirmed case from 2017 through 2024 and set outcomes against scar status and speed of care. Among 115,121 deliveries, seventy-four ruptures occurred, about six in ten thousand births.

More than half the ruptures struck wombs with no prior scar, defying the assumption that surgical history is the main warning. Four in five patients had little or no pregnancy care beforehand. Removing the womb was needed in about twenty-three percent of cases, concentrated among late-care cases. One mother died, while about thirty-five percent of babies were lost, deaths clustering in neglected and unscarred cases. Regular antenatal visits, an end to harmful labor practices, and fast referral would, in their reading, save most of the mothers and babies this emergency now claims.
pmc-13439101:
Youjin Kim and co-authors report a 2026 structural study of two enzymes that help cells sense nutrients and switch on growth signals. The enzymes, LARS1 and IARS1, belong to a larger complex that loads amino acids onto transfer RNAs. Beyond that core job, LARS1 senses leucine and helps activate mTORC1, a master switch for cell growth. How LARS1 sits in the complex and breaks away when fed was not known.

Cryo-electron microscopy, which freezes proteins for imaging, showed LARS1 gripping its anchor partner through a tail region. When amino acids arrived, three sites on LARS1 gained phosphate groups right at the grip surface. That change loosened the hold, freed LARS1 from the complex, and allowed mTORC1 activation. The work frames phosphorylation as a shared switch for this enzyme family.
pmc-13439301:
Giel J L van Neerven and colleagues compare two ways of placing long-term feeding tubes into the small bowel, in a 2026 Dutch hospital study. One route threads a thin extension through a stomach opening; the other places the tube directly through the bowel wall. The threaded route is easier to insert and usually chosen first, yet head-to-head outcome data were scarce. Records covered 93 patients treated between 2010 and 2022, including people fed this way and Parkinson's patients on gut-delivered gel medicine.

Patients with the threaded route needed far more repeat scopes per year, mostly after extensions slipped out of place. Tube problems struck three quarters of that group, against a quarter of the direct group. Quality of life scores matched, though direct-route patients reported more tube pain. The authors back the direct route at skilled centres when extensions keep failing.
pmc-13440001: Yuchen Ying, Xiaomei Chen, and Li Wang issue a correction to their study of mood symptoms among nursing interns in Ningbo, China. The correction fixes the author order, the corresponding author, an equal-contribution note, and a missing funding line. The notice is a correction only, with no new data or findings. It confirms Li Wang as corresponding author and restores the Zhejiang education research grant credited to Ying.
pmc-13441101:
Yu Liu and a large team ask how both parents' body builds together shape fetal growth, reporting a 2026 letter on a national Chinese cohort. Mother's size alone is a known driver of fetal size, yet fathers are rarely counted. The study enrolled 9,075 low-risk singleton pregnancies at twenty-four hospitals across eighteen provinces. Parents were grouped by clustering on mother's height and pre-pregnancy weight plus father's height, yielding four couple profiles.

Ultrasound tracks from week twelve to delivery traced growth curves for each profile. Babies of short, lean mothers ran smaller across weight estimates and head, belly, and limb measures than babies of medium-build couples. Babies of overweight mothers ran larger on the same measures. Small-for-dates and large-for-dates diagnoses appeared in notable shares of the cohort. The authors argue that fetal growth forecasts should read both parents' builds as one combined exposure.
pmc-13441401:
Nicholson and co-authors explain the 2025 ATS/ERS update of the classification of interstitial pneumonias. These are a family of lung-scarring and inflammatory diseases. The focus is what changes for pathologists reading biopsies. The scheme was first agreed in 2002 with seven patterns and grew in 2013. It anchors the team-based diagnosis these diseases require.

Five major changes headline the update set out for working pathologists in this review article. The scheme now extends beyond idiopathic disease to include secondary causes. It sorts cases into interstitial, fibrotic or not, and alveolar-filling patterns for clearer organization. New patterns such as bronchiolocentric interstitial pneumonia enter the list. Wording better reflects how lesions arise. Pathologists must also state how sure they are in their reports. The review covers cryobiopsy reading too. It urges reporting points that hint at a secondary cause, since treatment hinges on that split.
pmc-13441901:
Josh J Arbon and colleagues show that dwarf mongooses size up rival groups before trouble starts and adjust their behaviour to match, reporting ten years of field data in 2026. Group contests shape social animal life, yet anticipatory behaviour, and how it varies with the rival in question, was barely studied. Detailed observations and GPS tracks followed wild dwarf mongoose groups across a decade. Behaviour before possible encounters was sorted by the relative size of neighbouring groups.

Mongooses changed space use, information sharing, and resource defence depending on whether neighbours were evenly matched or dangerously larger. Each rival profile drew its own preparation pattern, tuned to the costs that rival could impose. Differences between home-range core and edge, by contrast, looked inconsistent as threat signals. The authors argue that evolution has equipped these animals to read specific rivals, not just risky places, when bracing for conflict.
pmc-13445601:
Abdullah and colleagues present a deep learning system that spots pneumonia on chest X-rays and shows its work, in a 2026 study. Pneumonia kills many children and older adults, and fast, sure reading of chest films guides care. Their system, HybridCATNet, blends two network types and reports how sure it is of each call.

The model reads nine image channels at once, mixing the raw film with lung outlines and edge maps. Training used 8,478 real chest films from several sites, checked with ten-fold cross-checks and two outside groups. Accuracy sat near ninety-seven in a hundred, and outside groups stayed above ninety-four. Heat maps of the model's focus matched the zones radiologists marked, which supports trust in its calls.
pmc-13446101:
Yongqi Ji and colleagues argue for a shift in how a body metabolite called alpha-ketoglutarate is used in medicine, in a 2026 review. The molecule sits at a hub of cell energy work and also steers gene marks, slows cell aging, and calms immune balance. Given as a plain drug, though, it fades fast and reaches tissues poorly.

The authors propose building the molecule into materials themselves, bonded into the frame rather than carried as cargo. They grade three stages of that plan, from protected cargo, to helper mixed in, to the frame itself. Uses in sight span bone and cartilage regrowth, soft tissue repair, immune tuning, and stronger cancer care. The review closes with open hurdles and a map for joining metabolism to material design.
pmc-13446201:
Henrik Mellström Dahlgren and colleagues follow Swedish children born in the first pandemic year to test whether low early exposure to germs raised later severe chest infections, in a 2026 cohort study. Lockdown steps cut the spread of common viruses, and infections bounced back as rules eased. The team set the 2020 births against like spans in 2015 and 2018.

Each group held more than ninety thousand children. The pandemic-born had far fewer hospital stays for chest infection in their first two years. Between ages two and four the pattern flipped: their hospital risk ran well above both older groups, for lung infection overall and for flu and RSV in kind. The authors link the swing to changed early-life germ exposure.
pmc-13446301:
Soh Youn Suh and colleagues ask whether a child's first year on weak atropine drops for short sight foretells the whole course of control, in a 2026 records study. Five hundred fifty-five children at one practice used the drops for at least a year, most at the weakest strength. Eyes were classed by whether yearly worsening stayed under a set line at month twelve.

About six in ten children met the line in both eyes, and their later control rate reached seven in ten. Children who missed the line in both eyes, about a fifth of the group, later controlled in under two in ten cases. Near half of all children stepped up to stronger care, sooner among the poor first-year group. The authors back first-year pace as a triage signal.
pmc-13447001:
Abhishek Jaiswal and colleagues survey women in an urban Faridabad neighborhood on cervical cancer and the HPV vaccine, in a 2026 study. Three hundred two residents aged nine to forty-five took part, most of them married. Symptoms were screened on the spot, and women with warning signs were sent on for checks.

Only about a quarter had heard of cervical cancer, and barely one in ten knew of the vaccine, with thin grasp of cause or prevention. Even so, near three quarters said they would take the shot. Among the unwilling, low drive led the reasons, ahead of having little say in health choices, while fear ranked low. The authors back public rollout with teaching and stronger say for women.
pmc-13447301:
Cong Kang and colleagues review digital tools for raising teenage physical activity in a 2026 systematic synthesis. Most adolescents worldwide fall short of recommended activity levels. Apps, wearables, games and chatbots promise scalable help, yet real-world results often fade, and the review asks what separates lasting success from early enthusiasm.

Studies from 2020 onward were gathered across trial, cohort and review designs, with quality checked by design-specific tools. Nearly two-thirds of tools showed a positive effect at first testing. Engagement still collapsed over time in one tracked cohort, falling steeply by the fifth month. Age fit mattered, with younger teens responding better to playful, movement-based designs. Success rested on matching development stage, sustaining motivation and keeping access fair, not on technology alone.
pmc-13448201:
Feilong Zhu and colleagues test online fine motor training for children with inattentive ADHD in a 2026 randomised trial. Children with the inattentive form often struggle with hand skills and executive functions, the mental controls for planning and inhibition, alongside focus itself. Live remote sessions could reach families who cannot attend clinics, yet structured tele-rehabilitation evidence for these outcomes was limited.

Sixty-six children aged six to ten were assigned to twelve weeks of thrice-weekly online training or to a waiting list. Parent-rated inattention fell more in the training group at twelve weeks, with a smaller edge kept at six months. Inhibitory control, immediate memory and flexibility also favoured training at both checks. Hand dexterity and hand-eye coordination improved more with training and held at follow-up, supporting remote delivery as a workable format.
pmc-13448901:
Maryam Rezaeianjam and colleagues test in 2026 whether adding a plant compound to dental filling materials makes them kinder to gum tissue. They loaded ellagic acid, an antioxidant from fruits, into tiny fat bubbles called liposomes and mixed it into discs of nano-glass ionomer and nano-dental cement. Human gum fibroblast cells were then grown on the treated and untreated materials in the laboratory.

Cells on the modified materials stayed over 96 percent viable and attached 1.3 times better by day three. Two inflammatory signals, IL-6 and TNF-alpha, dropped markedly, as did markers of oxidative stress inside the cells. The liposomes released their cargo steadily, reaching 56 percent by 72 hours. The authors propose the additive as a route to restorative materials that actively calm inflammation while they repair teeth.
pmc-13449001:
The editor of ACS Omega retracts in 2026 a 2023 article by Atiya Ayub, Muhammad Ikram, and colleagues. The retracted work concerned yttrium and carbon sphere doped lanthanum oxide nanostructures for dye degradation and antibacterial use. The notice gives concrete reasons rather than a bare withdrawal. In one figure, the X-ray diffraction patterns for two different formulations, noise included, look highly similar, pointing to inappropriate image reuse. Traces in another figure look more angular than expected.

Set beside irregularities in the data and analysis and concerns about accountability for the research, the editor judged the pattern serious enough to undermine the findings entirely. The same pattern touches two related articles, and the notice questions the reliability of all three publications. The original article appeared on September 27, 2023, and the retraction was issued on July 23, 2026.
pmc-13449601:
Sneh Parekh and co-authors confirm in 2026, with data from two large southeastern United States medical centers, that scarring lung disease travels with ulcerative colitis more than with Crohn disease. Interstitial lung disease is a rare but serious companion of inflammatory bowel disease. Their review of records from 2012 to 2022 covered 8,865 bowel disease patients, of whom 408, or 4.6 percent, also carried a lung diagnosis.

The lung condition's prevalence ran significantly higher in ulcerative colitis than in Crohn disease, while demographics between those two lung groups looked alike. Across bowel patients, having both diseases came with older age, more emergency visits, more hospitalizations, and more steroid use, plus less use of the gentler drug mesalamine. White patients showed higher recorded prevalence than minority patients. The authors say the utilization pattern marks a sicker, costlier subgroup deserving earlier lung attention.
pmc-13450001:
Mitra Shojania Feizabadi, James Paisnel, and Jelena Stanisic describe in 2026 a microfluidic method that forms droplets in fatty acid oil and steers their size with temperature. Droplet systems turn tiny volumes into isolated reaction chambers for cell and molecular work, yet the field leans on fluorinated oils now shadowed by concern over persistent PFAS chemicals. Emu oil, rich in unsaturated fatty acids, offers a more biologically familiar continuous phase, one the lead author's earlier work introduced as a new droplet class.

The team quantified how temperature shifts droplet size in this oil, giving users a dial rather than a fixed geometry. Working in a fatty acid medium at controlled, body-like temperatures also makes the droplets a more physiologically relevant stage for cellular analysis than harsh synthetic oils allow. The authors position phase-based thermal control as a greener, gentler route to droplet experiments in biochemistry and molecular biology.
pmc-13450501:
Mizuho Namba and colleagues present a 2026 case of blistering skin disease that kept returning after breast cancer care. Their patient, a woman aged 74, had surgery for cancer of the left breast, then radiation and hormone therapy. Blisters first rose on the treated breast about a month after radiation ended.

At first the rash was read as radiation skin damage, and steroid creams cleared it. Later flares spread to a limb and the back, and skin tests showed immune deposits along the base of the skin, a sign of a blistering illness driven by the immune system. Oral steroid pills settled each flare, and later blood tests found raised levels of an antibody tied to a blister target in skin.
pmc-13450901:
Mohsen Nakhaei and a large team present in 2026 a way to track heart valve leaflets in motion scans by leaning on physics models. Valve strain shapes how fast a faulty valve worsens, yet fast motion and odd shapes make leaflet tracking shaky. Their flow builds a patient-matched valve from heart scans and runs a physics play of its closing.

The play gives mid-step shapes that guide the scan match, which then fixes gaps between model and image. In twenty patients, the aided match beat a plain match on accuracy by two fifths. Strain measures followed for two- and three-leaflet valves in adults and children, with hints that size, not shape twist, drives age gaps in total strain.
pmc-13451901:
Abhimanyu Pavuluri and Adam Kohn study in 2026 how monkey visual brain areas lay out their replies to natural textures. Single-cell taste tests miss how whole groups code a scene, so the team read group reply shapes in the first visual area and the next one. Both areas saw the same rich texture images.

Replies in the second area sat in a lower-dimensional shape and lined up better across textures. That layout let the group tell apart new textures it had not trained on. Standard computer vision nets did not copy the brain's layout. The authors read the shift as a move toward a tidy, shared code for surface feel as sight climbs the chain.
pmc-13452301:
Yiaw, in a solo 2026 case report, describes rescuing a surgical complication with an improvised tool. A 33-year-old man with bladder exstrophy, a surgically created urinary channel, and chronic kidney disease was having a metallic ureteral stent exchanged through the skin. Such stents resist compression and can stay in long, but this extraction went wrong.

A suboptimal grip folded the rigid stent inside its working sheath, badly bending it. When the sheath came out, the stent's upper portion lodged in the fat under the skin. It sat beyond the reach of standard endoscopic graspers. Those tools lacked the strength to pull it free. Working under continuous live X-ray imaging, the author used a robust curved artery forceps, a general surgical clamp, to seize and extract the stent completely. Lessons cover grasping the stent's tip, sheath sizing, and fluoroscopy-guided retrieval.
pmc-13453001:
Abbasi and Masoudpanah show in 2026 how to rebuild a common battery cathode material from the innards of substandard cells that never passed quality checks. They converted the separated black mass from these out-of-line lithium iron phosphate cells into lithium and iron precursor compounds, then fired them with sugar as the carbon source.

Powders rebuilt from two of the precursors, at an equal molar ratio, performed best in testing. The regenerated cathode kept ninety percent of its capacity after 2,000 charge and discharge cycles at a fast rate. Other precursor mixes and ratios performed less well in the comparison. The authors present the carbothermal route, meaning heating with carbon, as a direct recycling path that skips separating every element, saving time and cost.
pmc-13454201:
Jing Li and five co-authors build a model of how audiences outside China come to accept traditional Chinese medicine. The medicine now sits in the ICD-11 disease manual, yet its whole pattern logic clashes with biomedicine's cut down approach, a gap translation alone cannot close. Their 2026 study drafts the model from three theories, then refines it with a panel of senior experts.

Acceptance runs in three stages in the model. First comes a pass of perception and feeling. Next, people map the ideas onto their own frame. Last, the system becomes part of a person's health identity. Three forces steer the path: felt compatibility, mental cost, and trust handed over from known institutions. Supports such as metaphor mapping plus official recognition ease the unease foreign audiences feel. The authors frame dialog, not one way messaging, as the bridge.
pmc-13454701:
Marx and co-authors report in this 2026 case study the first use of pulsed field ablation in a patient carrying a deep brain stimulator. The patient was a 66-year-old woman with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat. She had received the implanted stimulator years earlier to control severe muscle fasciculations. Standard heat-based ablation is discouraged near such devices for fear of interference.

Pulsed field ablation, which kills heart tissue with short electric pulses rather than heat or cold, offered a safer profile. The stimulator was switched off before the procedure, and a five-spline catheter treated her pulmonary veins, including an unusually large shared left vein, without complications. Reactivated afterward, the stimulator showed no malfunction or interference. The authors conclude the approach is feasible in carefully selected patients when device teams plan together in advance.
pmc-13455001:
Mingyu Zhang, Jiaju Tian, and Weiming Sun review, in 2026, how the immune system senses acidity and turns it into inflammatory action. Acidity was once viewed as a mere waste product of metabolism. Inflamed, infected, and tumor tissues all turn acidic, and immune cells carry dedicated proton sensors on their surfaces.

The review sorts the sensors into families: surface receptors such as GPR4 and GPR68, acid-gated channels, and inside-cell factors that read pH shifts. Each converts a sour environment into signals that reshape gene activity and cell behavior. The authors map how these routes plug into the wider inflammation network. They close with prospects for sourness-based diagnostic markers and drugs that tune the sensors. Their larger claim is that pH deserves treatment as a true immune signal, not background noise.
pmc-13455601:
Elizabeth Whidden and four colleagues report, in a 2026 interview study, how a food benefit delay during a government shutdown shook the daily care routines of people living with HIV. In November 2025, shutdown politics held up Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program payments for millions. The team interviewed 20 recipients inside a larger tracked cohort.

Four themes came through. Food access took constant planning even in normal months. The monthly benefit cycle itself taxed memory and organization, both vital for staying on daily medicine. The shutdown delay felt different, because not knowing when money would land broke routines. Community help cushioned some of the blow. Pill adherence across the wider group had sat at a median of 72 percent before the delay. Among the nine people tracked through it, the median fell to 40 percent. The authors argue benefit reliability matters as much as benefit size.
pmc-13456601:
Ana Paula Lobez, Mikael Oliveberg, and Peter Brzezinski study, in a 2026 paper, how electrons hop between two giant enzymes inside yeast mitochondria. The last steps of breathing pass electrons from complex III to complex IV aboard a small shuttle protein, cytochrome c. In soap-purified extracts, the shuttle's swimming speed set the pace of the whole relay.

Working instead with membrane-embedded sacs that keep the complexes in their natural sheet changed the answer. Up to one shuttle per supercomplex, the rate climbed steeply whatever the salt level. Past that point the pace leveled near 15 to 20 turns per second, set by complex IV's own catalytic speed. The authors conclude that inside a real membrane, the bottleneck is the enzyme's chemistry, not the shuttle's journey. Purified systems, they warn, can misplace the limiting step.
pmc-13457101:
Zhenyang Feng and thirteen colleagues engineer, in a 2026 study, a nanoparticle that delivers gene editing and a leukemia drug together to break drug resistance. Chronic myeloid leukemia often learns to shrug off its targeted pills. The last-resort drug, ponatinib, works against the toughest mutation but harms at high doses. The team's earlier work found a resistance circuit ending in a protein called IFITM3.

Their carrier is built from ginger-derived lipids, layered with two coatings for aim and entry. It ferries a CRISPR plasmid that knocks out IFITM3 plus a load of ponatinib, at about 84 percent packing efficiency. In resistant cells, the pair at its best ratio restored killing and halted growth. In mouse tumors, growth and spread slowed with no obvious organ harm. The authors show the resistance protein works by waking a survival pathway, which the knockout blocks.
pmc-13457701: Fever after prostate surgery — which medical factors predict it? Lei Huang, Fang Guo, and others analyze the cohort. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is urologic surgery research. It identifies factors behind postoperative fever after bipolar TURP and GreenLight laser vaporization procedures.
pmc-13459401:
Tohid Piri-Gharaghie and co-authors packaged a sea cucumber compound inside tiny fat bubbles to make it a stronger weapon against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium known for drug resistant biofilms in hospitals. The compound, Frondoside A, kills bacteria but dissolves poorly and degrades quickly. Their 2026 lab study put it in niosomes, inexpensive vesicle carriers. It measured particle properties, killing power, biofilm destruction, and effects on two biofilm related genes in the pathogen.

The optimized bubbles captured 78 percent of the compound loaded into them. Encapsulation cut the concentration needed to inhibit or kill the bacteria fourfold compared with the free compound, and enlarged killing zones by 45 to 60 percent in plate tests. Biofilm mass fell by 68 to 79 percent under the loaded drug, a highly significant drop. Gene measurements confirmed the treatment switched off the GacS and PslA biofilm genes.
pmc-13459901:
Adam Jurgoński and co-authors fed camelina seeds, an oilseed crop rich in protective plant chemicals, to genetically obese rodents to test protection against severe fatty liver. Their 2026 study ran two five week experiments. Obese Zucker rats received camelina seeds or their oil in the diet, and obese db/db mice received the seed's main glucosinolate compound, glucocamelinin, by mouth. Liver size, fat content, and tissue images were compared to find which seed fraction carries the benefit.

Camelina counteracted liver enlargement and fat build up in the rats, with several fold lower total fat, triglyceride, and cholesterol content in liver tissue, all statistically significant. The rat experiment pinned the benefit on the non oil fraction of the seed, not the oil itself. In mice, purified glucocamelinin reproduced the protection, cutting liver enlargement and steatosis on both inspection and microscopy. The results nominate this compound as the active principle.
pmc-13460101:
Jinde Wang and colleagues mapped in 2026 the research landscape of quantitative CT analysis in lung cancer, where scan numbers rather than impressions guide diagnosis, treatment checks, and prognosis. Searching the Web of Science for open-access work from 2005 to 2025, two reviewers screened records and kept 1,618 publications. Bibliometric tools then charted output growth, author networks, journal citations, and keyword patterns across the two decades.

Their map shows a rapidly expanding field with identifiable core journals, productive teams, and shifting frontiers. Narrative reviews had described pieces of this terrain, yet none had traced its evolution quantitatively. For newcomers and funders alike, the analysis flags crowded areas, neglected gaps, and the collaborations most likely to shape quantitative imaging of lung tumors next.
pmc-13460201:
Shirong Li and Hairong Bao examine in 2026 whether fibroblast growth factor 21, a hormone released by the liver, plays a protective role in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. This scarring lung disease progresses relentlessly, and current antifibrotic drugs only slow decline. Patients show higher blood levels of the hormone yet lower levels of its helper receptor in lung tissue, a puzzling pairing the review sets out to interpret.

Evidence from mice suggests genuine defense: animals lacking the hormone scarred worse after injury, while a long-acting version preserved the fragile air-sac lining cells. Proposed routes include stronger antioxidant responses and controlled cell recycling. Unresolved questions dominate the ending, especially whether high blood levels signal successful compensation or a body failing to respond.
pmc-13461501:
Ye and colleagues built in 2026 a rat model of cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome, a linked disorder of metabolism, kidney damage, and heart injury, that worsens step by step. Robust animal models and mechanisms for this syndrome are scarce. The rats were fed a high-fat, high-sugar diet and given a kidney stress agent, while the team tracked change over time and layered gene, cell, and tissue mapping methods.

Ye found early metabolic faults came first, with kidney and heart damage growing later, mirroring the human course. Every data layer pointed the same way: disturbed fat metabolism sat at the centre of progression. Three regulators, named PPAR-gamma, ESR1, and FASN, emerged as candidate control nodes, with fat programs enriched in kidney tubule cells and fat cells infiltrating diseased kidney tissue. A computer screen flagged one compound as a possible multi-target drug candidate.
pmc-13462301:
Afeef and colleagues examine how stress relates to body size in university students in this 2026 cross-sectional study. Stress has been tied to unhealthy eating, but evidence from young adults outside Western countries is thin. The team surveyed 297 students aged 18 to 26, measuring perceived stress, three eating behavior traits, body mass index, waist size, and handgrip strength.

Women reported more stress and more deliberate restraint around food, while men had higher body mass, waist size, and grip strength. Stress showed no direct link with body mass or waist size in this sample. It was connected indirectly, through emotional eating to slightly higher body mass, and through uncontrolled eating to slightly larger waists, though both effects were very small. The authors caution that a one-time survey cannot prove that stress causes the eating patterns.
pmc-13462901:
Ying Sun and a large team study, in a 2026 report, whether a bedside clotting test can warn of early clots after liver transplant in children. The device, Sonoclot, tracks how blood clots in real time, yet no warning threshold existed for children. The team followed 200 children who received living-donor liver transplants at a Tianjin hospital between 2019 and 2021.

Thirty-eight children, nineteen percent, developed clots after surgery, split between the liver artery and large veins. Of all test values taken one hour after blood flow returned to the new liver, only the activated clotting time stood as a risk factor. A threshold near 229 seconds sorted cases sharply: children below it clotted more often, above all in the liver artery. Keeping the value above that line went with fewer clots in this group. The authors stress that randomized trials must confirm whether holding that target prevents clots.
pmc-13463401:
Gopal Gowane and co-authors test a new shortcut for estimating the genetic parameters that livestock breeding runs on, in populations far too large for classical methods. Heritabilities and genetic correlations normally require statistical models that choke on millions of genotyped animals, and the values drift as selection proceeds. Their 2026 study proposes GPP, which recovers parameters from how accurately breeding values predict outcomes within and across traits. It validates GPP on simulated herds under strong genomic selection for ten generations.

GPP estimates closely matched the true simulated values in both scenarios, with only slight, variable bias. Feeding the method slightly wrong starting variances barely disturbed the results, a practical robustness. Classical REML on single generations proved highly variable on small data and slightly biased on large data, while a genomic variant had steadier errors. One quirk emerged: GPP genetic correlations are directional, depending on which trait benchmarks the other.
pmc-13464101:
Mansoureh Barzegar and seven co-authors chart the small RNAs that guide human oligodendrocyte growth. These cells wrap nerve fibers in myelin, the fatty coat that speeds signals. Most prior maps came from rodents, leaving human steps poorly known.

The team grew the cells from human stem cells and fished out each stage with a built-in marker. Sequencing found stage-locked microRNAs, counting several never tied to this cell line before. Computer checks tied the new RNAs to target genes and to AKT and SMAD paths, both known growth routes. The atlas gives researchers fresh markers and candidate levers for myelin repair work.
pmc-13464401:
Hye-Jin Kang and eight co-authors craft two new stevia sweeteners with two enzymes in sequence. Rebaudioside M tastes closest to sugar among stevia compounds, yet plants hold little of it and it dissolves poorly in drinks. Their route starts from stevioside, a plentiful stevia compound.

A first enzyme added glucose units in one pattern, and a second enzyme finished the build, converting nearly all of the mid-product. The two analogs dissolved over one hundred times better than the natural compound in water. Both held up under heat and across wide acidity, and they kept their sweetness about three times longer in a tart store drink. Taste sensors rated one analog balanced and the other sweetness-forward with little bitterness.
pmc-13464801:
Zakhi Zafrani, Sarah Suleman Khan, and Michael Zitzmann review whether GLP-1 drugs can lift low testosterone in men whose hormone axis is suppressed by obesity or diabetes. The drugs, now common for weight and blood sugar care, touch many hormone systems. Eight studies from 2021 to 2026 met the review's rules.

In men with obesity, diabetes, or low testosterone, the drugs paired with modest testosterone gains and better erections or sperm traits in some studies. In healthy men with normal levels, a placebo-controlled trial found no real change in hormones or sperm. Gains seem to ride on better metabolic health rather than a direct hormone push. The authors see a fertility-sparing option for selected men, pending larger trials.
pmc-13465201:
Marcel Wehmann and four co-authors report a rare aorta cancer that masqueraded as graft infection after aneurysm repair. A sixty-four-year-old woman came in with recurring belly pain and rapid loss of ten kilograms, five years after a stent repair of her abdominal aorta. Infection markers ran only mildly high, and she had no fever.

PET imaging showed a hot mass hugging the aorta, a picture that fits bad infection or cancer alike. A fine needle biopsy settled the doubt by finding malignant cells. Surgeons removed the tumor wholesale, replaced the aorta section, and added chemotherapy with two drugs. Tissue study confirmed angiosarcoma, a vessel-wall cancer, which shows how biopsy can rescue a misleading case.
pmc-13465601:
Zengchen Liu and colleagues investigate why some virus-positive throat and mouth cancers still spread to neck lymph nodes, in a 2026 study of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. Such cancers often end better than virus-negative ones, yet node spread still harms outlook and complicates care. The group worked with public single-cell and gene-activity data sets plus laboratory experiments.

They found a stem-like group of tumor cells tied to node spread. Early genes of the HPV16 virus seemed to lower levels of a protein called SERPINB3, and changes linked to the viral E7 gene connected with MYC pathway activity and stronger cell movement. The work offers one possible route by which the virus shapes how these tumors behave.
pmc-13466201:
Roepke and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the helper proteins that usher cargo through the type three secretion system. The rig is a needle germs use to inject attack proteins into host cells. It fires in order: needle parts, pore parts, then the attack set. Each cargo class has its own helper class. The review sets helper shapes and codes side by side.

Helpers guard cargo from firing too soon inside the germ. They hold loose cargo from clumping or rot, and walk it to the rig in rank order. Shape reads show kin helpers share a fold though their codes drift. One open ask closes the review: do all attack proteins need a helper, or can some ride free?
pmc-13466301:
Dalal Al-Mutairi and colleagues report a gene fault behind heart and skin disease in an Arabian family with four affected sisters, in a 2026 case study. The sisters shared a heart muscle disorder, thickened skin on palms and soles, and woolly hair, a combination known as Carvajal syndrome. The two eldest died suddenly as children.

Mapping of shared inherited stretches pointed to the DSP gene on chromosome six. Sequencing found a stop-signal change present in two copies in the sisters, hitting only one of the gene's two message forms, the one that builds desmoplakin I. Both parents carried a single copy. Heart scans in the surviving sisters showed both ventricles involved.
pmc-13466801:
Yumin Wu and six colleagues published this 2026 review of stage-adapted cryotherapy, treatment by freezing, for oral mucosal melanoma, a rare cancer inside the mouth. Surgery can cost patients speech, swallowing and chewing, so a repeatable freezing treatment that spares tissue is attractive. The authors set out their centre's approach, which matches treatment intensity to disease stage, and report survival and recurrence for their patients.

The team reviewed 43 patients treated between 2016 and 2026. Earlier-stage patients received cryotherapy alone, while stage IV patients had freezing plus wide surgery. Estimated survival for the whole group was 93.0 percent at two years and 69.8 percent at five years after treatment started. Local recurrence struck 2 of 11 earlier-stage patients but 18 of 32 stage IV patients. Spread to lymph nodes was tied to worse survival, with a hazard ratio of 3.342 in their analysis. The authors stress the study was small and non-randomised.
pmc-13467001:
Łukasz Florczak and Andrzej Sobkowiak review how complex fluoride compounds shape protective coatings grown on magnesium alloys by plasma electrolytic oxidation, in a 2026 article. The process sparks a ceramic-like layer onto the metal in a chemical bath, guarding against corrosion. Simple fluoride additives were the old recipe; complex forms carrying zirconium, titanium, silicon, aluminum, or phosphorus now draw interest.

Most of these complexes break down in water depending on bath acidity and stabilizers. Stopping that breakdown is the key step, the authors argue, because intact complexes put more fluorine into the coating and improve its structure, phase makeup, and corrosion resistance. Bath chemistry thus decides the armor's quality.
pmc-13467501:
Robert Błaszczyk and colleagues explore in 2026 whether common gene variants in matrix metalloproteinases, enzymes that reshape the tissue scaffolding around cells, relate to atrial fibrillation. Scarring of the heart atrium helps this rhythm disorder take hold, and these enzymes control how that scaffolding is built and broken down. The case-control study enrolled 179 patients with atrial fibrillation and 56 controls, all of Polish background, and tested eight variants across five enzyme genes.

Simple comparisons of variant frequencies showed no clear differences between patients and controls. A fuller model that assumed two copies of a variant were needed did find significant links for one variant each in the MMP1 and MMP2 genes. Haplotype analysis, which looks at variants inherited together, also showed a significant overall pattern. The authors read the results as hints that tissue-remodeling genes shape risk in combination rather than alone.
pmc-13467801:
Katielle Vieira Avelino and colleagues explore in 2026 whether growing mushrooms together changes the useful chemistry of their fungal threads. Four basidiomycete species were grown alone and in pairs, giving ten cultivation systems. Extracts of the mycelia were profiled for phenolic compounds and tested for antioxidant power, sun protection, and the ability to block tyrosinase, an enzyme tied to skin darkening.

Nine phenolic compounds appeared across the systems. Two of them, catechin and syringic acid, showed up only in selected paired cultures, proof that fungal neighbors alter each other chemistry. Some single cultures led on antioxidant activity, while sun protection reached a factor of 39 in several single and paired systems. Tyrosinase blocking peaked at 92.7 percent in one solo culture and stayed above 90 percent in some pairings. Computer-based screening then checked the found compounds for drug-like traits and safety.
pmc-13468901:
Sabina Szymoniak and Mariusz Kubanek review in 2026 how distributed artificial intelligence can defend the Internet of Things, a web of billions of devices no central guardian can watch. Central security hubs buckle under the scale, variety, and constant motion of these systems. The review focuses on local, cooperative intelligence: devices that learn together, flag intruders, and share warnings without surrendering all their data.

Federated learning and multi-agent systems receive the deepest treatment, weighed for benefits, limits, and deployment friction in real networks. Critical infrastructure gets special attention, because there a security failure threatens public safety and service continuity, not just privacy. The authors close with the research gaps: trust between cooperating agents, energy budgets, and standards. Their survey argues the defense of sprawling device networks must itself be sprawling and cooperative.
pmc-13469001:
Christoph Lange and four colleagues published this 2026 article on measuring the randomness of stochastic bit sequences. These unpredictable zero-one streams secure wireless sensor networks and enable signal separation. Standard test suites check whether bits behave as independent, identically distributed draws, but specialised checks are costly. The authors present a simpler gap-based approach. They analyse the spacing between non-zero elements and derive a gap density function and a burstiness measure. With a standard NIST test, these flag violations of the independence assumption.

They validated the method on sequences from polynomial and non-polynomial generators and on hardware-generated streams from devices, across use cases from structural health monitoring to fibre-optic sensing. The gap-based tests exposed non-independent behaviour that matters for security against brute-force, replay and eavesdropping attacks. The authors offer it as a low-complexity complement to full randomness suites.
pmc-13469901:
Minseok Kim, Taekwon Kim, Kyungsub Song, Sang-hun Lee, and Jonghoon Yoo chart in 2026 where the burden of fall injuries falls across stages of care in Korea. Falls send older adults to hospitals in large numbers, but the stage at which harm concentrates differs by age. The team analyzed the national injury statistics report for 2022, drawing on five sources from ambulance records to death statistics.

Emergency visit rates peaked in young children and in adults aged seventy five and older, at similar levels. From that point the paths split sharply. Admission after an emergency visit rose from under three percent in young children to about forty three percent in the oldest group. Hospitalization rates in the oldest adults ran about two and a half times those of adults aged sixty five to seventy four.
pmc-13470001:
Farhat and a large team report outcomes for a common leukemia subtype in this 2026 study from MD Anderson Cancer Center. The subtype is acute myeloid leukemia carrying a change in the NPM1 gene, which usually signals a better outlook, yet long-term results vary. The authors reviewed 396 newly diagnosed patients, who made up 18 percent of cases at the center, and compared treatments.

Patients given intensive chemotherapy lived a median of about 84.7 months, with just over half alive at five years. Those given a gentler drug pairing lived a median of about 23.3 months instead. Among intensively treated patients, older age, poor daily functioning, a FLT3-ITD gene change, or disease outside the marrow predicted worse survival. A cladribine-based lower-intensity regimen beat the gentler pairing in an age-matched comparison.
pmc-13471301:
Li and a children's hospital team reviewed in 2026 every head and neck case of lipoblastoma, a rare benign fat tumor of early childhood, over eight years. The series held 32 children treated between 2016 and 2023, median age near three, with tumors grouped by exact location, from face to deep throat spaces. Surgical completeness, leftover behavior, and recurrence were tracked over a mean follow-up exceeding five years.

Location shaped everything: the commonest sites were the shoulder-armpit junction, about 31 percent, and the front neck and deep throat space, about 19 percent each. Surgeons removed tumors completely in 24 children; eight kept residual tumor, usually where vital nerves and vessels block safe cutting. Of those eight, two leftovers shrank, four stayed stable, and two grew and needed a second operation. No child with complete removal relapsed. The authors recommend maximal safe removal that spares critical structures, with watchful follow-up for deep leftovers.
pmc-13471401:
Kantha and co-authors compared leg muscle quality between older adults who had fallen in the past year and those who had not. Their 2026 cross-sectional study enrolled 120 community-dwelling adults, split evenly into 60 fallers and 60 non-fallers with median ages near 70.

Muscle quality was read from phase angle, an electrical measure from body-composition scans that reflects cell health. Overall phase angle did not differ between groups, but left-right asymmetry in the legs at the 5 kHz frequency was greater in fallers, with a statistical link of rs 0.29 to fall status. Leg asymmetry also tracked poorer sit-to-stand performance, leading the authors to suggest it as an extra check in geriatric assessments. Prospective studies, they note, must still show whether the measure predicts future falls.
pmc-13471501:
Lee and co-authors assembled an umbrella review of treatments for adolescent suicidal behavior and self-harm to ground new South Korean clinical guidelines. Their 2026 synthesis searched five databases for systematic reviews from January 2015 to December 2024 covering ages 10 to 24, grading quality with AMSTAR-2 and certainty with GRADE.

Self-injury without suicidal intent affects an estimated 21.2 to 24% of Korean adolescents, well above the global average near 17.2% worldwide. The review weighs which therapies carry solid review-level evidence for the guideline panel.
pmc-13473101:
Zahid and co-authors propose a privacy architecture for the Internet of Vehicles, where cars broadcast location and behavior data to roads and clouds. Their 2026 paper borrows from Metaverse systems to replace identity-based trust checks with zero-knowledge proofs, letting a vehicle prove it is insured, inspected, and emissions-compliant without revealing who owns it.

The design pairs zk-SNARK proofs, compact cryptographic receipts, with Layer 2 blockchain settlement to keep verification fast and auditable while minimizing stored personal data. As related evidence, the paper cites federated-learning simulations with 100 devices and 10 edge servers reaching up to 92.2% model accuracy and cutting communication overhead by 20% against baselines. The authors frame ethical design, not raw security, as the bottleneck for connected transport.
pmc-13473301:
Panico and colleagues compared keyhole versus robotic surgery for ventral rectopexy, an operation that lifts a prolapsing rectum, in women treated at women's health centers. Constipation scores on the Wexner scale fell sharply with both methods: from 17.7 points to 2.5 after keyhole surgery, and from 15.2 points to 2.6 after robotic surgery. Incontinence scores dropped in step, from 11.6 points to 1.1 and from 10.7 points to 1.2 across the two methods, all highly significant. Posterior prolapse relapsed in just 1.0% of women, and no outcome significantly favored either technology. A combined front repair accompanied 70.6% of the operations.
pmc-13473501:
Salehi and co-authors compared the gene activity of nestin-expressing hair follicle cells, an accessible stem cell source, against bone marrow cells, dental pulp cells, astrocytes, and hypothalamic neurons. Their 2026 study measured growth-factor and neural-marker genes to judge the follicle cells' promise for nerve repair.

Their Tubb3, a neuronal skeleton gene, ran 2.1-fold above bone marrow cells and 1.4-fold above dental pulp cells. pmc-13474001:

Without LMO2, the signal stalls outside the nucleus. The authors conclude that LMO2 controls the activation and the delivery of STAT3, making it a chokepoint in this metastasis pathway.
pmc-13474501:
Wang and co-authors fed cherry tomato seedlings a fertilizer made of beetle dung: the frass of Protaetia brevitarsis larvae, insects that efficiently digest crop straw into humus-rich droppings. Their 2026 pot experiments mixed the frass into growing substrate at 1, 2, 4, and 8% by weight and tracked plant growth alongside the substrate's microbial community.

The middle doses worked: 2% and 4% frass produced stockier, more robust plants with heavier stems and roots, while 8% proved too much and was dropped from sampling.
